---
title: "5. Rival Ultimates"
---

Chapter 4 tested the metaphysical rivals: positions that contest the machinery of Time, Space, and Substance without proposing a rival ground beneath it. This chapter turns to rival ultimates — accounts that do propose one. Each names an ultimate offered as more fundamental than structure, asked to occupy the ground the tradition reserved for God.

The classical-theistic constructions are the most fully developed and take up most of the chapter, but they are engaged as one family of rival ultimates rather than as a category apart. Each is taken in its strongest available form and pressed on one question: can an ultimate be specified as prior to the structural conditions without merely relocating the roles those conditions play? The inquiry distinguishes three verdicts. Some candidates fail because their proposed grounding relation has no determinate content on the book's analysis. Some retain the structural roles under another vocabulary. Others remain coherent but carry a grounding or explanatory burden the chapter cannot close by contradiction. The bar is the strongest form the literature has yet produced; where a more powerful version exists or later emerges, the argument is answerable to it, not exempt from it.

The chapter works through three families of these, each gathered under its own cluster. The first are the theistic arguments that reach for a divine ground without presupposing structure: the cosmological and foundation arguments, the arguments from design and fine-tuning, the ontological and modal arguments, and the moral, pragmatic, and transcendental ones ([§5.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1)). The second are the doctrines of the divine nature built to keep that ground ultimate without regress, simple without composition, and independent of the structure it grounds: divine simplicity and the via negativa ([§5.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2)). The third are the accounts of the ultimate that are not classically theistic but make the same bid against structure: Spinozist pantheism, Neoplatonism, process theology, Madhyamaka emptiness ([§5.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3)). [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4) draws together what the engagements across these families reveal.

A note on scope: this chapter presses contemporary Christian-analytic theistic counter-constructions because that is where the literature has been most fully developed: Rasmussen, Plantinga, Pruss, Swinburne, Craig, Leftow, Stump, Dolezal. The structural pressures collected here are not in-house Christian difficulties. The same moves are made across the Islamic *falsafa* tradition (the medieval Arabic philosophical inheritance of Greek metaphysics): Avicenna's contingency argument, Al-Ghazali's *Tahāfut* (the *Incoherence of the Philosophers*) and the Kalām cosmological tradition the contemporary argument inherits. They are made too across the Jewish philosophical tradition (Maimonides on divine simplicity and negative theology). Where a parallel premodern development is doing the same conceptual work, it is registered in the relevant section. The argument is not against any one tradition but examines a structural pattern that recurs across traditions. It does not treat every use of divine, ultimate, or apophatic language as one undifferentiated target; each engagement is evaluated at the resolution and with the grounding commitments its own defenders specify.

A note on disaggregation: Aquinas's Five Ways are not answered in a single section because the structural analysis does not treat them as a single argument. Each Way targets a different structural condition: motion and efficient causation ([§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2)), contingency (Chapters 2–3 and 4), degrees of perfection (§[§6.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2)–6.6), teleology (Chapter 7). Each is taken up where that condition is derived, so the Five Ways are met across the book rather than in one place.

## 5.1 Theistic Arguments for a Divine Ground {#sec-5-1}

This first cluster gathers the theistic arguments that reach for a divine ground without presupposing structure: the cosmological and foundation arguments ([§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1)–[§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4)), the arguments from design and fine-tuning ([§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5)–[§5.1.6](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-6)), the ontological and modal arguments ([§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7)–[§5.1.8](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-8)), and the transcendental, moral, and pragmatic ones ([§5.1.9](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-9)–[§5.1.11](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-11)). Each reaches past the world toward a God offered as prior to and more fundamental than time, space, and substance.

Each is pressed on a single question: can it be carried through without leaning on the structural roles it was meant to stand free of? The recurring finding is often relocation rather than refutation. A ground that acts, knows, creates, sustains, or explains must at least bear directed dependence, relational differentiation, and real grounding content. Whether those roles entail the richer types of temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence depends on the specific form of the ground and must be argued rather than assumed. A candidate that posits an essence-prior or transcendent ground may remain a live metaphysical proposal; the chapter asks whether it has supplied an intelligible grounding relation or merely named one.

### 5.1.1 Rasmussen's Foundation Argument {#sec-5-1-1}

Among contemporary arguments for a divine ground, Rasmussen's foundation argument[@rasmussen2019] presses the case on the narrowest and most rationalist basis: no appeal to revelation, scriptural authority, or parochial religious commitment, only the demand that things have explanations. It belongs to a lineage running from Avicenna's contingency argument (*burhān al-ṣiddīqīn*) in the *Kitāb al-Shifā*[@avicenna1020], through Leibniz's *Monadology*[@leibniz1714, §32] and Clarke's demonstrative cosmology, to its contemporary reconstructions in Pruss[@pruss2006] and Koons[@koons1997]. Because it stakes everything on explanatory principles the present account also accepts, it earns engagement at full strength before any reply.

The argument proceeds in three moves.

1. *The Foundation.* Every contingent fact has a sufficient reason (the PSR), so the regress of reasons terminates in a being whose existence is not contingent on anything further, a Supreme Foundation.

1. *Maximal greatness.* Any limit on this Foundation's nature would itself be a contingent fact, and explaining the limit would require something beyond the Foundation, which contradicts its ultimacy, so the Foundation must possess every positive attribute to the highest degree.

1. *Personhood.* Consciousness is among the positive attributes, so the Foundation is personal.

The result is classical theism reached by explanatory first principles alone: a maximally great necessary being, argued for without a premise the naturalist has already refused. What makes the argument difficult to resist is its rationalist honesty: it does not retreat into mystery; it runs the Principle of Sufficient Reason (the PSR: every contingent fact has a sufficient reason for being so rather than otherwise) without flinching and lets the derivation land where it lands.

What the argument gets right is granted from the start: explanatory regress does not terminate in a brute fact. Where it goes wrong is the identity of the terminus. The terminus is located by [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) in the structural roles themselves: T, S, and Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) as the conditions under which anything is coherently a something-rather-than-nothing. Rasmussen accepts the PSR and rejects that terminus: the roles, he would say, are facts, facts require reasons, and the reason must be something outside them that can ground them without itself requiring grounding. The dispute is not about whether the PSR generates pressure; both accounts agree that it does. It is about where that pressure comes to rest. If the structural roles are themselves the conditions of coherent fact-hood, they do not stand in line with other facts awaiting a reason; they are what allows anything to be a fact waiting for one. The argument reaches its Foundation by three lines, and each, carefully followed, recovers the very structure it means to displace: the Argument from Limits, the Mind-Grounding Isomorphism, and the direct appeal to the PSR.

*First.* The argument from limits runs straight off the PSR: any limit on the Foundation's nature would be a contingent fact requiring further explanation, so the Foundation must possess every positive attribute without restriction. Each restriction would point beyond the Foundation. Maximal greatness follows from the PSR itself, requiring no independent theological assumption, which is why it lands even on readers suspicious of theism.

The move risks treating every determination as a limiting defect. At role-resolution, a proposed Foundation must at least be determinate, distinguishable from what it grounds, and stand in a real asymmetric dependence relation to it. None of that yet proves clock-time, spatial extension, or ordinary causal persistence in an atemporal ground. It does show that maximality cannot be obtained simply by subtracting every form of order, difference, and bearing; a wholly indeterminate posit supplies no intelligible grounding content. The Argument from Limits mistakes the conditions for existence for restrictions on a hypothetical limit-free existent, and concludes by describing ∅ under a greatness-theoretic heading.

A theist will object that this describes ∅, not the infinite plenitude classical theism intends: a Foundation lacking every limitation is maximally full, not empty. But the objection trades on an equivocation the reply can refuse. The limit at issue is not *privation*, some perfection the Foundation lacks, but *determination*: to be anything at all, even infinite fullness, is to be this and not that, full and not empty, being and not nonbeing. The principle descends from Spinoza's *determinatio negatio est* (determination is negation, Letter 50), generalized by Hegel into the *omnis determinatio est negatio* since quoted in his name, and pressed here to its theological conclusion. Determination is not a defect to be maximized away; it is what being a something costs, and a candidate that sheds it entirely does not rise above the roles but falls beneath them into ∅.

So the appeal to infinite fullness faces a fork: either it keeps that determinacy, and it is a determinate, therefore structured, ground, the floor already conceded; or it renounces determinacy, and the plenitude is ∅ under a superlative. Answering that the Foundation merely cannot be empty, since emptiness is no perfection to lack, guards it against privations it never faced and leaves untouched the determinacy it cannot shed. A bolder theist welcomes the second horn: the God of the *via negativa* is "beyond being," so naming it ∅ merely fails to rise past determinate categories. But "beyond being" either marks something determinate, this and not that, and falls back into the first horn, or it marks no determination at all, which [§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1) establishes is not eminence beyond being but ∅, nothing under the honorific "beyond."

*Second.* The mind-grounding isomorphism extrapolates from the way finite minds ground propositional content to the way the Foundation grounds existence itself: if minds carry meaning across cognitive acts (entertaining truths, sustaining explanatory relations, grounding one content in another), a maximally unrestricted version of that same relation is the best candidate for grounding reality. So Mind is the most general category of grounding, its range of configurations exceeding what structural mediation could confine.

Range of configurations is idle if the capacity to host configurations is missing. Any mind that entertains a proposition must carry that proposition across its articulation (Time), distinguish it from neighboring propositions (Space), and persist as the same mind across the act of entertaining (Substance). A mind that performs no such act is not a mind; it is the word *mind* with no referent. A classical theist will protest that this pictures only a finite, discursive mind: the divine intellect entertains nothing across an interval but grounds all truths timelessly and without succession, in one simple act or in nothing beyond its own nature. Grant the disclaimer entirely; it changes nothing, because grounding of any kind, timeless grounding included, rests on a minimal floor. An intellect that grounds truths without performing any temporal act must still stand to what it grounds in an asymmetric order of prior and posterior (T as grounding-order), remain distinct from those truths rather than collapsing into them (S as relational distinction), and retain its identity as their ground across the relation (Φ as identity-retention). A timeless, non-discursive intellect that grounds anything has thereby conceded the floor; one that meets none of these conditions grounds nothing at all. Timelessness lifts the mind above succession, not above structure. Rasmussen attributes to his Foundation everything a mind does (entertaining truths, grounding reasons, sustaining explanatory relations), which means the Foundation is already operating on the structural conditions the argument is supposed to explain. Run carefully, the Principle does not elevate Mind above T, S, and Φ. It shows that Mind is where T, S, and Φ operate most densely, which makes it a high-order instance of structure, not an alternative to it. The wider reach of mental grounding is not its escape from the roles. It is the roles running richer.

*Third.* The direct appeal to the PSR skips theistic content altogether and invokes the PSR unadorned: the structural roles are facts, facts require reasons, and the reason must be a necessary being that grounds them without itself requiring a ground. This version is difficult to answer without appearing to abandon rationalism, because refusing the PSR's demand at the structural level looks like allowing a brute fact at the foundation.

The PSR has no purchase against the structural Conditions if the proposed contrast class is simply their total absence: [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) argues that ∅ is not a coherent alternative state. That result blocks a demand for a cause of the Conditions construed as an ordinary contingent fact. It does not, by itself, eliminate an essence-prior proposal that takes the Conditions to depend on a primitive metaphysical ground; such a proposal incurs a further explanatory burden rather than being answered merely by the absence of ∅. The present reply is that Rasmussen has not yet shown why a necessary structured ground requires an additional personal Foundation, not that every possible grounding gloss is already contradictory.

The Foundation, moreover, inherits a structural burden. Rasmussen can press that the relevant grounding or explanation need not be causal or temporal: the Foundation may ground without producing, explain without sustaining-through-time, or source without performing a causal act across an interval. The reply should therefore remain at role-resolution. Any intelligible source/ground relation must at least distinguish source from grounded, order the dependence asymmetrically, and obtain as a real explanatory or grounding fact rather than as a bare label. The book identifies these as the S-, T-, and Φ-roles in their minimal forms: relational distinction, asymmetric grounding-order, and real bearing or identity-retention. This does not by itself prove that an atemporal Foundation instantiates clock-time, spatial extension, or causal persistence; it establishes that the Foundation is not wholly structureless.

Analogical predication is the classical theist's natural recourse at exactly this point: God grounds not univocally but analogically, so the floor is granted only in an eminent, non-creaturely mode. It changes nothing here. Either the analogical relation has determinate content, in which case it carries the ordering, distinction, and identity-retention the floor names, and a structured ground has been conceded under an analogical description; or it has none, in which case the relation specifies ∅ ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)). There is no third term between structure and ∅ for the analogical move to occupy. The full pressure on the classical *via negativa* runs at [§5.2.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-2) and [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4); the reply here needs only the floor, and the analogical move cannot slip it.

Reading the roles at this minimal level is not a retreat from the fuller T, S, and Φ the book defends elsewhere, nor an equivocation that proves a thin conclusion and asserts a thick one. The minimal reading fixes only the *floor* any grounding relation must meet (relational distinction, identity-retention, asymmetric ordering), and the reply needs only that floor: no candidate ground, however the theist refines it, drops beneath it. Whether the ground's temporality, extension, and substantiality also take their richer everyday *type* is a further question the reply here neither needs nor settles. The richer type-upgrade is secured only where the separate change-realizer arguments apply; an atemporal ground stands outside that conclusion by hypothesis, so the reply against it rests on the minimal role floor alone. That is enough: a ground that refuses even the floor — asymmetric ordering, relational distinction, identity-retention — specifies ∅ ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)), while a ground that grants the floor has thereby conceded a structured ground, whatever it declines at the level of everyday type. There is no loophole by which a ground might satisfy the minimal conditions while escaping the roles themselves: that the floor (asymmetric ordering, relational distinction, identity-retention) simply *is* T, S, and Φ read at role level is fixed upstream, by the role-definitions of [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4) and the Structural Requirement ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)), not asserted afresh here nor borrowed from [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4). Condition-Individuation ([§2.6.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-11)) secures separately only that there is no fourth axis, and the remaining disagreement, whether a structured ground is aptly named God, is the one [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4) takes up.

The classical admission that God cannot make a square circle was always a concession that coherence binds the Foundation. The present argument names what coherence consists in: the description of what T, S, and Φ together require, read at the level of relational distinction, identity-retention, and asymmetric ordering rather than specifically causal-temporal production. A Foundation bound by coherence is a Foundation operating within structure, not outside it.

The abductive variant on these arguments reaches the same terminus by inference rather than demonstration: best-explanation reasoning rather than deductive PSR application, as in Koons[@koons1997]. The reply is parallel. A posit must be able to do the explanatory work attributed to it; doing that work requires determinate ordering, differentiation, and bearing at role-resolution. An abductively posited Foundation therefore carries structural commitments. Whether those commitments reduce the Foundation to the book's structure or remain features of a distinct personal ground is the live abductive comparison, not something the role-floor alone decides.

Two objections press at this site. The selection-among-possibilities challenge asks: if Nature is the necessary structural foundation, what selects which contingent configuration it realizes? The question is internal to Nature: which configuration obtains within the necessary structure, not a question about Nature itself. The modal PSR as applied to contingents within Nature ([§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)) answers the explanatory pressure without an external intentional selector, while the absence of a coherent contrast class for Nature's non-instantiation ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)) blocks projecting the question back onto the Conditions; the level-distinction at [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4) fixes why, since contingency is a property of configurations within Nature, not of the necessary structural ground. The aggregation challenge asks: if T, S, and Φ are each necessary, why are they not three independent necessary foundations that aggregate to one, the structural form of monotheism? Because T∧S∧Φ is not a conjunction of three independently necessary grounds but one structural fact under three logical-categorical readings. The Triunity of Nature ([§2.6.9](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-9)) and Condition-Individuation ([§2.6.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-11)) establish that instantiation of any one Condition analytically requires the others, so there is no coherent specification of T, S, or Φ as a foundation prior to their conjunction. Rasmussen's aggregation move, which correctly collapses multiple independent necessary foundations to one, does not reach T∧S∧Φ, because the Triconditional identity forecloses the independence it requires.

*What converges.* Each of the three lines to Rasmussen's Foundation recovers the structure it set out to replace: the Argument from Limits mistakes the structural conditions for restrictions on a hypothetical limit-free existent and ends up describing ∅ under a greatness-theoretic heading; the Mind-Grounding Isomorphism attributes to the Foundation everything a mind does (entertaining truths, grounding reasons, sustaining explanatory relations), so the Foundation is already operating on the structural conditions it was meant to explain; and the direct PSR line has no purchase where the proposed contrast class is ∅, which fails before it has been described; the essence-prior gloss that survives carries a further explanatory burden rather than an answer, leaving a Foundation bound by coherence as a Foundation operating within structure.

Rasmussen is right that explanatory regress must terminate somewhere, and right about nearly everything the terminus must be. The one divergence is its identity: not a necessary being standing over the roles, but the roles themselves, which are necessary because nothing is a something without them. What classical theism has been pointing at under the name Foundation *is* what Chapter 1 and §2 have been proving under the name T ∧ S ∧ Φ. For neighboring contemporary positions in the same methodological cluster, the engagement runs at [§3.4](convergence.html#sec-3-4) and [§3.5](convergence.html#sec-3-5) rather than here: Pruss and Rasmussen[@prussRasmussen2018], and Pizzi[@pizzi2025]. The cluster reaches □∃x x; the five-domain convergence reaches □(T∧S∧Φ); the latter closes candidates the former leaves open. Pizzi[@pizzi2025] is the closest in formal method, and explicitly leaves the identity of the necessary existent open in his §7, a stop-point this argument crosses. Divine simplicity is taken up next, at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1): whether the necessary ground can be identical with its attributes in a way that exempts it from the structural conditions this section has established apply to any ground capable of the grounding work. Rasmussen's personalist last stage (the move from necessary foundation to intentional selector, and from intentional selector to personal being) is engaged directly at Chapter 6: [§6.4.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-1) (Awareness), [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) (Knowledge), and [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) (Power) test whether awareness, knowledge, and agency are genuine additions to the necessary structural ground or configurations it realizes. The lever Rasmussen would press hardest is the book's own Recursive-Depth → Phenomenal-Interiority arc (Chapter 8): the place where the framework most invites the personalist conclusion, since it is the book's own account of how interiority arises. That recursive structural depth gives rise to phenomenal interiority is not a concession that the ground is antecedently personal, but the explanation of how persons arise within the structure rather than standing over it. Two precision notes on scope govern the divergence. The book's necessity claim is *de dicto* with respect to the structural role (necessarily, any ground that discharges the modal-grounding function is T∧S∧Φ as a co-instantiated conjunction), not the *de re* claim that this particular token instantiation is necessarily this token. The modal-collapse risk (whether necessary identity collapses contingent configurations of Nature into necessities) is foreclosed by the level-distinction [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4) establishes: necessity attaches to the Conditions, not to the configurations they permit to vary.

### 5.1.2 Cosmological Argument {#sec-5-1-2}

The First Cause demand is natural theology's oldest cosmological move and its most systematic: if T, S, and Φ are necessary, what caused them to be? The demand presses the account of §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6 to either produce a cause outside the structural order or concede that necessity has a source the account has not named. Three claims carry the reply. First, the Kalām traversal argument is a spatial metaphor applied to a successional order, and Oppy's deflation of Hilbert's-Hotel absurdities[@oppy2006] shows the metaphor does not transfer. Second, the contingency-of-the-whole move conflates the contingency of individual events with the contingency of the order they occur in and illicitly exports the former to the latter. Third, the PSR appeal, pressed as a demand for something rather than ∅, presupposes a contrast class whose incoherence [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) has already established; pressed as the Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact, it demands a necessary explainer outside Nature that the PSR alone does not deliver, as [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3) shows.

The three forms sort into two wings the reply treats differently: the necessity-seeking wing (Leibniz, Koons, Pruss) is answered by being grounded, since □(T∧S∧Φ) already supplies the necessary terminus it reaches for; the causation-seeking wing (the Kalām and its kin) is answered by being dissolved, since a boundary is a feature of the order, not an event outside it.

The argument concedes at the outset that the Leibnizian tradition is correct on a narrower point: causal series within the structural conditions do admit, and often require, further explanation. The claim pressed here is weaker than the target that tradition is built to refute. The order through which causal series run is not itself a series. Causal vocabulary applies to what occurs within the order, not to the order itself. A framework that makes causation possible is not among the candidate effects causation explains.

The cosmological tradition offers a resilient natural-theological resistance to the sufficiency of structural necessity. Its core commitment is simple: something must have started things. The universe is a vast succession of causes and effects extending backward in time; either that succession is infinite or it has a first member. An infinite past, the objector contends, is incoherent: actual infinities cannot be traversed, and we could never have arrived at the present if infinitely many prior moments had to elapse first. A finite past therefore requires an originating cause, and such a cause cannot itself lie among the events it initiates. The argument's classical roots run through the Islamic *kalām* tradition (medieval speculative theology that pressed dialectical-rational defenses of revealed doctrine): Al-Kindi's *On First Philosophy* [@alKindi850] gives the earliest systematic case for the impossibility of an infinite past, and Al-Ghazali's *Tahāfut al-Falāsifa* [@alGhazali1095] develops the mature premodern version that the contemporary recovery directly invokes.^[@craig1979, ch. 1; @davidsonH1987 traces the Islamic transmission.] The point has been refined by its contemporary inheritors into three distinct argument forms: the Kalām appeal to traversal, the Koonsian appeal to mereological contingency, and the Pruss appeal to the Principle of Sufficient Reason.[@craig1979; @koons1997; @pruss2006; @prussRasmussen2018; @rasmussen2019] Each converges on the same conclusion: a necessary being outside the causal order, identified with God. The present account lands next to the Leibnizian wing of this tradition — □(T∧S∧Φ) and their necessary ground being adjacent endpoints — and diverges from it only on the line taken and the commitments incurred along the way.

The challenge bears directly on §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6. T, as defended there, is a necessarily instantiated structural role, derived without PSR machinery and without any external originating cause. The First Cause objector grants the necessity and demands a cause for it: the account has explained why Time must obtain, not what started it. Three forms of the move take up the objection; the narrower point that individual causal series within the order admit explanation stands untouched.

*First.* The Kalām traversal argument, regimented, runs:

1. *Causal principle.* Whatever begins to exist has a cause.

1. *Finite past.* The universe began to exist: an actual infinite sequence of past events cannot be traversed, for if infinitely many moments had to elapse before now, now could never arrive, so the past is finite.

1. *Conclusion.* The universe therefore has a cause; and a cause not itself in time must be a timeless agent, which is God.

The traversal argument is a spatial metaphor dressed as a structural claim. 'Traverse' treats the past as a finished road Now had to travel down, a road whose length must be completed before the traveler arrives. But in a successional order, Now is not a traveler reaching a destination. It is the current coordinate of the order's state. You do not need to 'finish' infinity to be at a specific point within it, any more than you need to visit every point on an infinite plane to be at coordinate (0,0). Oppy[@oppy2006] formalizes the point: the absurdities of Hilbert's Hotel require the simultaneous rearrangement of discrete objects, a spatial and substantial paradox that does not map onto temporal succession. You cannot shift past moments aside to make room for the present. The mathematical tools Craig invokes to generate absurdity do not apply to the domain he applies them to.

Craig[@craigSinclair2009, §3; @craigMoreland2000] has pressed a generalized version of the point in reply: the absurdities follow from the actuality of the infinite itself, not from any rearrangement procedure; Hilbert's Hotel is a vivid illustration of a more general impossibility rather than its only form. Granting actual-infinite-absurdity in general (the cases involving completed infinite collections accessed as totalities), the question is whether a temporal past counts as that kind of completed-collection-accessed-as-a-totality. It does not. On a tensed or passage-centered theory, the past need not be treated as a completed collection accessed from outside; on a tenseless block theory, the past can form a completed ordered totality. The traversal objection therefore depends partly on the theory of time and cannot be dismissed by one model alone. The tensed/tenseless question is the standing pivot of the Kalām dialectic, but the account need not adjudicate it here: on the composition defended at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), tenseless order and tensed passage are not rival readings of Temporality but the two features it jointly requires, and the reply holds on each. Taken as ordered dimension, the traversal worry does not arise: there is no formation to complete, only an ordered manifold at whose interior Now sits. Taken as directed passage, grant the finitist the point in full — successive addition, if it establishes anything, establishes that the past is finite; that much is conceded below, since the account is compatible with a finite-past cosmology. A finite past is a chronometric boundary within T, the earliest coordinate the passage has reached from within, not a moment-prior-to-T from which T departed. So the theological inference fails on both features alike: what it needs is not a boundary but a cause outside the order, and the boundary is a feature of the order ([§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2)). The Kalām's own conclusion about finitude is granted; only the step from finitude to an external cause is refused. Craig's stronger reply keeps open the question whether a beginningless temporal order can be actually infinite without anyone traversing it from an external vantage. Oppy's response weakens the traversal metaphor; it does not by itself settle every argument against an actual infinite past.

Craig's empirical prong is separable from the conceptual one. The Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem[@bordeGuthVilenkin2003] is standardly cited as proving the universe had a past boundary, and Craig treats it as empirical confirmation of Kalām's second premise. Two points cut the weight. First, BGV establishes only that geodesics with positive average Hubble expansion are past-incomplete, not that the universe as such began. Aguirre and Gratton [@aguirreGratton2002] and Carroll [@carroll2010; @carroll2016] describe eternal cosmologies in which past-incompleteness of inflating geodesics is compatible with an eternal ambient spacetime. Craig and Sinclair's *Blackwell Companion* reply [@craigSinclair2009, §4] presses that Aguirre–Gratton requires a quiescent low-entropy past boundary that itself functions as a beginning, and that Carroll's eternal cosmologies require thermodynamic time reversal at a past boundary that operates likewise; the 2014 *Greer–Heard Forum* exchange with Carroll restates the point.

Granted: the quiescent boundary, where one is required, is a beginning in the chronometric and thermodynamic senses. It is not a beginning in the categorial sense the Kalām requires. A past boundary is the first coordinate of T along the dimension (the earliest position the passage has reached from within), not a moment-prior-to-T from which T departed. The chronometric beginning is a feature within T (§[§2.4.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-6), 7.2.2); the categorial beginning, which the Kalām needs and the cosmological model does not deliver, is foreclosed by Parasitic Negation on T (§[§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), 5.1.6).

Second, even if the universe has a finite past boundary in its own time-coordinate, that boundary is a feature within T, S, and Φ: the first chronometric coordinate of the successional order, not an event caused by anything outside it. A boundary of the order does not transport the order's explanation outside the order. The argument concedes the empirical finding and denies the theological inference it is supposed to underwrite.

A newer wave of anti-infinite-past work has migrated away from actual-infinity absurdities toward paradox-based causal finitism. Koons[@koons2014] presses Grim Reaper cases (scenarios in which an infinite staggered sequence of potential killers generates contradiction) as evidence that infinite causal sequences are metaphysically impossible even when mathematically coherent. Pruss's *Infinity, Causation, and Paradox*[@pruss2018] generalizes the point into a systematic case. These arguments are not touched by Oppy's Hilbert deflation, because they do not turn on Hilbert-style rearrangement; they target the supposition that infinitely many prior events could each causally produce the next. The present reply does not contest causal finitism in general (the account is compatible with a finite-past cosmology) but denies that causal finitism, even if sound, establishes what Kalām requires. A finitely-extended past is still a past within T; its first chronometric coordinate is the earliest position the passage has reached from within, not an event caused by something outside the order it would initiate. The Kalām framework presents this as a forced choice between (i) the first moment of T has no cause (denying Premise 1) and (ii) the cause is not within T (and so outside T). The present account takes a third position. The present account treats the first chronometric coordinate as a boundary of the temporal order rather than automatically as an effect of something outside it. The Kalām defender can contest that category assignment and argue that the universe's beginning is an event falling under the causal principle. The dispute therefore turns on the scope of causation, not on a contradiction generated merely by asking for a cause. The categorial-vs-chronometric distinction is developed directly at [§5.1.6](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-6): what is foreclosed is a moment-prior-to-T from which T departed; what is admitted is a chronometric boundary as the first coordinate of T itself. Grim Reaper considerations constrain the shape of causal series; they do not relocate causation to the order's exterior.

A further reply is available, though the categorial response does not require it. Grim Reaper cases idealize location, propagation, and mechanism in order to isolate a causal-structural paradox. The idealization cannot be rejected merely because it omits ordinary physical realization; the relevant question is whether the causal stipulations are jointly satisfiable and whether their contradiction generalizes from the constructed series to every beginningless causal past. Physicality is a substance carrying causal power across T-succession through S-extension ([§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4), [§2.4.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-11)); a putative cause that occupies no region and transmits nothing across one is not a faint or limiting-case cause but no cause at all. The dilemma this poses to the causal-finitist deployment is exact. Either the reapers are genuine causes — located in S, carrying Φ, propagating at finite speed — in which case the impossibility the converging series generates is located in Spatiality and Physicality rather than in infinity or in causation as such: infinitely many physical signals converging on a single instant drive their spatial separation toward zero and their energy density without bound, a merely physical impossibility that establishes nothing about a metaphysically necessary First Cause. Or the reapers are the idealized spaceless triggers the paradox in fact stipulates, in which case what it proves impossible was never a causal sequence on the present account, and 'infinite causal sequences are impossible' mislabels a result about an unsatisfiable non-causal stipulation. A beginningless past is untouched on either horn: it is not a staggered swarm of located conditional agents racing to act inside a shrinking window, but the past-directed order of T itself, whose earliest coordinate is a boundary rather than an effect. The Grim Reaper thus constrains, at most, the arrangement of embodied causes; it does not reach the successional order those causes run within, which is the only thing the Kalām needed it to reach.

This verdict converges with the critical literature rather than standing alone. The unsatisfiable-pair diagnosis — Shackel's demonstration that Benardete constructions merely encode two jointly unsatisfiable conditions[@shackel2005], pressed against causal finitism by Schmid and Malpass[@schmidMalpass2025] — locates the contradiction in the stipulation rather than in the infinity, and observes that purely non-causal Benardete variants (in which each reaper's action brutely correlates with its predecessors' rather than being caused by them) generate the paradox with no causal chain for finitism to sever. That non-causal variant is decisive here: if a swarm carrying no causal power at all yields the same contradiction, the impossibility was never a fact about causation reaching infinitely back. The present account agrees on the diagnosis and adds only that the past-directed order of T is not a Benardete series to begin with, so nothing in the family bears on whether that order has a first coordinate.

Loke[@loke2017] presses a further refinement: the only coherent transition from a timeless cause to a temporal effect is free agential initiation, so the first cause must be personal. The refinement inherits the structural reply already given. A 'timeless cause' stands outside T by hypothesis, and standing outside T is standing outside the conditions under which causing has content; a free agent who initiates temporality must persist as the same agent across the initiation (Substance), distinguish its pre- and post-initiation states (Space), and stand in a before-and-after relation to the effect it initiates (Time). The personal-agent refinement does not escape the structural conditions; it concentrates them. Loke's argument is a contribution to the personalist question deferred to [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4), not a distinct way past the present response.

Morriston presses two further objections the account can absorb. The first is inductive: the causal principle that anchors the Kalām, that whatever begins to exist has a cause, draws its support only from cases of rearrangement within the order, so its warrant does not extend to an absolute beginning of the order itself.[@morriston2000; @morriston2002] The account does not lean on this objection, since its own reply is categorial rather than inductive, but the objection reinforces from a second direction that the causal idiom is at home within the order and strains when lifted outside it. The second objection is sharper against the personalist fix: a timeless agent's producing a first effect is itself a transition from not-creating to creating, and a transition is a succession, so the agential initiation Loke and Craig invoke reintroduces the very order it was meant to precede.[@morriston2000; @morriston2013] That is the structural reply already given, reached from the opposite side: the transition presupposes Time, Space, and Substance rather than delivering them from outside.

A corollary follows if the theist absorbs Morriston's point rather than resisting it. The standard absorption denies the transition outright: God's willing of the world is timeless and immutable, so there was never a state of not-creating for the first effect to succeed. The absorption then leaves one exit from necessity: a willing immutable in fact yet able to have been otherwise, the necessity of supposition Aquinas distinguishes from absolute necessity [@aquinas1947, I.19.3, I.19.7]. The exit keeps the world contingent, but at the price of a modal contrast (a possible circumstance in which the changeless willing is absent) that nothing in the timeless picture grounds; whether that contrast survives divine simplicity is the modal-collapse question pressed at [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) and engaged at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1). The theist who declines the exit, identifying the timeless willing with the necessary divine essence so that no modal distinction remains between what God is and what God wills, delivers the present account's conclusion in theological dress: there is no vantage, temporal, volitional, or modal, at which God exists and the world does not, and obtaining in every circumstance is necessity under its ordinary modal name. Those premises yield a necessary natural order directly: □(T∧S∧Φ) with a divine middleman attached. And the middleman contributes nothing to the necessity itself, since it is the modal closure of the willing, not any further feature of the agent, that closes off every circumstance lacking a world. What remains in dispute on that horn is not whether the order is necessary but whether its necessity needs an owner, and that is the personalist question already deferred to [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4).

*Second.* The contingency-of-the-whole move grants, with Koons [@koons1997], that an infinite past is possible. The series still consists entirely of contingent beings, events that did not have to happen. A series of contingent beings, even an infinite one, is itself contingent. The contingency of the whole demands a necessary cause outside the series. That cause is God.

The move trades on two senses of *contingent*. Individual events may be contingent even if the structural possibility of an order is necessary. It does not follow that this particular total history is necessary. Koons's argument gets traction if the Big Conjunctive Fact or total series is itself a contingent fact requiring explanation, whether or not it is an additional concrete object over and above its members. But a succession is not a thing over and above what succeeds; it is just the parts in the order they take. And that order obtains within a necessary framework whose conditions are what make succession possible at all. Member-level contingency is real. Whole-level contingency, treated as a further fact requiring a further ground, is a misattribution: a property that belongs to what sits inside the framework has been exported to the framework holding them. Hume's *Dialogues* IX [@hume1779] and Paul Edwards [@edwards1959] diagnosed the underlying slip as a fallacy of composition, treating a property of the parts (contingency) as a property of the whole, and the diagnosis is sound and worth crediting. The reply does not, however, rest on the Hume–Edwards explanatory principle that explaining each member thereby explains the conjunction, the very inference Pruss's contingency argument is built to reject. Its load-bearing move is the one already made: whole-level contingency is a misattribution because the order obtains within a necessary framework, and the demand for an external ground of the series-as-a-whole has no coherent target once ∅ and a necessitating Nature are both foreclosed ([§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)). Koons's mereological premise is precisely what is supposed to rescue the argument from the composition charge; denying that the whole is an entity over and above its members withholds that premise without leaning on the Hume–Edwards inference. What Koons locates at the top of his derivation (necessary ground) is already present at the bottom, as T, S, and Φ. The accounts share a destination. This one arrives without the mereological premise that the series is an entity additional to its elements, a premise Koons himself flags [@koons1997, §3] as load-bearing and contestable.

*Third.* The PSR appeal presses, with Pruss [@pruss2006], that every contingent fact requires a sufficient reason. The entire sequence of contingent events is itself a contingent fact: it could have gone differently in countless ways. Its sufficient reason must be a being whose existence is not itself contingent, and whose nature explains why this history rather than another obtains. That being is God.

The PSR question splits into two the reply must keep apart. Read as 'why an ordered history rather than none at all?', it presupposes ∅ as the contrast, and ∅ is no contrast: [§2.7.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-2) closes it on independent modal and temporal grounds, and sufficient reason bottoms out where alternatives run out, which is at the roles that make alternation possible. Read as 'why this configuration rather than another?' — Pruss's Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact, the conjunction of all contingent configurations of Nature — the alternatives are genuine and the PSR does real work: rival configurations compete within the structural conditions, and each contingent fact keeps its contingent explanation there.

What does not follow is the further step, that the conjunction as a whole requires a necessary explainer outside Nature. The book denies that this demand automatically requires an explainer outside Nature. But the alternatives are not exhausted by ∅ and a Nature that necessitates every configuration: a theist may posit a necessary personal ground whose contingent intention explains one history without necessitating it. That proposal must face the grounding, freedom, and modal-collapse burdens developed in §[§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1)–5.2.1 rather than being eliminated by the PSR split alone. The dissolution does not run through the Hume–Edwards principle that explaining each conjunct explains the conjunction, the inference Pruss's argument is built to reject; it denies that the external demand has an automatic target, as [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3) develops in full.

Hume anticipates the move in *Dialogues* IX [@hume1779]: Cleanthes' reply to Demea is that if a necessary being must be posited at all, the material universe itself is a candidate, and the theist offers no non-theological ground for disqualifying it. The present argument completes Cleanthes' gesture. The 'necessary material universe' Cleanthes floated was not specified enough to bear the weight; □(T∧S∧Φ) specifies it. The Humean cosmological option the *Dialogues* left undeveloped is the one the structural account takes up. Pruss's own defense of the PSR against Humean attack [@pruss2006, chs. 2–7] is uncontested here; the present argument simply does not conscript the principle into service outside the domain where it has purchase. The standard critical literature presses harder, rejecting the principle rather than confining it: Rowe [@rowe1975] argues that the PSR is not rationally compelling and can be denied without irrationality, and Mackie [@mackie1982] presses both the causal principle and the demand for an explanation of the totality as unmotivated once every member has been explained. The reply here needs neither rejection. It grants the PSR full force within the structural conditions and withholds only its application to them, a narrower and less contestable claim than the outright refusal Rowe and Mackie mount.

A kindred deflationary move presses from the opposite side: the call for a first cause is a pseudo-question, Rundle [@rundle2004] and Grünbaum [@grunbaum1998] argue; 'why is there something rather than nothing' has no grip because no coherent answer-space exists. The role account agrees with half of this and rejects the other half. It agrees that 'what caused the structural order?' terminates, because the idiom of causation applies within that order rather than to it. It rejects the dismissal of the further question 'why is the order necessary rather than absent?', because that one does have an answer: §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.8 give it. The cosmological demand is not empty; it is a question with a structural answer where theism has given a theological one. Rundle and Grünbaum close the inquiry without resolving it; the present argument resolves it without closing it.

Kant frames the deepest version of the critique. The cosmological argument extends causality beyond the field of possible experience, where alone the concept has warrant, and so misapplies a category whose jurisdiction is the world of appearances (*Critique of Pure Reason* [@kant1781, A603/B631]); Kant presses further that the argument covertly relies on the ontological proof it claims to do without. The First Antinomy sharpens the impasse (*KrV* [@kant1781, A426/B454]): equally compelling cases can be built for a first beginning in time and against one, which for Kant shows the question has outrun the conditions under which causal reasoning stays legitimate. The account agrees that causation does not apply to the order as a whole, and for a recognizably Kantian reason: the idiom belongs to what occurs within the field, not to the field itself. It parts from Kant on the status of the conclusion. His verdict is epistemic, that reason cannot settle the question and must fall silent; the verdict here is metaphysical, that the question is malformed, because the order is necessary (§[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6) and its necessity has a structural ground rather than a causal one. Where Kant reaches a limit of knowledge, the account reaches a categorial boundary.

One objection cuts across all three forms and is the family's most resilient. Schopenhauer[@schopenhauer1813] named it the Taxicab objection: the Principle of Sufficient Reason is hired to carry the argument as far as a first cause and then waved off once the destination is reached, the terminus exempted from the very demand that powered the regress. Oppy [@oppy2006] presses the contemporary form as a symmetry: whatever explanatory privilege the theist claims for the divine terminus, whether necessity, self-explanation, or brute factuality, the naturalist can claim with equal right for the universe or its fundamental laws, so the demand for a cause of the order underdetermines the theological answer. The objection lands against any account that stops by fiat. It does not land here. The account exempts nothing: it grants the structural order no standing waiver from a demand that otherwise applies, but denies that the demand was ever well-formed against the order, since causation relates elements within the order and the order is not one of its elements. The symmetry Oppy exploits is real, and it is conceded rather than resisted, because it is not met by making the necessary ground simpler or more unified than a physical candidate. It is met by locating necessity in T, S, and Φ themselves (§[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6), which are neither a divine terminus nor a rival physical one but the conditions any candidate terminus, divine or physical, would have to instantiate. The taxicab is never hired, so there is no fare to dodge.

A note on division of labor. Several adjacent theistic moves belong to neighboring sections and are deferred there rather than redeployed here. The personalist extension (why think the necessary ground is a mind rather than a set of structural roles?) receives its dedicated engagement in [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4) (Swinburne's simplicity argument) and [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1) (Rasmussen's Mind-Grounding Isomorphism). Divine simplicity as the classical counter-ground runs through [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1). The Thomistic *per se* causal series and the Aquinas/Feser/Kerr pure-actuality response are handled in §[§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3) and 5.2.1. The Boethian eternal present is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The worry that structural necessity propagates to Spinozan modal collapse is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). The PSR as a standalone rationalist demand (distinct from its deployment here as a first-cause lever) receives its fullest engagement in [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3). The present section confines itself to the specific demand that the order require a cause; the surrounding terrain is covered in those sections.

A final consideration turns the objection back on the conditions of its own statement, a move called retorsion: the call for a first cause presupposes what it is calling on to be caused. The asking unfolds across moments, the words occupy relational positions, and the thought persists across its articulation and transmission: an objection to the necessity of T, S, and Φ raised within T, S, and Φ. The obvious reply is that enacting the structure while demanding its cause shows only the structure's actuality in the world where the demand is issued, not its necessity. Granted, but modal necessity does not need to be closed here; §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6 did that. This section defends the sufficiency of that closure against calls for an additional explanatory step. What the retorsion shows is that every idiom in which the call can be issued (temporal succession, spatial articulation, substantial persistence) is parasitic on the very order the call purports to require a cause for. Causation explains moves inside the field. It cannot explain the field: not because the field is mysterious, but because 'cause' is a relation between elements of the field, and the field is not one of its own elements.

*What converges.* Each of the three forms concedes the very order it means to extend: the Kalām traversal treats the past as a finished road Now had to travel down, a spatial metaphor that does not map onto successional order, where Oppy's Hilbert deflation blocks the rearrangement absurdities and any finite past boundary is a feature within T rather than an event outside it; the contingency-of-the-whole move concedes a necessary framework and then misassigns member-level contingency to it, committing the fallacy of composition Hume and Edwards diagnosed; and the PSR appeal either presupposes ∅ as a contrast the structure forecloses or, in its Big-Conjunctive-Fact form, demands an external necessary explainer the PSR split alone does not deliver ([§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)), leaving the personal-ground variant to the burdens of §[§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1)–5.2.1, with sufficient reason bottoming out where alternatives run out.

The narrower point (that individual causal sequences admit further explanation) stands; the argument does not contest it. What the argument contests is the step beyond: the assumption that the order through which sequences run is itself a sequence, that the language of causation lifts from elements to their ground, and that the call for a first cause can be satisfied by anything other than what makes calls, causes, and sequences possible in the first place. The regress objector runs on Nature while asking what Nature rests on. It does not rest on anything; it is what makes resting on possible at all. With the First Cause demand answered, [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3) turns to the mechanism classical theism offers the First-Cause picture: the *per se* series of simultaneous causation. Swinburne's probabilistic recovery of the inference — theism pressed as a simpler hypothesis than its rivals — is [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4).

### 5.1.3 Simultaneous Causation {#sec-5-1-3}

The order of cause-before-effect is not the only order causation admits. A hand moving a stick that presses a stone illustrates concurrent dependence: while the contact and applied force obtain, the stone's acceleration is produced without a temporal gap between the applied force and its effect. Releasing the hand need not stop all motion instantaneously, because inertia remains. Simultaneity is a causal structure too, and Aquinas sees in it the template he needs: an eternal God could simultaneously ground every moment of a temporal world without entering the time of what it grounds. The *per se* causal series runs through a stack of concurrent dependencies rather than a sequence of prior ones. Cause at the top, effect at the bottom, no temporal interval between them. Remove the top and the whole column falls in the same moment. If the picture works, the stack can be finite upward while terminating in an atemporal source, and the atemporal cause at the summit never needs to enter the time of the stones it moves.

Simultaneous causation is the mechanism that lets classical theism have both the atemporal God and the temporal world. The tradition developed the doctrine to resolve a specific problem: how an atemporal, unchanging being could cause a temporal, changing world without either being changed by the causing or leaving a gap in the causal order. Aquinas (*ST* I.2.3) deploys simultaneous causation in the First Way, the *per se* series that stops at an Unmoved Mover. Aquinas's *De Aeternitate Mundi* addresses explicitly the coexistence of eternal cause and temporal effect. Avicenna's continuous-creation doctrine in the *Kitāb al-Shifā* develops the parallel position in the Islamic tradition: God is the necessary, atemporal cause whose causing of contingent existents is itself eternal even though the existents are temporally extended [@mcginnis2010; @adamson2013]. The continuous-creation model is not a separate escape but the same atemporal-sustaining picture in Islamic dress, and it meets the reply given below to the occasionalist and conservationist kindred: a continuously creating cause must still individuate what it sustains (S), order it (T), and carry it across (Φ). Kant's *Critique of Pure Reason* refines the concept in the Second Analogy, distinguishing logical from temporal priority and illustrating with the ball resting on the pillow. Stump and Kretzmann's "Eternity" [@stumpKretzmann1981] proposes ET-simultaneity as a relation between the eternal present and each temporal moment. Craig's *God, Time, and Eternity* [@craig2001b] develops the contemporary version closest to biblical-theism commitments: God timeless without creation, temporal with creation. Against the doctrine: Wolterstorff's "God Everlasting" [@wolterstorff1975] presses the case for divine temporality against Boethius and Aquinas. Padgett's *God, Eternity, and the Nature of Time* [@padgett1992] defends a relative-timelessness alternative. Mullins's *The End of the Timeless God* [@mullins2016] presses the most sustained contemporary argument that timelessness is internally incoherent. Morriston [@morriston2002; @morriston2010] has pressed the simultaneous-causation move specifically for two decades: if the cause is eternal, the effect must be equally eternal. The present reply sits closest to the Mullins–Wolterstorff wing in holding that timeless grounding does not cohere, and adds what that wing does not specify: the failure is not primarily biblical or doctrinal but structural; the logical priority the doctrine requires is itself a structured relation, and the structure is what was supposed to be escaped.

Applied here, the move offers the theist a path to concede the structure's dominion over the created order while preserving God as external ground. The argument holds that any ground of the structure must itself instantiate the roles. The simultaneous-causation theorist counter-claims that grounding need not be temporal, spatial, or substantial: it can be purely logical, a relation of eternal dependence that places the effect within T, S, Φ (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) without placing the cause there. On this picture, the demand that grounds instantiate what they ground fails at the central claim: God grounds the structure atemporally, the structure grounds creatures temporally, and the argument's reach stops one level short of fundamentality.

The move bears directly on the Cartesian Certainty for change of [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2), the Intermediate Necessity of [§2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-3), the identification in [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) of the modal constraint with T, S, and Φ, and the Triconditional account in [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) of the Conditions as Nature. Simultaneous causation is the specific mechanism by which classical theism tries to exempt God from the structural conditions while accepting their application to creatures. If the exemption holds, a changeless ground is possible after all, provided the ground relates to change by logical rather than temporal priority. Three forms of the move take up the objection: the *per se* causal series, Kant's logical/temporal distinction, and Craig's modal refinement. The replies below argue that each discovers temporal asymmetry inside the logical priority it was supposed to replace.

*First.* The *per se* causal series, regimented, runs:

1. *Two series.* A *per accidens* series (events in time) differs from a *per se* series (grounding relations that hold at every moment).

1. *The First Way.* Aquinas's First Way holds that a *per se* series of causal dependencies requires no temporal extension: it is a relation of ontological priority rather than temporal sequence.

1. *Conclusion.* So God can be the *per se* cause of the world without being in time: the world depends on God at every moment, and the dependence relation is not itself a temporal event.

If C is a sufficient cause for E, whenever C obtains E obtains. The will of the Maximally Great Being (MGB) is held to be eternal, changeless, and sufficient. An eternal sufficient cause entails an eternal effect. Morriston [@morriston2002] presses the point: if the cause is eternal, the effect must be equally eternal; if the effect is finite, a simultaneous cause must be equally finite. (The Stump–Kretzmann ET-simultaneity reply to this eternal-cause/eternal-effect point is engaged at [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1).) The *per se* series resolves nothing, because the structural question reappears within it: how can an eternal, changeless ground produce a finite, changing effect without the ground itself being modally or structurally differentiated between its producing and its non-producing state? The doctrine gestures at logical priority while silently importing the temporal directionality it was supposed to avoid. If temporal priority is denied, the causal relation must still supply asymmetric dependence; otherwise the remaining relation is structurally indistinguishable from simultaneous coexistence, two things obtaining together without one producing the other. The issue is not whether every cause must come earlier in clock-time. The issue is whether “cause” has determinate content without ordered priority, distinguishable relata, and a stable dependence relation. Those are the structural roles in non-clock form. That identification is not stipulated here. The minimal floor was established independently at [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1), showing that even a timeless grounding intellect must exhibit asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction, and identity-retention across the relation in order to count as a ground at all. Asymmetric ontological priority is not being relabeled temporal by fiat; it is being held to the floor that any grounding relation must clear, and that floor is T, S, and Φ read at their most minimal. The simultaneous-causation theorist cannot keep the priority while refusing the floor, because the priority is precisely what the floor articulates.

The deeper problem cuts across all three forms: whatever the priority relation is called, simultaneous causation turns the contingency of creation into a dilemma. If God is necessarily creator or sustainer, and the sustaining relation is sufficient, then the sustained order follows necessarily from God. A necessary sufficient sustainer does not leave the sustained order contingent unless the sustaining relation is itself contingent. But if the sustaining relation is contingent, creatorhood is not necessary in God; and if the sustaining relation is necessary, the particular order God sustains is necessary with God. It will not do to answer that Nature is necessary in any case: the necessity of the structural conditions is affirmed here (□(T∧S∧Φ)), and [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) shows why necessary structure does not necessitate any particular configuration within it. That reply is available for the structure and unavailable for a contingent created world. A necessary complete sufficient cause would necessitate its effect. The classical theist therefore distinguishes God's necessary existence from a contingent free willing or from the contingent obtaining of the creation relation. Whether that distinction is coherent under timelessness and divine simplicity is the modal-collapse question; simultaneous causation alone does not settle it. The doctrine alone has not preserved a free creator beyond Nature; it has purchased the atemporal ground at the price of leaving in dispute the contingency it was meant to protect.

A second pressure compounds the first. Creation, considered not as a clock-time event but as a dependence relation, has structural requirements of its own. A creating relation has an asymmetric order: source and recipient are not interchangeable, and the dependence runs from ground to grounded rather than the reverse. It has a distinction: creator and creature must be distinguishable relata rather than one undifferentiated item. It has relation-stability: the recipient must be something whose being is held by the source, not a label that vanishes as soon as the relation is named. Those are the structural roles in non-clock form. Strip T from the relation and there is no directed dependence, only co-obtainment. Strip S from it and there is no creator/creature distinction. Strip Φ from it and there is no recipient whose being is sustained or produced. Eternal creation avoids a first temporal moment only by shifting the issue from temporal beginning to asymmetric dependence; it does not remove the structure that makes dependence intelligible. There is no third option in which creating obtains without order, distinction, and a bearer of the relation: that description names the absence of a creating relation, not a special kind of one.

Feser's defense of the per-se series through the act/potency distinction merits direct engagement at this point. The per-se causal series is, on Feser's reading in *Aquinas* [@feser2009] and *Five Proofs* [@feser2017], not merely a sequence of concurrent dependencies but an analysis of what it is for one thing to be the *actualizer* of another: the cause supplies actuality that the effect has only potentially, in the very instant of causation. The causal series terminates in *actus purus* (pure act without potency) because any cause that retains potency is itself in need of actualization.

The structural reply does not contest the act/potency analysis on its own terms; it shows that T, S, and Φ are what the analysis describes. Actualization supplies asymmetric dependence and distinction between actualizer and actualized, directly yielding thin order and difference roles. Thomistic concurrent actualization need not be a temporal transition from an earlier potential state, and dependence need not by itself be spatial extension. The richer T, S, and Φ types require the separate realizer arguments. Feser's act/potency machinery, taken on its own terms, is an analysis of what asymmetric causal dependence consists in, and the structural roles are what that analysis bottoms out in. The conclusion is the same as the main reply: the per-se series, whether described in the language of actualization or in the language of asymmetric dependence, presupposes the structural conditions at the terminating cause rather than exempting it from them.

The engagement with the *actus purus* form of simplicity and with the analogy-of-being machinery that underwrites it lives at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1); the structural question raised there and here is the same: whether a fully-actualized being can bear the causal roles the doctrine requires without bearing the structural conditions those roles presuppose.

*Second.* Kant's logical/temporal distinction pushes the case further. A cause and its effect can be simultaneous in time (the ball resting on a pillow creates the indentation at the moment it rests there) while the cause is logically prior: the indentation depends on the ball, not vice versa. Classical theism uses this template for God's relation to the world.

Kant's distinction is real and defeats the move rather than rescuing it. Logical priority without temporal priority requires a structural relation that holds between simultaneous states, a relation of asymmetric dependence between distinct elements within a single moment. Such a relation requires distinguishable relata, asymmetric dependence, and determinate obtaining at role-resolution. Logical priority within one moment is not thereby temporal asymmetry, and relation-stability is not automatically ordinary persistence. The ball-and-pillow analogy illustrates this vividly: the indentation depends on the ball because mass, resistance, and gravity are structurally active between them. The analogy works because ball and pillow are both in time, both in space, both substantial. Remove the structural roles and the analogy collapses: there is no ball and no pillow, only two labels with nothing between them. Kant's distinction describes the structure carrying the logical priority, not an escape from it. Without what the pillow supplies, the ball has nothing to indent, and the asymmetric-dependence relation the analogy illustrates has no content to carry.

*Third.* Craig's modal refinement goes furthest. God exists timelessly without creation and temporally with creation; the transition is not an event in God but a relational change: God stands in new relations to creatures without changing intrinsically. Simultaneous causation on this reading is what timeless grounding looks like at the temporal interface.

The refinement concedes the point while renaming the concession. If God stands in new relations to creatures with creation, then God's relational profile changes from no-relation-to-creatures to standing-in-relation-to-creatures. A change in relational profile is a change, and a change requires before-and-after, a prior state differing from a subsequent state.

Here the strict-timelessist will invoke the distinction between real and merely Cambridge change: God's coming to stand in relations to creatures is, on this reply, an extrinsic Cambridge change (as Socrates comes to be shorter than a growing Theaetetus without himself altering), not a real change in God, so timelessness survives untouched. The distinction is genuine; the Mullins–Padgett objection is that it does not cover this case. Craig's view is pressured by the claim that becoming temporal changes the subject's mode of existence rather than merely adding an external predicate. Craig denies this and treats the change as relational. The Mullins–Padgett objection holds that the Cambridge-change distinction does not cover this case: becoming temporal changes the subject’s mode of existence rather than merely adding an external predicate, and the move from real to Cambridge change requires defense rather than mere assertion. Cambridge change is the correct description of “shorter than”; it is the wrong description of “timeless, then temporal.” (The kindred ET-simultaneity reply, which relates the eternal present to each temporal moment without either term changing, is engaged at [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1).) Timelessness-without-creation plus temporality-with-creation requires God to occupy two distinct modal-relational states and a transition between them. That transition is itself a structural event. Craig has not avoided making God temporal at the moment of creation. He has made God's atemporality conditional on not-creating and God's temporality conditional on creating, a structural description of a being whose modal status varies with its relational context. The result is not a being outside the structure, but a being whose structural position depends on which relational role it occupies.

Mullins [@mullins2016] pushes the critique further: if God's atemporality is contingent on God's non-relations, then God's atemporality is not a necessary feature of the divine nature but a contingent fact about the divine's relational profile, and classical theism was supposed to deny exactly that. Padgett [@padgett1992] presses from a different direction: the transition Craig posits (from timeless-without-creation to temporal-with-creation) is not coherent unless God was already in some temporal frame within which a transition could occur, which is why Padgett opts for relative-timelessness from the start rather than trying to combine strict atemporality with a creative act.

A kindred variant is Malebranchean occasionalism: God is the sole genuine cause, and what appear as natural causal relations are divinely ordained regularities holding between occasions rather than mechanisms. The reply is the same in thinner vocabulary. For God to occasion distinct events, the creaturely occasions must be differentiated and ordered, and the decree must supply determinate explanatory bearing. Occasionalists may construe the divine intention as one timeless decree rather than a persisting mental episode, so the move secures the minimal roles while leaving the loaded divine types contested. Occasionalism has not eliminated the structural conditions; it has relocated them into the divine willing itself. Another kindred: the conservationist account [@freddoso1991], on which God continuously sustains creatures in existence without directly causing their operations. The sustaining relation is a constant causal contact that persists across time, and persistence across time is the admission the doctrine was trying to avoid.

The changeless-ground objection is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The simplicity variant, which grounds the atemporal-cause picture in *actus purus*, is [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1). The probabilistic-simplicity variant is [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4). The PSR-demand variant is [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3). The Modal Collapse worry that necessity propagates from ground to grounded is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9).

*What converges.* Three forms of the exemption, each discovering temporal asymmetry inside the logical priority it was supposed to replace: the *per se* causal series must either supply asymmetric dependence, conceding the structural floor at its terminating cause, or strip directionality and lapse into simultaneous coexistence, and Morriston's point stands that an eternal sufficient cause entails an eternal effect; Kant's logical/temporal distinction requires asymmetric dependence between distinct elements within a single moment, where distinction, persistence, and directionality are T, S, and Φ at the single-moment level and the ball-and-pillow analogy works only because ball and pillow are both in the structure; and Craig's modal refinement concedes the point while renaming it, since a change in relational profile is a change and Mullins's critique cuts through, atemporality contingent on non-relation being no necessary feature of the divine nature.

Plato set the problem in the *Timaeus*: time is the moving image of eternity. The formulation gave Western metaphysics its longest-running project: to describe a relation between the eternal and the temporal that did not collapse one into the other. Augustine inherited the project; Boethius articulated eternity as the complete and simultaneous possession of illimitable life; Aquinas formalized simultaneous causation as the mechanism; Kant sharpened the logical-temporal distinction; Craig, Stump, and Kretzmann refined the apparatus across the last half-century. What simultaneous causation loses across the refinements is the still point: the eternal ground from which the world was supposed to hang. Two and a half millennia of work on the eternity/time interface converge on the same structural conditions the doctrine was designed to hold at arm's length: simultaneity, relational priority, and donation of being are all structured relations, and the structure is what the doctrine was attempting to transcend.

### 5.1.4 Argument from Simplicity {#sec-5-1-4}
