Richard Swinburne develops a mathematically precise case for theism in the analytic tradition. *The Coherence of Theism* [@swinburne1977] establishes that the concept of God is internally consistent. *The Existence of God* [@swinburne1979; 2nd ed. @swinburne2004] argues that, given the evidence of the natural order, consciousness, religious experience, and the moral phenomena, the posterior probability of theism (its probability after the evidence is taken into account, in the technical Bayesian sense) exceeds one-half. *Simplicity as Evidence of Truth* [@swinburne1997], his Aquinas Lecture at Marquette, articulates the underlying epistemology: simpler hypotheses have higher prior probability as a matter of methodological necessity, not sentimental preference. The argument stands apart from the Five Ways not as a refinement but as a genre change. Swinburne does not try to demonstrate God exists; he calculates the odds. And on the metric he specifies, the odds favor a single infinite mind.

The Swinburnean case concedes more ground than any other contemporary theist move. Swinburne does not deny the structural roles are present, does not deny they admit coherent formulation, does not deny the argument for their necessity has some force. He argues rather that a divine mind is a simpler, more probable explanation for why the structure obtains at all. The move is a sharp one: probabilistic rather than structural, comparative rather than exemptive. Swinburne [@swinburne2004] argues that a single infinite mind, a being with a single, infinite degree of each positive property (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness), constitutes a simpler hypothesis than the complex, multi-component physical universe. By Occam's razor, the simpler hypothesis has higher prior probability as an explanatory ground. The physical universe, with its vast array of particular constants, particles, and forces, is maximally complex by comparison. The theist hypothesis wins on comparative parsimony.

Applied to the argument, the move is elegant. Swinburne does not deny T, S, and Φ are present; he argues they are better explained by positing a simpler posterior ground than by accepting them as brute or self-grounding. If the structural proof is valid and its premises are true, comparative simplicity cannot lower its conclusion's probability. Swinburne's case instead pressures the premises or explanatory sufficiency of the structural account: it argues that, given contested background assumptions and evidence, theism is the better overall explanation. The move requires a simplicity metric that operates across ontological levels and favors infinite-mind posits over structural-role posits. Secure the metric and the argument is defeated by comparative probability rather than refutation.

The contemporary literature on simplicity runs thick, and the picture is less favorable to Swinburne than his standing in the field might suggest. On simplicity as a truth-indicator: Sober's *Ockham's Razors* [@sober2015] gives the most sustained philosophical analysis of simplicity's role in scientific inference, and concludes that simplicity functions only relative to background assumptions, never as an unconditional criterion. Huemer [@huemer2009] presses the deflation further: the standard rationales for parsimony hold in scientific settings but fail to transfer, leaving ontological simplicity without evidential value in typical philosophical contexts. Against Swinburne: Mackie's *The Miracle of Theism* [@mackie1982] presses the Bayesian prior-assignment problem most trenchantly: prior probabilities are stipulated, not derived, and Swinburne's stipulations do the theological work before the calculus runs. Philipse's *God in the Age of Science?* [@philipse2012] presses the scientific-methodology angle: Swinburne's criterion is alien to the actual practice of inference in physics. Oppy's *Arguing about Gods* [@oppy2006] catalogs the failures of the probabilistic arguments across their range. Dawkins's *The God Delusion* [@dawkins2006] offers the rhetorical version of the deflation (a God who continuously monitors and controls every particle in the universe cannot be simple) whose analytic substance was already present in Mackie and later refined by Philipse. The present reply sits closest to Sober on simplicity's background-relative operation and to Philipse on the scientific-methodology point, and adds what neither alone specifies: the background relative to which Swinburne's simplicity claim would have to be evaluated is T, S, and Φ themselves, which forecloses the comparison in principle.

The argument turns against the necessity claim of [§2.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-5) and the exhaustion claim of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). If simplicity favors theism over structural necessity, the modal conclusion of the argument is defeated by comparative probability even if its logic is sound. The reply runs on two levels, and the order matters. The load-bearing level concerns the *candidate*, not the comparison. Whatever wins the parsimony contest is offered as the ground of the structural order, and being a ground of any kind requires the minimal floor established at [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1): asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction from what is grounded, and identity-retention across the grounding relation, which is T∧S∧Φ read at the structural level. A single infinite mind that grounds the roles thereby instantiates them; it cannot be the simpler thing the roles reduce to, because it already presupposes them. This level says nothing about who performs the comparison, so it is untouched by the rejoinder that the book's own case for the roles is equally an exercise of embedded reasoning. The second level concerns the comparison itself, is genuinely weaker, and is placed second for that reason: comparative parsimony ranks candidates within a fixed background of alternatives, and it has no purchase on a background weighed against its own absence, because [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) has already shown there is no coherent contrast class in which the roles fail to obtain. With no articulable alternative on the menu, there is nothing for the razor to weigh the roles against. This is not the claim that the roles are exempt from rational support; the transcendental case of §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6 supports them. It is the narrower claim that comparative parsimony is the wrong instrument, since it requires a slate of rivals the roles do not sit on. Three forms of the move take up the objection: one-mind parsimony, cross-level simplicity, and Bayesian refinement.

*First.* The one-mind parsimony move holds that an infinite mind has a single unified essence (one being with one set of infinite properties) while the present account posits three distinct roles each requiring separate grounding. Occam's Razor, the objector presses, favors the one over the three: infinity in a single subject is simpler than multiplicity across structural roles.

The objection misapplies Occam's Razor by confusing ontological levels. The razor governs explanatory entities within a background of structural possibilities: it operates by comparing candidate explanations of contingent facts against a stable background against which simplicity judgments have meaning. It is coherent to ask whether electrons or fields are the simpler posit for explaining electromagnetic phenomena, because both are candidates within structure and the simplicity comparison has a stable background. It is not coherent to apply the same criterion to structure itself: structure is not a candidate explanation within a background of structural possibilities; it is the background.

That structure is background rather than candidate is not asserted but earned at [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7), which shows there is no coherent contrast class in which the roles are absent; with no such alternative, the roles are not one posit among rivals but the condition any posit occupies. The one-versus-three arithmetic the objection runs never gets started either: [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1) shows T, S, and Φ are not three independent posits but one structural fact under three categorial readings, so there is no count of three for a count of one to beat.

Actual simplicity comparisons are structured cognitive acts, but that act-side fact does not prevent them from evaluating hypotheses about the structure of reality. The stronger reply must concern the candidate and the metric: whether the divine-ground hypothesis already incurs structural commitments, and whether any background-neutral simplicity measure favors it. Occam's razor was made to cut entities within a shared background. It cannot cut the background itself.

*Second.* Cross-level simplicity raises the stakes. Simplicity applies across ontological levels and not merely within them, the objector presses: a single infinite mind is simpler than the structural conjunction even as an ultimate explanation, and the comparison evaluates whether structure or the mind is the better ultimate posit rather than presupposing structure as its background.

The cross-level move raises the altitude of the comparison but not the standing of its candidate. To rank the mind against structure as ultimate posits is still to offer the mind as the ultimate ground, and a ground of any kind carries the [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1) floor: asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction from what it grounds, identity-retention across the relation. There is no altitude at which a grounding mind sheds those and remains a ground. So the cross-level comparison never reaches a vantage where structure is one optional posit among others; it relocates the contest to a level where the theistic candidate has already instantiated the structure it was meant to displace. Swinburne's argument does not offer an alternative to structure; it describes a configuration of it. The evaluator-side point reinforces this without bearing the weight: any such comparison is performed by a structurally embedded reasoner, with no unstructured vantage from which to weigh the conditions of weighing. But the decisive fault lies in the candidate, not in the one comparing.

*Third.* The Bayesian refinement turns the comparison probabilistic. The prior probability of the theistic hypothesis, given its internal simplicity and explanatory scope, exceeds the prior probability of a necessary structural architecture; updating on the evidence of a contingent-looking, complex physical universe, the posterior favors the infinite-mind hypothesis. The inference is not deductive but probabilistic, and the probability calculus is on the theist's side.

The Bayesian refinement's real weakness is not that priors are computed by embedded reasoners; pressed that way the point would prove too much, sweeping in the book's own reasoning along with Swinburne's. The weakness is that the prior assigned to "the theistic hypothesis" is already doing the theological work before the calculus runs, as the comparison-class problem below makes plain.

Set the prior-assignment problem aside and the candidate-side reply still binds: for an infinite mind to be a coherent posit, that mind must stand in determinate cognitive and grounding relations to what it knows and what it grounds. Its omniscience covers what-is-the-case, and what-is-the-case has structural content: distinguishable objects, temporally articulated states of affairs, persisting carriers of becoming. The mind's mode of cognition need not be discursive (running through premises and conclusions in succession, the way a finite intellect does) for the point to bind. Even non-discursive cognition, where the divine intellect grasps all things in a single timeless act rather than thinking them through step by step, cognizes content that is structurally articulated; and the grounding relation a mind bears to what it grounds is itself asymmetric, sustained, and obtaining between distinguishable relata. Aquinas's intuitive cognition, the Boethian *tota simul*, and the Stump–Kretzmann ET-simultaneity are engaged at length in [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1), which shows each variant requires structural conditions through the relations it bears to what it knows and what it grounds even where it denies them in the *mode* of cognition. T, S, and Φ are required by what the mind cognizes and what it grounds, not by how it cognizes. The non-discursive exit narrows the line through the *mode* of divine cognition; it does not eliminate the structural conditions on its *content* or on the grounding relation that connects the mind to what it grounds. A mind so related to its contents and to what it grounds carries more articulated commitments than the bare role-floor. That does not yield a theory-neutral numerical simplicity ranking, because Swinburne counts properties and laws under a different metric. It does undercut any claim that the divine hypothesis is obviously simpler before the metric and background assumptions are defended. The classical rejoinder that the divine mind has no composition at all, and so is not a configuration of anything, is the *actus purus* line; it is taken up at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1), where the strict-simplicity claim must still meet this floor, since even a metaphysically simple mind stands in an asymmetric, distinct, identity-retaining grounding relation to what it grounds. The reply here needs only that floor and leaves the *actus purus* case to its own site.

The infinite mind is not a cheaper ontology. It is a configuration that presupposes the full structural architecture at maximum richness, and simplicity comparisons conducted at that level run on the conditions they are trying to weigh.

One underlying premise of Swinburne's cumulative case deserves direct engagement in this section. Swinburne holds that personal explanation (explanation in terms of an agent's intentions) is an irreducibly distinct form of explanation, not reducible to structural or scientific explanation, and at least as fundamental as structural explanation [*The Existence of God*, @swinburne2004, ch. 2; *Mind, Brain and Free Will*, @swinburne2013, ch. 1]. The premise carries weight independent of the simplicity comparison: even granting the structural-conditions reply above, if personal explanation is irreducibly distinct from structural explanation, then an irreducibly personal ground remains a live explanatory terminus. The book's reply concedes the irreducibility claim while denying the entailment. That personal explanation is irreducible to the vocabulary of physics is true: intentions are not fully translatable into particle velocities or field configurations. Ordinary personal explanation involves an agent, an intention directed toward a distinguishable outcome, and continuity between intending and acting. A timeless theist will deny that intention is formed across time. The role-level point survives—content, direction, and explanatory bearing remain—but the loaded temporal and persistence types cannot be inferred from personal explanation alone. The irreducibility of personal explanation to physics is compatible with T, S, and Φ being necessary conditions for personal explanation to occur. Swinburne's canonical examples (the agent who freely decides, who selects among possibilities, whose intentions cause outcomes) each instantiate the structural conditions in the act of being a personal explanation. The irreducibility claim survives; what it does not establish is that the irreducible personal level is free of T, S, and Φ or prior to them. A personal explanation that instantiates T, S, and Φ in its own performance is not an alternative ground to the structural conditions but a high-order configuration of them.

A separate line of pressure runs through the comparison class itself. Swinburne ranks one infinite mind against the complex physical universe and concludes the mind is simpler. The class, presented as theism versus its rivals, is gerrymandered against the strongest alternative theisms. Process theism [@whitehead1929; @hartshorne1948] posits one dipolar deity whose abstract pole carries fewer essentially distinct attributes than the classical theist mind. Panentheism [@clayton1997; @peacocke2007] posits one substance with internal differentiation rather than a divine substance externally related to a created one, reducing the number of fundamental ontological categories. Open theism [@hasker1989; @pinnock1994] drops the strong omniscience condition that does heavy work in the Swinburnean parameter count. On Swinburne's own metric (fewer essentially distinct properties scoring as simpler) several sibling theisms score equal or better than the Swinburnean theism his prior assignments single out, and the calculus does not adjudicate among them without theological commitments that precede it. The simplicity case, pressed honestly through its full class of rivals, narrows to a contest among theisms rather than a contest between theism and structural necessity. Mackie's [@mackie1982] prior-assignment objection sharpens here: the priors Swinburne assigns to "the theistic hypothesis" elide which theism, and the elision does the disputed theological work before the Bayesian calculus runs.

A kindred move drops the Bayesian apparatus for an aesthetic-simplicity appeal: simpler ultimate posits offered as intrinsically more credible than complex ones, independent of probability calculus. Huemer [@huemer2009] has already cut the move off from within the parsimony literature, finding the aesthetic rationale delivers no evidential value in ontological disputes; the structural reply explains the residual pull. Aesthetic simplicity is an assessment made by embedded reasoners, structurally configured to find the simpler posit more satisfying because structural cognition naturally compresses. The aesthetic judgment is not a view from outside structure; it is a feature of how structure evaluates itself. Another kindred: Dawkins's [@dawkins2006] inverse parsimony argument (a mind capable of monitoring every particle cannot be simple) arrives at an adjacent conclusion by a different way. The present reply sharpens it: not only is the mind not simple in the information-theoretic sense, but its simplicity is uncomputable without the structural background, and the structural background is what the simplicity claim was meant to explain away.

*A note on direction.* The reply does not depend on which direction the parsimony comparison is run. Oppy [*Arguing about Gods*, @oppy2006; *The Best Argument against God*, @oppy2013; *Atheism and Agnosticism*, @oppy2018] develops the naturalistic counterpart most thoroughly: where Swinburne argues theism wins on parsimony, Oppy argues naturalism wins on the same metric, one ontological category, no additional minds, a necessary-or-brute natural terminus reached without theological posits. The present account is stronger than Oppy's at the structural level. Any appeal to parsimony presupposes the necessary standards against which the evaluation runs, and those standards are T∧S∧Φ themselves. The within-structure-versus-of-structure distinction that blocks Swinburne's pro-theism parsimony blocks Oppy's pro-naturalism parsimony with equal force: parsimony does not adjudicate between structure and an alternative to structure in either direction, because parsimony requires the conditions it would have to evaluate. The reply runs at a second layer as well. The candidates being compared are themselves causes (Swinburne's mind that grounds structure, Oppy's structure that grounds phenomena), and being-a-cause requires causally structured temporal succession (T), which by the Triconditional Cross-Entailment ([§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7)) requires also relational extension (S) and a persistence medium across which influence is transmitted (Φ). Neither candidate can be specified as a cause without the full conjunction T∧S∧Φ. Parsimony's evaluative standards and the candidates it was meant to evaluate both run on T∧S∧Φ; the reply blocks the move at both layers.

The strict-simplicity variant, which presses parsimony through *actus purus* rather than probability, is [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1). The simultaneous-causation variant is [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3). The foundation-argument variant is [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1). Rasmussen's stage-by-stage personalist construction (the move from necessary foundation through selection-among-possibilities to personal being) receives its primary reply at [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1) and is carried to Chapter 6 ([§6.4.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-1) Awareness, [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) Knowledge, [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) Power) rather than being developed here; this section engages Swinburne's probabilistic simplicity case specifically. The PSR-demand variant is [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3). Swinburne's case is cumulative by design (simplicity sets the prior, and fine-tuning, the existence of consciousness, and the moral phenomena are aggregated toward a posterior exceeding one-half), so dismantling the simplicity wing in isolation would leave the aggregate standing if the other weights did. Each component must therefore be assessed at its own site (fine-tuning at [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5), the PSR at [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3), consciousness and moral awareness elsewhere). Weakening one component lowers the cumulative case, but it does not establish that every remaining evidential weight is zero. The §5 replies are reckoned together at [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4).

*What converges.* Three forms of the simplicity move, each running on the architecture it was meant to outrun: Occam's Razor is a within-structure evaluative tool that compares candidates against a stable structural background, and applied to structure itself the razor has no background to cut against; cross-level comparison never reaches a vantage where structure is one optional posit among others, since a grounding mind at any altitude carries the asymmetric order, distinction, and identity-retention of the [§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1) floor; and the Bayesian refinement imports the problem it was meant to solve, since the prior assigned to "the theistic hypothesis" does the theological work before the calculus runs and an infinite mind capable of grounding is a configuration at maximum structural richness, not an obviously simpler posit.

Swinburne's work is the kind of work only a theist who takes secular philosophy with complete seriousness could produce: at every juncture he accepts the standards of the field and argues the theistic hypothesis wins on those standards. The precision is what lets the reply be precise too. The simpler hypothesis the objector recommends is a configuration of structure, not an alternative to it. Comparative parsimony, pressed against the architecture of comparison itself, collapses into a comparison the architecture had to underwrite to be performed. Hume gives the move its final form in *Dialogues concerning Natural Religion* (posthumous [@hume1779]): if a necessary being must be posited at all, the material universe itself is a candidate, and no non-theological consideration disqualifies it. Cleanthes' suggestion was underspecified in 1779. The present argument supplies the specification: □(T∧S∧Φ). The necessary being Cleanthes gestured at is the structure Swinburne's simplicity comparison was trying to outrun.

### 5.1.5 Fine-Tuning Argument {#sec-5-1-5}

Precision is the fine-tuning argument's wedge. Several fundamental parameters appear to lie in ranges compatible with complex structure that are narrow relative to commonly discussed comparison ranges. The often-cited 10¹²⁰ figure for the cosmological constant primarily expresses the discrepancy between observed vacuum energy and a naive Planck-scale estimate, not straightforwardly the width of a life-permitting interval. The tradition reads the broader sensitivity evidence as evidence of selection and the selection as evidence of a selector. The resulting inference is a serious empirical challenge to the necessity claim for T, S, and Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) defended in §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6. The fine-tuning argument is a single inference (from narrow-window precision of the constants to selection) with two extensions the theist presses when the core inference meets resistance. The reply follows this shape rather than treating the three versions as independent objections.

Against the core inference, two lines apply pressure: McGrew, McGrew, and Vestrup [@mcgrewMcgrewVestrup2001] challenge the choice of measure, while Carter [@carter1974] and Bostrom [@bostrom2002] show that observer selection must be included in the likelihood model. Against the multiverse extension, the reply asks whether the higher-order mechanism and its parameters receive independent support or merely move the explanatory burden. Against Swinburne's Bayesian cumulative case [@swinburne2004], the issue is whether theism and its rivals supply justified comparative likelihoods for embodied observers of our kind.

Beneath all three forms lies a prior question: what alternative configurations and comparison class the probability model is licensed to range over. And beyond the bare inference lies a stronger reading (that the universe is not merely life-permitting but life-intended) which separates cleanly from the core argument and fails on its own terms.

The reply takes the prior question first, then the three forms, then the teleological gloss. The observation behind the argument is not in dispute. The constants of this universe do sit within narrow ranges compatible with complex structure. The account contests the inference from the observation to selection, not the observation itself.

The fine-tuning tradition is the empirical wing of natural theology's design inheritance. Where Paley's watchmaker reasons from biological complexity to a designer, the post-Paley inheritors ([@collins2009]; [@barnes2012]; [@swinburne2004]; and [@plantinga2011] at selective points) reason from the values of the fundamental physical constants to the same conclusion. Substantial changes in the effective cosmological constant relative to the observed value can prevent galaxies and other complex structures from forming; the exact life-permitting range depends on the model and on which parameters are varied together. Vary the strong force coupling by a few percent and stable atomic nuclei do not form. The quantitative sensitivities have been catalogued with professional care. What is contested is whether precision of this kind, against the background of no further specification of the alternatives, is genuinely evidence of selection. The naturalist reply has two heads. Anthropic reasoning ([@carter1974]; [@bostrom2002]) notes that observers can only observe observer-permitting conditions. This supplies a selection effect, not by itself a complete explanation of why any observer-permitting universe exists; its force depends on the cosmological ensemble and observation-selection model adopted. The probabilistic critique [@mcgrewMcgrewVestrup2001] argues that the likelihood calculations the theist runs presuppose a measure over an unbounded parameter space for which no canonical measure exists. The present account absorbs both replies and adds a third: the precision is not a feature of a configuration picked out from among rivals but a feature of what a configuration within T, S, and Φ must look like to be a configuration at all.

The challenge bears on [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) most directly. T and S, defended there as necessary structural conditions, admit no variation: not because the values of physical constants are fixed at a particular numerical setting, but because the roles T and S discharge are logically prior to anything a numerical setting could register. Fine-tuning compares this configuration to alternative configurations. The comparison is coherent only at a level where 'configuration' has content, which is within the structural order. What follows presses the point that the argument's demand for a tuner applies the idiom of selection one level above where it has purchase. One question stands upstream of the entire dialectic and is taken first; three forms of the move then take up the objection at the level of the inference itself.

*The prior question.* Probability is downstream of possibility. Before assigning a physical chance distribution, one must establish a genuine space of alternative outcomes. A Bayesian confirmation argument can instead use epistemic probabilities over rival hypotheses, but it must still justify its comparison class, priors, and likelihoods. Mere ignorance about whether the constants are necessary does not by itself provide a canonical distribution over their values. This question sits upstream of the normalizability problem: McGrew, McGrew, and Vestrup [@mcgrewMcgrewVestrup2001] show that even granting a space of alternatives, no canonical measure over it exists; the prior question asks whether the space has been shown to exist at all.

The proponent has a practiced escape. Probability, they note, need not wait on metaphysics; rational agents assign credences to propositions whose modal status is fixed but unknown all the time. Goldbach's conjecture is either necessarily true or necessarily false, yet a mathematician may rationally hold it to 0.99 on inductive grounds; so (the move runs) one need not first prove the alternative constants metaphysically possible in order to spread a credence across them and call the actual values surprising. The escape shows that a Bayesian design argument can use epistemic probabilities without positing an objective chance process that sampled the constants. Rational credences can be evidentially responsive even when the proposition is necessarily true or false. The remaining burden is comparative: the proponent must justify the likelihoods and priors under theism and its rivals, rather than infer an ontic selector directly from an objective frequency distribution. Epistemic probability can support an abductive conclusion, but only through defensible comparative likelihoods; it cannot be treated as if it revealed a literal sampling process over constants.

A second escape runs the other way: perhaps the alternatives only seem possible. Kripke [@kripke1980] shows that some truths are necessary but knowable only a posteriori (that water is H₂O, that Hesperus is Phosphorus) so that what presents itself as a contingent setting can be a necessary one wearing the appearance of contingency. If the constants are necessary a posteriori, the apparent space of alternatives is an illusion of contingency, and the fine-tuning improbability never gets started. The present account does not lean on this claim, and notes the standing counter: Chalmers [@chalmers2002] argues from modal rationalism that ideal conceivability does track genuine possibility, so the appearance of contingency cannot be dismissed so cheaply. The dialectic is unsettled, and the account does not rest on settling it. It rests only on the asymmetry the prior question fixes: the burden lies with the proponent to establish that the alternatives are possible in the sense the measure requires, and that burden has not been discharged. And the account's own positive footing is insulated from the dispute in any case. What it asserts of complex structure (that a structure-permitting, life-permitting configuration is always available to necessary T, S, and Φ) is a necessary possibility, not a claim that the constants could not have differed; a claim of that form stands whether or not ideal conceivability tracks genuine possibility, since conceiving the constants otherwise leaves a necessary possibility exactly where it was. The dispute the proponent would need to win to revive the inference is therefore one the account can decline from either side.

One discipline must be observed in pressing this. The claim is not that the numerical values of the constants are necessary: that is a separate and stronger thesis, argued elsewhere and not needed here. The claim is that the structural conditions T, S, and Φ are necessary, while the contingency of the particular numerical settings within them is unestablished. The argument requires that contingency as a premise and has not earned it. The conclusion is not 'the values are necessary' but 'the values have not been shown to be contingent in the sense the inference needs', and an inference that presupposes an unestablished premise does not transmit its conclusion.

*First.* The precision argument, in its contemporary form, runs from likelihood ratios rather than intuition. Collins and Barnes do not rely on intuition; they rely on comparative probabilities. If life is extraordinarily rare across the space of possible constants under naturalism, and non-rare under theism, then the narrow-window observation confirms theism. The form of the argument is Bayesian: P(tuning | theism) / P(tuning | naturalism) is large, and observing tuning updates credence toward theism.

The calculation requires a probability measure over the space of possible constants. McGrew, McGrew, and Vestrup [@mcgrewMcgrewVestrup2001] press a serious measure problem: an unbounded parameter space admits no uniform normalizable measure, and the ratio of life-permitting to life-forbidding regions is undefined without additional constraints. Defenders answer with restricted ranges, scale-sensitive priors, or direct likelihood comparisons, so the objection imposes a burden rather than refuting every Bayesian formulation. 'One part in 10¹²⁰' presupposes a flat measure over an interval that extends to infinity in both directions; a log-uniform measure would yield a different ratio; a measure weighted by physical plausibility another; and the argument offers no principled reason to prefer any of them. The sensitivity of the conclusion to the measure chosen is as large as the purported fine-tuning itself. Stenger's *The Fallacy of Fine-Tuning* [@stenger2011] observes that many of the 'fine-tuned' constants are only fine-tuned relative to a particular parameterization; under different but empirically equivalent parameterizations, the apparent precision dissolves. Carroll [@carroll2016] notes that whether the tuning is 'fine' depends on what set of possible universes one is comparing the actual one to, a set the theist has not specified.

The most developed reply on the theist's side is Collins's [@collins2009], which concedes that the full parameter space admits no canonical measure and restricts the comparison to an *epistemically illuminated* range: the interval of values across which the life-permitting effect of variation can actually be assessed, within which, Collins argues, a normalizable measure is available and the life-permitting sub-region is vanishingly small.

The restriction relocates the problem rather than resolving it. An epistemically illuminated range is bounded by what inquirers can currently model, not by what is metaphysically possible, so a measure defined over it is a measure over the reach of present physics, and confidence drawn from it is confidence about that reach, not about a space of ways the constants could have been. This is the objective-epistemic conflation the prior question already isolates, reappearing one level in: Collins secures a normalizable measure by substituting an epistemic boundary for a modal one. And even granting the illuminated range as a genuine space of alternatives, the measure over it is still unfixed, since a uniform and a log-uniform measure on the same finite interval deliver different ratios and the argument supplies no principled reason to prefer either. The coarse-tuning observation that the life-permitting band is narrow on any reasonable measure survives the restriction, but it establishes only that the band is narrow relative to the illuminated range, which is a fact about the range our physics can survey, not evidence that the constants were drawn from a wider space and selected from it.

Anthropic reasoning makes a complementary point that does not duplicate the measure problem. Carter [@carter1974] and Bostrom [@bostrom2002] argue that observers can only find themselves in observation-permitting conditions: not because observation causes the conditions, but because the selection effect is built into what it is to be an observer making an observation at all. Were the constants otherwise, no one would be measuring them. The present account extends the anthropic point rather than replacing it: T, S, and Φ are not conditions that happen to be observer-permitting; they are conditions that make observation possible in the first place. An observation that these conditions obtain is made from within them. That fact requires an observation-selection correction, but it does not by itself show that the observation has no evidential bearing beyond the conditions.

*Second.* The multiverse-insufficiency extension presses the design inference up one level. Conceding everything naturalist cosmology asks for (a universe-generating mechanism, an ensemble of universes, a stochastic process sampling parameter space) the theist ([@collins2009, §6]; [@barnes2012]) argues that the fine-tuning demand reappears at the meta-level rather than dissolving. Any universe-generating mechanism must have its own structure: laws governing what universes it produces, a range of constants it can assign, a probability measure over outcomes. Those higher-order parameters are themselves either contingent (so the fine-tuning demand reappears at the meta-level) or necessary (so the theist concedes the destination of the present account). The regress of designers, the theist argues, does not terminate in the multiverse; it terminates in whatever fixes the multiverse.

Two replies. Hacking's inverse-gambler objection warns that observing one apparently unusual outcome does not automatically support many unobserved trials. Contemporary multiverse arguments often add independent cosmology and an observation-selection rule, so the objection constrains naive inferences rather than every multiverse explanation.

The sharper reply is available within the modal framework defended in §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6 rather than from the fine-tuning dialectic's neutral empirical register; conditional on that framework, S5 preserves the necessity of any genuinely necessary higher-order parameter. It does not identify the parameter or explain its high-resolution content. Necessary meta-parameters would be invariant features of the ensemble theory, but T, S, and Φ are too coarse to determine their specific values or probability law. The structural roles constrain any genuine universe-generating realizer; they do not identify every higher-order parameter or meta-tuner with the triad. Readers unconvinced by the prior modal framework can rely on the McGrew normalizability point alone: that closure is framework-neutral, and the S5 closure is a further sharpening available only on top of it.

*Third.* The Bayesian cumulative case, pursued most carefully by Swinburne [@swinburne2004], takes the argument in a more restrained probabilistic direction, retreating from entailment to confirmation. Swinburne does not claim the fine-tuning observation entails a designer; he claims it raises the probability of theism relative to naturalism by a non-trivial factor, and that when combined with other probabilistic considerations, the cumulative case for theism becomes compelling: simplicity (the prior-from-simplicity wing of Swinburne's case, engaged at [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4)), the existence of consciousness, and the phenomenon of moral awareness. Fine-tuning is one weight on a larger scale.

Monton [@monton2006] isolates the structural problem with the fine-tuning weight specifically. If God is omnipotent, God can instantiate conscious beings in any logically possible configuration. The present configuration is not therefore necessary for the existence of conscious beings. But if it is not necessary for the existence of conscious beings, the theist cannot explain why God selected this one rather than another except by appeal to divine preference, which does no Bayesian work: preference is compatible with any observation and discriminates between no hypotheses. The probability P(this configuration | theism) is as free as divine preference allows; which is to say, unanchored; which is to say, unable to contribute a determinate likelihood ratio.

A sharper version presses on the theist's own commitments rather than on Bayesian bookkeeping. God is held to be a conscious being not in this universe. If the constants of this universe are necessary for the existence of conscious beings, no conscious beings exist outside this universe, and God does not exist as characterized. If these constants are not necessary for consciousness simpliciter, the fine-tuning argument must be stated more narrowly in terms of embodied observers or life of our general kind. That limits the conclusion but does not make the observation evidentially null; comparative likelihoods may still differ over how readily rival hypotheses produce such observers. The fine-tuning premise concerns embodied life or observers generated by physical laws, whereas God is proposed as an unembodied mind. That is not a simple equivocation, but it narrows the evidence: the likelihood comparison must explain why theism predicts a physically life-permitting cosmos of this sort rather than merely the existence of consciousness somewhere.

*The teleological gloss.* The inference examined so far concludes only that the constants were selected; it is silent on what for. A stronger reading is almost always present in the tradition and rarely separated out: that the universe is not merely life-permitting but life-intended, tuned for life, with life as the purpose the tuning serves. This gloss is separable from the bare inference, and it fails on its own terms, independently of whether the bare inference succeeds. It is also the reading that carries the argument's rhetorical force, so its collapse matters.

*Any-tuning.* The gloss assumes that this configuration is specially suited to conscious life: that life is what these constants are for. But that only configurations near ours could host conscious beings is precisely what the argument has not shown. For all that is known, most configurations might support life of some kind; our inability to imagine it reflects the limits of our physics, not the limits of the possible [@ikedaJefferys2006]. Worse for the gloss, the theist's own ontology already contains conscious beings that hold none of this universe's constants fixed. God is a conscious being with no physical parameters at all. Angels and demons, on the traditional commitment, are conscious without bodies. The saved in heaven and the damned in hell are conscious persons in conditions that are not this universe's physics, on the doctrine, not even this universe. If consciousness can obtain in God, in heaven, and in hell, then this configuration is not necessary for consciousness on the theist's own accounting, and the 'tuned for conscious life' gloss contradicts the metaphysics it is meant to serve. The example is not a hostile construction; it is drawn from the proponent's own creed.

*The reversal.* Scoped to the gloss rather than to the bare inference, the fine-tuning observation runs the other way. If God is omnipotent, the space of means by which conscious life could be realized is enormous: God could sustain life in any configuration, or with none, or by direct fiat. A universe that must be threaded through a needle's eye of constants to permit life is therefore a strange choice for a being to whom all means are open: it is exactly the expedient a maker without options would be forced into, not one a maker with every option would prefer. The likelihood reversal makes this precise [@ikedaJefferys2006]: once observability is taken as background, learning that the universe is naturalistically life-permitting cannot raise the probability of a supernatural tuner, and on the for-life gloss specifically it lowers it, since an omnipotent intender had no need of a delicately balanced mechanism at all. The positive thesis follows: life that needs no apparatus to be created, yet is given a vast and precarious one, is evidence against the apparatus being for it.

*Function.* The sharpest form of the objection turns on how teleology is individuated. A thing made for a purpose is identified as such by its serving that purpose: the test of 'made for X' is 'succeeds at X.' An omnipotent maker cannot fail at function: whatever such a maker intends, obtains. So if the universe were made for life, it would be unmistakably, abundantly, securely hospitable to life, because nothing could have constrained the maker to do less. What is observed instead is a cosmos in which life clings to a vanishing margin, sustains itself against constant threat, and is extinguished with ease. A product that barely and precariously discharges its supposed function is, by the only test teleology affords, not made for that function. This wing is immune to the 'precious because rare' reply: rarity is evidence of difficulty, and difficulty is exactly what omnipotence does not face.

*Scale.* Three observations reinforce the functional point. Qualitatively, life does not find a hospitable world; it engineers itself against a hostile one. Survival is a labor of building shelter, regulating temperature, and defending against an environment that is not arranged for the organism; cities are monuments to how much must be done to make a patch of the world habitable. The relation runs opposite to the gloss: life is tuned to its environment by adaptation, not the environment to life by design. Quantitatively, the life-permitting region is a vanishing measure of a cosmos overwhelmingly lethal to life: near-absolute vacuum, lethal radiation, temperatures at both extremes, durations and distances on scales that dwarf anything life occupies.[[1]](cosmic-scale-disparity) Structurally, the narrowing recurs one level down inside that vanishing region: the fraction that is habitable is not itself one hospitable environment but a partition of mutually exclusive niches, where crossing from one into another is lethal rather than merely difficult, an ocean drowns what land life requires, open air suffocates what ocean life requires, and each further subdivision (pressure band, temperature range, salinity, atmospheric composition) forecloses what its neighbors permit. There is no environment hospitable to life as such, only a fractal series of disjoint environments each hostile to whatever is not already fitted to it. The fracturing recurs even inside a single generalist species. The Bajau of maritime Southeast Asia carry a genetic adaptation, an enlarged spleen serving as an oxygen reservoir, that lets them free-dive to depths and durations unadapted humans cannot match, while Tibetan and Andean highlanders meet the same challenge of high-altitude hypoxia by two different physiological routes: lower hemoglobin concentration in the one population, higher in the other. Ethiopian highlanders answer the same hypoxic pressure a third way, holding hemoglobin at sea-level norms while still reaching oxygen saturation levels neither of the other two groups matches by their own route. Inuit and Yup'ik populations carry a variant of the gene *CPT1A* that lets a near-zero-carbohydrate, fat-heavy diet fuel the body without the metabolic cost that same diet would impose on someone without it. The Haenyeo free-divers of Jeju evolved their own route to breath-hold diving in cold water, independent of the Bajau's. None of this is a claim of lethal incompatibility of the ocean-and-land kind; it is a claim about differential fit. Even the species most often cited as nature's generalist exception has already sorted into sub-populations locally optimized for extremes the rest of the species only tolerates. A universe that is for life is, on inspection, almost entirely against it.

What unifies these wings is omnipotence. Each dysteleological observation invites the reply that the hostility is instrumentally necessary: that a universe capable of producing life must be large, old, and governed by laws that are lethal elsewhere. That reply binds a constrained maker, not an omnipotent one. The moment the maker is granted omnipotence, every appeal to instrumental necessity lapses, and the hostility, scarcity, and precariousness become unforced features of the product, which is to say, evidence about its purpose. This is the cosmological specialization of the evidential structure Draper [@draper1989] presses for pain and pleasure: the distribution of good and ill in the world is more expected on indifference than on benevolent intention, and the gap is evidence.

Three replies are available to the gloss, and each fails for a stated reason. The instrumental-necessity reply binds the process, not the agent, and an omnipotent agent is not bound by the process. The minimalist-masterpiece reply (that a great maker might sign a single, spare, improbable work) does no Bayesian work, since 'a great maker would do this' is compatible with any observation whatever, and it collides directly with the suffering the spare work contains. The soul-making reply (that hardship is the point) concedes that the universe is not made for life's flourishing but for its testing, which is a different purpose, post-hoc with respect to the fine-tuning data, and which reactivates the problem of evil rather than answering it.

*The Fall.* A last rescue holds that the tuning was once benign and was broken: that the world's hostility postdates a fall, an original sin, a derangement of nature. The rescue faces a trilemma and forfeits its setting. Which conditions changed? If the physical constants changed, the claim is a physical hypothesis with no physical evidence, and one that runs against the very constancy the fine-tuning argument relies on. If only the biological or moral order changed, the cosmic hostility (vacuum, radiation, scale) was there from the start and is unexplained. If the change is purely spiritual, it does no work against the physical dysteleology at issue. And the rescue forfeits the project: an inference licensed only by an ancient text is no longer natural theology, which was the genre the fine-tuning argument entered to occupy. The collective form of the doctrine compounds the cost. A penalty visited on all conscious beings for the act of two, through a headship none of the penalized consented to or could have refused, is a moral structure an omnipotent maker had every means to avoid, who could, for instance, have created each pair on its own world to stand or fall for itself, with no representation imposed. That the collective arrangement was chosen when non-collective ones were available is not a necessity to be excused but a choice to be assessed, and it is assessed under the problem of evil, engaged in its own right elsewhere.

The eliminativist wing of the fine-tuning debate presses harder than the present argument does. Stenger [@stenger2011] argues that the appearance of fine-tuning is a statistical artifact: that under a full accounting of the possible parameterizations, no remarkable precision remains to be explained. (The Ikeda–Jefferys reversal, a distinct claim, is engaged above against the for-life gloss rather than against the bare observation.) The present account does not commit to the eliminativist's stronger claim. Some sensitivity is real; the question is what the sensitivity is of. The eliminativist answers: of nothing in particular, once the parameterization is normalized. The present account answers: of the configuration to the conditions prior to configuration. The two answers converge on rejecting the design inference and diverge on whether any feature of the observation survives the rejection. The present account preserves the observation and denies the inference; the eliminativist denies both. Where the eliminativist says the theist is chasing nothing, the present account says the theist is chasing the structure.

*Probability rides on modality.* The three forms share a structure worth stating directly: every probability is conditional on the modal frame that fixes its sample space, so probability questions are asked within a structure, never of it. That cuts against the tuner from two sides. Tuning requires a standard to tune toward, and the standard admits no tuner: if it is contingent, fine-tuning collapses into preference-matching and a regress of standards opens; if it is necessary, there is nothing to tune, since what holds necessarily holds in virtue of its necessity, not by being selected for. And the precision of any probability assignment tracks the resolution of the modal map beneath it, so a coarse map that under-distinguishes necessity from contingency inflates apparent contingency and, with it, apparent improbability. The narrow-window number is calibrated against what, at the structural level, is not itself a probability-bearer; precision against an ill-formed structure is fool's-precision, and the argument presents that precision as evidence about the very structure it was conditioned on.

A note on division of labor. The adjacent constructions that extend the fine-tuning debate are covered in their own sections. The Platonist reading of physical laws (whether the constants are prescriptive features of a separate domain or descriptive features of structural necessity) is [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4). The Wigner problem of mathematical applicability runs close to fine-tuning and is engaged in [§4.3.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-6). The multiverse taken as full-blown modal realism is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). Swinburne's broader cumulative case for theism, of which fine-tuning is one component, is engaged on its simplicity wing in [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4). The cumulative structure does not rescue the fine-tuning weight: Swinburne's method aggregates several individually-weak considerations toward a posterior above one-half, but each faces the same structural-presupposition reply and its own comparative burdens wherever it is pressed (fine-tuning here, simplicity at [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4), the PSR at [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)), so the contribution of this weight must be reassessed before the cumulative posterior can be claimed. The §5 replies are reckoned together at [§5.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-4). The problem of evil (reactivated above by the for-life gloss and by the appeal to a fall) is engaged in its own right in its own treatment, to which the present section defers. The present section confines itself to the direct inference from narrow-window observation to a tuner, and to the for-life gloss laid on top of it; the companion moves are handled where they belong.

*What converges.* A prior question, three forms, and a separable gloss converge on a qualified verdict. Fine-tuning can enter a Bayesian case, but only after its comparison class, priors, measure, and observation-selection effects are defended. The multiverse extension can move rather than remove the explanatory burden, yet necessary higher-order parameters are not thereby identical with T, S, and Φ. The cumulative case must show that theism predicts embodied observers in a cosmos like this more strongly than its rivals; the existence of an unembodied divine mind neither proves nor disproves that likelihood claim. Finally, the for-life gloss, separable from the bare inference, fails on its own terms: on the theist's own ontology consciousness obtains without this configuration, an omnipotent maker cannot fail at the function the gloss assigns, and the world's overwhelming hostility is evidence against its being for life rather than for it.

A final consideration: the argument for a tuner is delivered within the configuration it calls tuned. The precision of the constants is measured across moments, in laboratories configured in space, using instruments that persist through measurement; the inference from precision to selection is run by minds that instantiate the very structural roles whose contingency the argument is trying to leverage. The observation 'these constants are precisely set' is a report from within a world where the constants obtain; the inference 'therefore a setter' imports the idiom of selection from domains where selection has content (domains where unselected options also obtain) into a domain where no such options are available to compare against. The actual measurement and argument are structured acts, but a classical theist denies that divine selection is a temporal engineering process using pre-existing space and material. Retorsion establishes the structure of inquiry, not the absence of an external selector. The stronger objections remain the comparative-likelihood, measure, and grounding burdens developed above. The precision is a feature observed from within one structured configuration. Whether it is also evidence of selection remains a comparative explanatory question rather than something retorsion settles.

[[1]](cosmic-scale-disparity): The scale disparity, quantified. The observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years and roughly 13.8 billion years; a single known planet has hosted life for about 4 billion of those years, and reflective life occupies a fraction of a percent of that span. The precondition compounds the disparity: the mammalian radiation that eventually produced humans followed directly from the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction roughly 66 million years ago, in which an asteroid impact eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs and most other species then living; the ecological niches that opened were what primates, and later humans, expanded into. A universe built for a species that arrives this late, by way of a mass extinction, and occupies this little of it, is a strange one to have spent 13.8 billion years preparing, most of it filled with sterile voids.

### 5.1.6 Intelligent Design {#sec-5-1-6}

The intelligent design argument is the biological-scale version of the design inference engaged at cosmological scale in [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5). Its proponents, Behe [@behe1996; @behe2007], Dembski [@dembski1998; @dembski2002], Meyer [@meyer2009; @meyer2013], and Plantinga[@plantinga2011, ch. 9] at selective points, argue that biological complexity exhibits features (irreducible complexity, specified complexity, information content) that no unguided process can produce, and that the inference to a designer is the best explanation of those features. The Discovery Institute has carried the position into legal and pedagogical fora, and the *Kitzmiller v. Dover* (2005) decision rendered its legal status in the United States, but the underlying philosophical structure is what concerns the present argument.

ID is not simply fine-tuning at biological scale. Its core commitment is the forward design inference from specified or irreducible biological complexity to intelligent agency. Some religious deployments add special creation, an initially perfect order, or Fall-based explanations of dysteleology, but these are not commitments of ID as such and should be treated as optional extensions rather than the defining package. The Fall-based extension is what makes the religiously extended package self-sealing in a way fine-tuning is not. Fine-tuning claims forward tuning of constants and faces straightforward probabilistic and structural rebuttals. ID has a built-in absorber for every poor-design rebuttal: the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the human spine, the ichneumon wasp, the long catalogue of biological inefficiencies and cruelties[^5-1-6-dysteleology-catalogue]: these are read not as evidence against design but as evidence of *fall from* design. The argument flips dysteleology into confirmation. The present reply engages the core inference and both extensions, not just the core.

*First.* Against the design inference, the present reply draws on the four probability–modality couplings developed at [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5), named here for ease of reference: the standard-side dilemma (a tuner needs a standard, contingent or necessary, and both options foreclose the tuning), the consciousness self-application (the designer cannot be exempted from the constraints that motivated the inference), the modal-structure mask (improbability claims at the structural level are modal questions disguised as probability questions), and the resolution bound (modal-map coarseness inflates apparent contingency). Where [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) reads "constants" the argument reads "biological configurations." Where it reads "tuning," it reads "designing." The transfer is not automatic, because the two scales do not pose the improbability in the same key. Cosmological fine-tuning is a claim about the modal status of the constants, whether they could have been otherwise. Biological improbability is pressed as something nearer a first-order probability over a space of chemical and genetic configurations, and that is where the argument's intuitive force actually sits.

The biological case cannot be closed merely by transferring the cosmological objections. It turns on empirical models of mutation, selection, drift, developmental constraint, and the causal history of particular systems. Modal and probability questions still matter, but the decisive comparison is whether evolutionary mechanisms or design better explain the evidence under defensible likelihoods.

A further pressure bears on the inference from within its own founding image. Paley's[@paley1802] watch is recognized as designed only against a backdrop that is not: the artifact stands out because the heath it lies on does not bear the same marks. The design inference is therefore contrastive at its root, reading "designed" off a difference between the worked object and the unworked ground. The theistic use of the inference then extends the verdict to everything, the watch and the heath alike, since the same designer is said to have made the ground the watch rests on no less than the watch. But that extension consumes the contrast that licensed the first step: if the ground is designed too, there is no unworked backdrop left against which the watch's design could register, and "designed" stops marking any detectable difference. The inference cannot both earn its conclusion locally (this object, unlike its surroundings, is designed) and generalize that conclusion globally (the surroundings are designed as well) without dissolving the very contrast that gave the local reading its content. Universalized design is indistinguishable from no design at all: not because nothing is designed, but because the predicate has lost the difference it was introduced to track.

The analogy that anchors the inference also marks where it fails. A watch cannot produce another watch, and it is that incapacity, not the watch's intricacy alone, that makes an external maker feel mandatory: nothing about a watch could bring a second watch about. Living things have exactly the capacity the artifact lacks. They reproduce, vary, and are filtered, so the inference cannot be carried from the watch to the organism without importing the watch's sterility as a silent premise, which is to assume rather than show that life, like a watch, could not have come about unaided. The point can be put as a controlled comparison. A kennel holds a hundred dogs. In the first case a breeder selects two of them whose cross yields an animal well suited to a particular hunt: the mating is intended and the result is designed. In the second case the same two dogs are simply the last pair left together and breed as dogs do, with no one intending anything: the litter is identical to the breeder's. Set the two animals side by side. Nothing in either records which history produced it. One was designed and one was not, and the designed one carries no mark of the fact. What the comparison demonstrates is that agency is the sole variable differentiating the two cases; all product-level features are held constant. That result grounds a general claim about the domain the design inference operates in. Design is a prospective process: the designer models a function and selects for it. Selection is a retrospective process: the environment tests against function and retains what fits. Both are function-tracking processes; they differ only in whether the specification precedes or follows the production. For any functional product a designer can yield — any product whose distinguishing features consist in fitness to a function — a sufficiently calibrated selective filter operating on that same function can yield the same, because the features the designer specified-for are precisely the features selection retains. Functional similarity alone may underdetermine whether a trait was designed or selected, because different histories can converge on similar products. But causal histories can leave traces in genealogy, constraint, redundancy, and error-patterns. The design inference must therefore compare full historical models rather than assume either that function uniquely reveals agency or that products can never contain evidence of their origin.

This closes the appeal to specified complexity. A specification is a function-profile: the set of functional properties an object must instantiate to serve its purpose. Selection is differential reproduction based on fitness to the environment. Fitness to the environment is a function-profile. Selection can cumulatively retain variants that function better in a given environment, but it is not literally intentional specification: fitness landscapes emerge from organism–environment relations rather than from a prior semantic target. Dembski's design filter claims to detect specifications that are improbable given chance but probable given design; they are equally probable given cumulative selection operating on the same function-specification — which is the core of the cumulative-selection reply Sober develops.[@sober2008] A specification reliably hit by selection is not a signature of design; it is the predictable output of any process, intentional or not, that tracks function over sufficient iterations. The inference therefore requires a premise that rules out functional-equivalent selection, and that premise cannot be established by examining the product — only by examining the causal history the product-level evidence is being used to infer.

The empirical critique of ID's specific apparatus, Behe's irreducible complexity, Dembski's design filter, Meyer's information argument, lives in evolutionary biology and is not the structural argument's burden; that work has been done there, notably by Sober.[@sober2008] One strand of Behe's case is not purely empirical, however. The *Edge of Evolution* claim (that specified biological information is a quantity the unguided process can generate only within narrow limits) is a thesis about what generates structural information, not only about what the biology shows; the structural reply to it, how the immanent operators of change, composition, and constraint generate form rather than merely presuppose it, is developed where the operators are (Chapter 7), and the information-theoretic features are taken up at [§4.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3). The couplings at [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) and the comparative-history burden above bear on the design inference here, however that generative question is settled. The present argument shows what the inference must establish before it runs; the biological literature contests the empirical premises themselves.

*Second.* A historical Fall narrative posits an earlier condition within temporal history from which later corruption proceeds. It need not posit a moment outside T or a categorial origin of time. The relevant objections are empirical and theological—whether there was such an initial condition, what changed, and whether it explains the evidence—not Parasitic Negation alone. There is no moment-prior-to-T from which the first change departed, no temporal position at which "perfect creation" was instantiated as an initial condition outside the order it would initiate (§[§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), 7.2.2, 7.6). The quantitative question of how far back along the dimension the passage runs (whether the past is chronometrically finite or infinite) is a separate question within T, engaged at [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) against the Kalām's traversal and BGV arguments. The fall narrative in its privileged-t₀ form needs the categorial t₀; the Kalām presses the quantitative question. The two are dispatched at different sections by different machinery. Parasitic Negation applied to T (§[§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), 2.6.6) is the move ID's privileged-t₀ commitment cannot survive: any beginning would already instantiate the order it claims to begin. The question "when did time begin?" admits two readings. The quantitative reading (how far back does succession run) has a numerical answer within whatever cycle one is asking from. The categorial reading (what moment yielded T) is malformed: a moment is what T provides, not what produces T. A moment of perfect creation followed by decay is structurally describable as an event within time. Its difficulty is that ID evidence does not establish such a moment and the biological and cosmological records may count against particular versions of it. The categorial closure dispatches the fall narrative's t₀; it does not dispatch the Kalām's quantitative question, which is the work of [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2).

*Third.* The asymmetric decay vector, the third commitment, reads observed imperfection as evidence of fall from initial perfection. The reading conflates two distinct phenomena: entropy increase (a structural feature of T running) and moral or teleological decline (a normative feature attributed to history). The conflation is what gives the fall claim its empirical footing: every ad hoc construction, vestige, inefficiency, and cruelty in the biological record is reabsorbed as evidence of a perfect prior state from which the present has departed. Entropy increase should not be identified without argument either with moral decline or with Temporality itself. Thermodynamic arrows depend on physical laws and boundary conditions; a Fall theology that links them to corruption owes an additional empirical and doctrinal account. Reading entropy as moral-teleological decline imports a normative direction the present account locates nowhere. T running is not T falling. The fall reading also lacks a historical anchor. It requires a moment at which a first human moral agent acted in a way that initiated decay, but roughly half a billion years of metazoan suffering predate any organism that could be such an agent, and contemporary population genetics rules out descent of *Homo sapiens* from a single founding pair within the span the lineage permits.[@venemaMcknight2017] Plantinga's *O Felix Culpa*[@plantinga2004] relocates the fall into a privileged theological moment whose empirical anchorage is set aside; the move preserves the theological structure at the cost of giving up exactly the historical fall the original argument needs. Without the entropy-as-fall reading, and without a historical fall to anchor it, the dysteleology cases revert to what they were before being absorbed by the theodicy: evidence against the design inference, not evidence for it.

A note on scope. The fall claim also makes a directional empirical prediction (that observed history runs away from an initial perfection), and there are aggregate gradients in human social life and in religious demand that appear to run the other way. Those gradients are contested empirical terrain, and the present section does not rest on them: the fall narrative is already foreclosed structurally, by the categorial-t₀ argument and the entropy misreading above, whatever the long-run social data ultimately show. The substantive case that these gradients positively confirm the structural account is made where that work belongs ([§8.12.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-4) on the moral arc and [§8.14.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-14-4) on declining religiosity) and is left to stand or fall there on its own evidence.

*What closes.* The core inference and its two extensions dispatch separately, and the package does not survive their separation. The design inference carries the couplings at [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) and the comparative-history burden developed above. The privileged origin moment is foreclosed by the present argument that T has no exterior or prior origin moment, a categorial closure that leaves the quantitative question of a finite chronometric past to [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) and Chapter 7. The asymmetric decay vector misreads entropy as moral decline. A Fall-based absorber can make a religious design theory resistant to dysteleological evidence, but it is an optional theological auxiliary rather than part of ID's core. It incurs empirical and explanatory burdens concerning the initial condition, mechanism, and scope of corruption. Without the absorber, the design inference at biological scale inherits the burdens of the design inference at cosmological scale, which [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) leaves undischarged.

[[1]](dysteleology-catalogue): The catalogue extends to reproduction itself. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists estimates that as many as one in four recognized pregnancies ends in miscarriage (ACOG estimate, cited in Deshpande and Kucirka, *StatPearls*, 2023), and a substantial further share of fertilized eggs are lost before implantation is ever detected. A designer credited with intending the birth of every child inherits, on the same accounting, a design in which a large fraction of attempts at that outcome fail before term.

### 5.1.7 Modal Ontological Argument {#sec-5-1-7}

Plantinga's modal ontological argument[@plantinga1974b] runs as follows.

1. A being is *maximally great* just in case it is omniscient, omnipotent, and morally perfect in every possible world, so that maximal greatness includes existence in every possible world.

::: {.argument}
1. *Possibility premise.* Possibly, a maximally great being is instantiated: ◇□G.

1. *S5.* Possible necessity yields necessity: from ◇□G, □G.

1. *Conclusion.* A maximally great being exists in every possible world, the actual one included: □G, and so G.

:::

The crux is the possibility premise: is maximal greatness coherent?

The argument has antecedents and successors that sharpen what is being claimed. Hartshorne[@hartshorne1962] develops an earlier modal version of the argument from Anselmian materials, and Adams[@adams1971] defends the broader thesis that the modal-ontological strategy survives the Kantian objection that existence is not a predicate. Plantinga's own assessment in *The Nature of Necessity* is more modest than the argument's later reception: the argument shows that belief in a maximally great being is rational, not that disbelief is irrational. The objection developed below establishes a stronger result. It does not merely show that disbelief is rational alongside belief; it shows that the classical version of the argument cannot succeed even at its more modest target.

The argument's modal core relies on the same fixed-domain S5 framework the present book operates within. The present account does not contest the transfer rule; it contests whether the classical possibility premise supplies a determinate candidate within the global domain of real possibility.

*Try to conceive of an atemporal, aspatial, immaterial being.* The conception fails not because the being is alien or unlike anything in experience but because the description subtracts from its object the conditions of statehood itself: temporal location, spatial-relational differentiation, substantial bearing. The collapse of the conceiving act (succession of imaginative acts, distinction of the imagined being from background, sustained representational substance, each withdrawn by the very content entertained) is the symptom of that subtraction rather than the engine of the argument; the load is carried by what the description withdraws from its object, made exact in the conditions-for-statehood argument below. The general result has already been pressed at [§3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3): structural absence cannot be coherently conceived, because every attempt to represent it instantiates what it denies, and the asymmetry between conceivability-to-possibility and inconceivability-to-impossibility favors the downward direction when the inconceivability is of this structural kind. The maximally great being is the case where structural absence is dressed in classical-theistic predicates. What follows works the same point through Plantinga's machinery directly.

Plantinga's possibility premise concerns maximal excellence—omniscience, omnipotence, and moral perfection—instantiated in every world. Atemporality, aspatiality, immateriality, and strong divine simplicity are additional classical-theist doctrines, not premises of the modal ontological argument itself. Coherent possibility, in the relevant sense, requires that the conjunction's content be specifiable in a way that does not contradict itself or contradict the conditions on which content is possible. If a defender adds the strongest negative classical attributes, the book can press whether a personal being so characterized retains determinate cognitive, volitional, and grounding roles. That pressure does not show that Plantinga's thinner maximal-greatness predicate is contentless; it challenges one theological development of the candidate.

A defender may attempt the Plantingian reply: vehicle and content come apart. One can conceive a colorless object using a colored display; conceiving an atemporal being does not require the thought itself to be atemporal. The reply works for single properties: color, mass, charge, shape, all can be absent without the object collapsing. T, S, and Φ fail the test categorically. An object lacking temporal location is not an object existing timelessly but an object of which no moment can make 'this exists' true; an object lacking spatial-relational differentiation is not an object with unusual geometry but an object with no interval separating it from anything else; an object lacking Substance is not an object existing for zero duration but an object with no being through which predication could run.

T, S, and Φ are not properties within a state of affairs; they are conditions for statehood. The colorless-object analogy does not carry here, not because the maximally great being is missing more properties, but because it is missing the conditions under which properties could be instantiated at all.
