The claim is scoped to concrete existents. Abstract objects (numbers, propositions, the possible worlds Plantinga's own abstract-worlds actualism reifies) bear properties without instantiating T, S, or Φ, and nothing here denies it; the status of abstracta is treated in its own right at [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4). But the maximally great being is not an abstract object. It is a concrete person who knows, wills, and acts, and those are the very acts that require succession, distinction, and a persisting subject. The Platonist's atemporal existents are no refuge for it, and neither is a third category: the classical theist may reply that God is neither a structural concretum nor an abstractum but sui generis, pure act on the divine-simplicity model, and so exempt from the dilemma. The reply relocates the burden rather than discharging it. A being that knows, wills, and acts has already been given a personal profile whose exercise requires succession, distinction, and a persisting subject, whatever category label is invoked to secure the exemption; the constitutive case that a bearer of those acts must instantiate T, S, and Φ is pressed against the *ipsum esse* construal directly at [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1).

Because these are conditions for statehood and not features within a state, the description does not specify an object that then proves impossible (an impossibility would make the possibility claim about it false, true in no world) but fails to specify a possibility-candidate at all.

The diagnosis should not be placed automatically before truth-value. Standard semantic treatments can assign falsehood, presupposition failure, or undefinedness to defective descriptions. Here the safer verdict is dialectical: the defender owes a coherent account of how the added classical attributes combine with personal agency; semantic emptiness does not follow merely from their negations. Where standard modal semantics assigns falsity to an impossible proposition, the fully classical candidate leaves no determinate proposition for any world to evaluate: the presupposition on which the description's content depends is exactly what the description withdraws. The possibility premise, read with the full classical conjunction, is not false but empty: it carries no modal content for S5 to operate on.

::: {.corollary}
**Possibility-Premise Emptiness** · **R13** · *Result of the Conceivability Asymmetry*

The possibility premise of Plantinga's modal ontological argument carries no modal content: the conjunction of classical attributes specifies ∅ under personal description, and S5 cannot transmit necessity from an empty input. The argument is therefore not unsound but inapplicable. The local Chapter 5 verdict rests on the [§3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3) conceivability-asymmetry result and the §5 machinery already established; the Result form anticipates Supernatural Preclusion ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)) via Horn 1 of the Trilemma Closure, where the same result is restated under Supernatural Preclusion once that result is in place downstream. ([§3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3), [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1))


:::

The standard objection remains central: S5 transfers the possibility premise but does not support it. The structural critique can add that some classical enrichments of the candidate create tensions with personal agency. It should not claim that Plantinga's possibility premise carries no modal content simply because those additional doctrines are contested. What is described by the conjunction of the classical attributes is not a genuine possibility-candidate, because what is described is not a possible configuration but the absence of the conditions for any configuration.

The present objection should also be distinguished from the symmetry objection developed by Oppy[@oppy1995] and Sobel[@sobel2003]. The symmetry objection observes that the same modal apparatus generates a parody: possibly there is no maximally great being, therefore necessarily there is no maximally great being. The objection's force is that the argument and its parody share a form, so neither tells us which possibility actually obtains. The present objection does not rely on parody. It denies that the classical maximally great being is in the possibility space at all. The parody objection is consistent with the possibility premise being meaningful; the present objection denies that the possibility premise carries the kind of modal content that being true or false would require. Where the symmetry objection leaves the modal-ontological project a stalemate, this objection denies the project its starting move.

The S5 inference is intact. The modal framework is intact. What fails is the input. A *modus ponens* (the inference from P and 'if P then Q' to Q) transmits a conclusion only from a premise that carries modal content; a possibility premise that specifies no possibility-candidate carries none, so nothing is transmitted, regardless of how impeccable the inference rule. The failure is not that the premise is false (a false premise would still be a premise) but that no modal content is present for truth or falsity to attach to.

A second front is available, independent of the foregoing rebuttal. Van Hamme[@vanHamme2025a] argues that modal logic alone does not supply a substantive account of a necessary *personal* God. This should be stated precisely. S5 can transfer necessity to any determinate proposition in the global domain W; it does not restrict its scope to structural vocabulary. What it cannot do by itself is establish that personhood-attributing predicates — omniscience, omnipotence, moral perfection — form a coherent necessary package or that they apply to the candidate described. The modal-ontological argument therefore needs more than the transfer rule: it needs an independently supported, determinate possibility premise for a personal being.

This front constrains the present account too, harmlessly: the book does not derive the personal or the axiological from S5 alone. Chapter 6 must ground its claims about value, agency, and greatness in the structural and dialectical arguments specific to them. The two rebuttals therefore do different work. The first challenges the classical candidate's content; the second blocks the inference from a bare modal rule to the full personal-theistic conclusion. Together they show that S5 neither repairs an empty specification nor substitutes for an argument about the attributes.

*The formal derivation.* A more rigorous version of the modal ontological argument does not assert the possibility premise but derives it. Gödel's ontological proof (his axiomatization of *positive properties*, sharpened in Anderson's emendation against modal collapse and analyzed in Hájek's formal treatment) lays down that every property is positive or its negation is, that positive properties are closed under entailment, and that necessary existence is positive, and from these proves as a theorem that a God-like being, one bearing every positive property essentially, is possibly instantiated; S5 then delivers necessary existence. Deriving the possibility premise looks to answer the present objection at its root: the premise is no longer left unsupported but established by proof.

It does not answer it. Gödelian derivations shift the burden to the positive-property axioms, their consistency, and the definition of God-likeness. Those axioms do not by themselves encode atemporality, aspatiality, or immateriality, so the earlier structural critique cannot simply be transferred to them. Formal derivability still does not show that the axioms provide the intended theological interpretation. Formal derivability manufactures no more modal content than the axioms supply: the proof is valid, and whether its input carries the intended theological content is exactly what the axioms leave unsecured.

The personhood front closes the same gap from the other side: Gödel's positive properties include the personhood-attributing predicates, omniscience and omnipotence and moral perfection, that fall outside the structural vocabulary any modal logic can certify, so even granting the axioms their domain the apparatus cannot necessitate the personal. The Gödelian formalization raises the rigor of the derivation; it leaves untouched the status of what is derived.

A respondent may revise maximal greatness to drop the classical attributes, making the maximally great being temporal, extended, and embedded. The revision changes the subject in two respects. First, the present argument does not dispute such a being's possibility, only the inference from possibility to necessity by S5: the inference depends on the being's maximal greatness across worlds, which the revision has redefined and which now requires independent argument. Second, the revised being instantiates T, S, and Φ rather than grounding them, and a being so embedded depends on structure for its existence. The aseity the modal-ontological tradition was specifically trying to secure (necessary existence as a feature of the being rather than of its conditions) is the property [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1) and [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) (Horn 3) establish the embedded deity cannot have. The revised argument may go through to a different conclusion, but the conclusion is no longer the conclusion the classical modal-ontological project was constructed to deliver.

*What is established.* S5 validates the transfer from possible necessary existence to necessary existence, but it does not establish the possibility premise or the coherence of the full theological package. Structural tensions arise when strong negative classical attributes are added to a personal agent; those tensions qualify the candidate without making Plantinga's thinner premise semantically empty. The personhood front closes the same line from the inference side: modal logic cannot necessitate the personal even where the structural conditions are present. Revising the maximally great being to drop the classical attributes preserves the inference at the cost of what the classical project was specifically trying to secure: aseity as a feature of the being rather than of its conditions.

*No rescue by changing the modal logic.* A defender may retain the classical candidate while rejecting S5, so that ◇□G no longer transfers to □G. This is not self-undermining merely because it is stated in modal vocabulary; it is a rival account of real possibility and its global domain. But it is self-defeating for Plantinga's specific derivation: the step from possible necessary existence to necessary existence is the inference that makes the modal ontological argument go. Rejecting S5 does not save that derivation; it replaces it with a different argument that needs its own modal semantics and its own defense of the possibility premise. The present account maintains the fixed-domain S5 analysis of [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1). Granting it, the argument still needs a determinate classical candidate; rejecting it leaves the Plantingan transfer unavailable. Either way the original possibility line has not been secured.

*A parallel epistemological line.* Pascal's wager is taken up at [§5.1.11](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-11), where the temptation to run the same possibility-of-classical-necessary-being premise through a probability claim is closed off and the wager is returned to its own decision-theoretic ground.

*Plantinga's reserve: de re/de dicto and EAAN.* Plantinga would press two further questions on the present account. First, the modal-scope question: □(T∧S∧Φ) can be read de dicto (necessarily, whatever constitutes the modal constraint on change instantiates the three roles) or de re (these specific structural occupants necessarily exist). The two readings differ on whether contingent states of Nature inherit necessity from Nature's necessity. The de dicto reading is the intended scope: what is necessary is that the roles be instantiated, not that any specific instantiator is necessary. Contingent states of Nature remain contingent within a necessary structural framework ([§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4)); the scope-limit argument at [§2.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-5) ('P4's necessity attaches to F, not to every item within the field F makes possible') is the relevant disambiguation; and the co-instantiation claim at [§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5) secures the de dicto reading without collapsing into de re necessity for contingent occupants. Second, Plantinga's Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (*Warrant and Proper Function*[@plantinga1993]): the present argument is delivered by cognitive faculties selected for survival; whether such faculties can reliably track necessary structural conditions is the EAAN question. The structural account's response (that any functioning cognitive faculty operates within T, S, and Φ by the transcendental conditions on operation itself) lives in Chapter 8.

### 5.1.8 Modal-Grounding Argument {#sec-5-1-8}

Arguments of this kind reason toward a divine being. The modal-grounding argument reasons toward God as the explanation of modality itself: of why there are necessary truths and real possibilities at all, rather than nothing modal to speak of. Because it leans on the same modal facts the present account is built from, it is the most direct theistic competitor to the book's own grounding of necessity, and it warrants engagement on its own terms rather than as a restatement of the ontological argument [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7) handles.

The argument's most developed form is Leftow's. Historically, theist modal theories based all necessary truth on God's nature; Leftow (*God and Necessity*[@leftow2012]) argues instead that necessary truths about possible creatures and kinds are fixed by God's unconstrained imagination and choice, with the broadly logical modalities reduced to causal modalities seated in God and events in God's mind. The distinctive move is a *global economy* argument: theists are committed to some theist modal theory, and the explanatory merits of a good one (its economy against the heavy ontologies of Lewisian modal realism and abstracta-laden ersatzism) are offered as an argument for God's existence. Adjacent constructions press the same thought from other directions: Plantinga's suggestion that propositions are best construed as divine thoughts, since there are far more of them than finite minds could entertain ("Two Dozen (or So) Theistic Arguments"[@plantinga2007]); and the theistic activism, or absolute creationism, of Morris and Menzel[@morrisMenzel1986], on which abstracta (modal truths among them) depend for their existence on God's intellectual activity. The shared structure is an inference to the best ground:

1. *Grounding demand.* Modal and necessary facts are real and cannot be brute: they require a ground.

1. *Mind as ground.* A mind is the best or only adequate ground for them.

1. *Conclusion.* A divine mind exists as the ground of modality.

Grant the demand in full. The argument is right that modal facts are not free-floating: that "possibly P" and "necessarily P" cannot be ungrounded surds, true with nothing about Reality to fix them. Grant, too, that a plurality of concrete non-actual worlds (Lewis), or a Platonic heaven of modal abstracta, is a heavy and contestable ontology. The demand for a ground for modality is legitimate, and the dissatisfaction with possible-worlds Platonism is one the present account shares rather than resists.

What the argument adds to that demand is a mind to satisfy it, and the structure satisfies it first. Reality's fixed global domain of real possibility grounds modal status at [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1): Modal Stability derives S5 from evaluation over one complete domain W, while the Bottleneck distinguishes that global modality from local reachability. Transition Closure is a narrower auxiliary result concerning onset from capacitylessness, not a third derivation of proposition-wise S5. Modal status is therefore not conferred by an intellect entertaining worlds; it is fixed by the global modal structure the account articulates. The explanatory work Leftow credits to God's imagination and choice, and Morris and Menzel to God's intellectual activity, is already discharged one level down, by the conditions any possibility presupposes. This bears directly on the global-economy form: the theist theory is advanced as the *best* ground precisely because its rivals are taken to be Lewisian realism and abstracta-Platonism. A structural account is a third option that grounds the modal structure without a mind and without a plurality of worlds, so at that level the inference from "best available ground" to God is blocked at the comparative step it depends on.

This front must be drawn at its real scope. What [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1) grounds is the modal *structure*: that modal status is determinate, and determined by structure. The modal structure is schematic and existence-silent: it rigidifies what is possible and necessary without settling which contingent things exist or which specific creaturely natures populate the space of the possible. Leftow's theory reaches further than the modal structure, aiming to explain why *these* creaturely kinds are the possible ones. The present account does not, on its own resources, fix that *de re* creaturely content; it fixes the modal structure, not the full roster of what the modal structure permits. A defender can therefore concede that the modal structure needs no mind and still press that the content of creaturely possibility does. Taken alone, this front narrows the argument's reach; it does not close it.

The argument's deeper trouble is independent of how much of modality the structural account claims to ground: the proposed ground cannot do the grounding without carrying a structural burden of its own. A classical divine intellect is typically described as atemporal, non-spatial, and immaterial. The relevant pressure is whether it can bear determinate modal content and stand in an asymmetric grounding relation to possibilities without instantiating at least thin order, difference, and bearing roles. The revised [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7) verdict does not make the candidate semantically empty by definition; it leaves a substantive grounding burden. Actual finite imagining involves succession, distinction, and persistence, while the classical theorist proposes one timeless intellectual act. Even on that proposal, determinate contents and asymmetric dependence remain. This secures a minimal structural burden; whether it entails the loaded temporal, spatial, and physical types remains disputed.

A defender might relax the ground to an embedded, temporal mind, one that does instantiate the conditions. Then it is no longer the classical God whose aseity the theory was built to secure, and a mind so described instantiates Time, Space, and Substance rather than grounding them: it depends on the structure for its own operation, and so cannot be modality's ultimate ground. The revision keeps a grounder by giving up the ground's ultimacy.

The argument points at something real: modality is not explanatorily idle. The present account locates its modal structure in Reality's fixed global possibility-domain and the structural Conditions later derived for worlds in that domain. The general result of [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10) is narrower than an absolute sourcelessness thesis: no candidate whose own status is modal can confer the modal domain it already inhabits. A mind posited as an internal modal item therefore cannot ground W from outside; an essence-prior or transcendent mind remains a further metaphysical posit whose grounding credentials require independent argument.

*What is established.* The modal-grounding argument is right to refuse free-floating modality, and the structural account supplies a non-theistic ground for the global modal domain. That blocks the global-economy inference to God at the comparative step. A classical divine mind stripped of every structural role also fails to supply an intelligible active grounding relation on the present account. A defender may instead posit an essence-prior or transcendent ground, but then the proposal has moved beyond a modal-grounding explanation and owes an independent metaphysics of that ground. What the argument sees — the need for modal explanation — the structure supplies; what it adds — a specifically divine mind — remains unearned by the modal facts alone.

### 5.1.9 Transcendental Argument {#sec-5-1-9}

The transcendental argument for God presses logical necessity as its strongest case. The Laws of Identity, Non-Contradiction, and Excluded Middle are absolute, universal, and not plausibly derivable from any contingent feature of the world; something must secure their status, and a purely structural account can seem too thin to carry that weight, so on this argument the securing ground is God. In its most ambitious form the claim widens past logic to intelligibility as such — the very possibility of making sense of anything — but logic is where it bites hardest, and that is where the engagement begins. Pressed for the relation that ground bears to logic, the argument divides into three genuine positions: classical presuppositionalism ([@vanTil1955]; [@bahnsen1998]) — the transcendental argument in the strict sense — places logic outside God, as externally grounded by a necessarily rational being; theistic conceptualism ([@morrisMenzel1986]; [@plantinga1980]; [@leftow2012]; [@welty2014]) places logic inside God, as a structural feature of divine thinking; Cartesian voluntarism places logic downstream of God, as the free output of divine will. The three moves cover the principal theistic grounding strategies considered here (logic external to and grounded by God, logic internal to divine nature or thought, and logic dependent on divine will) and none secures a distinct theistic ground without unpaid burdens: voluntarism appears to presuppose the alternatives it would decree, presuppositionalism owes a non-circular account of its Author, and conceptualism converges on the structural conditions under a theistic description.

Regimented, the argument runs:

1. The laws of logic (Identity, Non-Contradiction, Excluded Middle) are absolute, universal, and necessary.

1. Their necessity cannot derive from any contingent feature of the world; something must secure it.

1. Only a necessarily rational being can secure necessary rationality.

1. Therefore a necessarily rational being, God, grounds logic.

The presuppositionalist move is, in its contemporary form, the most philosophically developed of the three. Van Til's *The Defense of the Faith* [@vanTil1955] and Bahnsen's *Van Til's Apologetic* [@bahnsen1998] stand at the head of the presuppositionalist tradition, which argues that any non-theistic worldview cannot account for the preconditions of intelligibility (logic, induction, morality) without borrowing from the theism it purports to reject. Morris and Menzel [@morrisMenzel1986] reframe the tradition with the view that has dominated the last three decades: theistic activism, on which God's necessary thinking constitutes the realm of abstract objects, including logical truths. Plantinga's *Does God Have a Nature?* [@plantinga1980] had earlier pressed the companion question whether God stands subject to the logical laws or is identical to them, and settled on a version of the conceptualist reply. Leftow's *God and Necessity* [@leftow2012] is the most systematic contemporary treatment: defending a modal conceptualism on which the modal facts are grounded in God's nature. Welty [@welty2014] develops a theistic conceptualist position that locates logic inside God rather than outside. Craig's *God Over All: Divine Aseity and the Challenge of Platonism* [@craig2016] presses the same aseity motive to a different destination: surveying divine conceptualism among the realist options and finding it wanting, Craig concludes that abstract objects (propositions, properties, logical truths) are not entities of any kind, so the apparent Platonic realm is dissolved by anti-realist deflation rather than relocated into divine intellection. The voluntarist position runs through Descartes's letters to Mersenne [@descartes1630] and has few contemporary defenders, though Frankfurt [@frankfurt1977] and Curley [@curley1984] give it sympathetic reconstructions. Against these stand anti-theistic-grounding positions: Sober's [@sober1993] Humean line that logical truths require no grounding beyond their formal character; and Sher's [@sher2016] logical realism, which treats logic as objective but not as requiring a rational ground.

The present account is closer to Sher's realism than to any of the theistic positions, but the reason is specific: logic describes formal constraints on determinate contents and relations. Where a manifold is offered as a concrete change-realizing reality, the structural Conditions identify the roles it must realize. Logic alone does not derive the full T, S, and Φ types from any arbitrary manifold of relata.

The challenge bears directly on [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) and [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7). T, S, and Φ are identified at [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) as the Triconditional Identity. Questions of the form “why is there something rather than nothing?” are dissolved at [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7), which argues that ∅ (the Null State: the configuration in which none of T, S, or Φ is instantiated) is incoherent on multiple independent grounds. The divine-logic objection presses both: against the structural account, that logical necessity is a distinct domain requiring its own ground; against [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7), that the positive necessity of the laws ruling out ∅ requires a ground of its own, and the ground must be a necessary rational being. The reply grants the necessity and universality of the core logical laws. T, S, and Φ can supply concrete instances of determinacy, difference, and ordered dependence, but logic is more general than any particular physical manifold. The structural account therefore offers an interpretation of logic's application; it does not derive all logical truth from the loaded types alone.

The three moves share a prior assumption worth naming: each treats the laws of logic as prescriptions, edicts that hold because something with the authority to lay them down has done so, which is why a legislator seems required to account for their force. But the “law” in “laws of logic” is descriptive, not prescriptive. It issues no command that a manifold of distinct relata could obey or flout; it states what being such a manifold already comes to. A description needs something to describe, not someone to enact it, and once the laws are read this way the office of lawgiver the three moves compete to fill stands empty before any of them is assessed.

The distinction can be put as one of prepositions. What holds necessarily of God, that a given act is necessarily open to him or that his nature is what it is, is a law *of* God, not a law *from* God: it describes him rather than issuing from his authority, and he could not have prescribed it to himself, since to prescribe anything already presupposes the modal space in which the prescription would hold. A lawgiver who must stand under the laws in order to legislate them has not grounded them but exemplified them, and the appeal to divine authority regresses at the very point it was meant to terminate. Three forms of the move take up the objection.

*First.* The classical presuppositionalist treats logic as externally grounded. On Van Til and Bahnsen's view, logical truths require something outside themselves to secure their necessity, and the only candidate is a necessarily rational, necessarily existent being whose nature underwrites the laws without being reducible to them. Every argument presupposes logical laws; every use of logical laws presupposes their ground; every ground of necessary rationality must itself be necessary; and the only necessary thing that can ground necessary rationality is a necessarily rational being. Call this the *authoring relation*: God authors logic by being the kind of being whose existence makes logical truth possible.

The authoring relation generates a modal dilemma at its own level. If the necessarily rational being (call it the Author) is the source of logical possibility, then the counterfactual “were the Author not to exist, logic would not obtain” must be true. But 'were the Author not to exist' is itself a logical possibility, a consistent hypothesis about what could fail to obtain, and its being a logical possibility presupposes the laws of logic holding. If the Author's non-existence is logically possible, logic cannot depend straightforwardly on the Author's actual existence. If it is logically impossible, the theist may say that logical necessity is grounded in the Author's essence rather than externally governing it. That answer faces a circularity or explanatory-priority burden, but it is not formally inconsistent merely because logical predicates apply to their proposed ground.

The regress completes the point. If logic is grounded in the Author's existence, what grounds the fact that the Author's existence has the relevant logical character? The presuppositionalist's candidate is the Author's necessary nature, but “necessary nature” is itself a logical characterization, and the grounding runs in a circle. Bahnsen's transcendental formulation (“the impossibility of the contrary”) concedes the point when pressed: “the impossibility of the contrary” is a logical modal claim, and the impossibility it invokes is the very kind of necessity the argument is trying to ground. The presuppositionalist account, pressed for substance, supplies a name for what underwrites logical necessity rather than an independent grounding of it.

*Second.* The contemporary conceptualist relocates logic inside the divine mind. On the conceptualist view ([@morrisMenzel1986]; [@plantinga1980]; [@leftow2012]; [@welty2014]), logical truths are not external to God and grounded by God; they are constitutive of God's thinking. The Law of Identity is not a law God obeys and not a law God creates; it is a structural feature of how God necessarily thinks. Logic is God thinking. The view is a substantial improvement on the classical presuppositionalist version: it eliminates the authoring relation (which the previous move showed to be incoherent) and replaces it with an identity-style grounding that avoids the regress. Leftow's *God and Necessity* develops the most careful version of this position, and it is genuinely resilient to the reply given to move one.

The concession is real. The reply is that the position succeeds only by locating structured content inside the divine mind. The point should not be put as though divine thinking must be discursive in the creaturely sense. The conceptualist explicitly denies that God reasons through logical truths one after another. The pressure is weaker and harder to evade: if logical truths are grounded in divine intellection, then divine intellection must contain determinate logical content. The Law of Identity requires determinacy of content; the Law of Non-Contradiction requires the distinction between a content and its negation; the Law of Excluded Middle requires an exhaustive contrast between a proposition and its negation. T does not enter because Excluded Middle is itself a temporal sequence. It enters through the asymmetric grounding and inferential roles the conceptualist needs: ground to grounded, premise to consequence, alternative-space to exhausted alternatives. These are not temporal episodes in a divine psychology. They are structural features of the content the conceptualist places in God.

Leftow [@leftow2012, chs. 10–12] is explicit that the divine modal activity is not temporally successive and does not involve distinguishable mental states. But if the content of that activity is genuinely modal (if it fixes the space of possibilities and the laws governing it) it must still be determinate, internally articulated, and capable of grounding asymmetric entailment relations. That is structure. Plantinga [@plantinga1980] entertains exactly this worry under the heading “the bootstrapping objection”: if God's nature grounds logic, and logic applies to God's nature, then the grounding relation runs in a circle. The standard conceptualist reply distinguishes the explanatory priority of God's nature from its logical priority, but the distinction requires logical apparatus to state, and the apparatus is what the account is trying to ground. The conceptualist account converges on the same structural conditions the argument names; the remaining disagreement is whether those conditions are best described as features of a divine mind or as features of structure as such.

*Third.* The Cartesian voluntarist makes logic the free output of divine will. On Descartes's letters to Mersenne [@descartes1630], the eternal truths (including the laws of logic and mathematics) are established by God as a king establishes laws in his kingdom. God could have decreed otherwise; the fact that God decreed these laws rather than others is what makes them necessary; and the modal force of the laws traces entirely to the divine will. Frankfurt [@frankfurt1977] reconstructs the view as genuinely coherent: a position on which God's omnipotence extends to the logical as well as the natural order. Curley [@curley1984] gives a more cautious defense, reading the Cartesian view as a limit position rather than a settled doctrine.

Voluntarism faces the deepest difficulty of the three: the act of decree appears to presuppose what it was meant to create. A temporal decree would involve succession, distinction, and persistence. Cartesian voluntarists can instead construe God's willing as eternal. The remaining objection is that free selection among alternative logics appears to presuppose determinate alternatives, identity, and consequence relations already available to the will; this yields a logical-priority problem without assuming a temporal divine psychology. The source of logic must already be inside logic to perform the act of sourcing. The objection is sharper than the parallel regress in move one, because voluntarism is committed to the contingency of the decreeing (God could have willed otherwise) and contingency is the mode of choice between alternatives. For there to be alternatives, there must be a space of distinct options; for a choice among them, an asymmetric dependence of outcome on selection; for the choice to hold, a chooser distinct from and stable across what is chosen. Voluntarism demands every structural condition the theory is trying to explain, in the very act of explaining it. This is why contemporary theism has largely abandoned the position: not because the motivation is wrong (the motivation is to protect divine omnipotence from external constraint) but because the machinery is self-defeating at a level even the conceptualist can see. Leftow [@leftow2012, ch. 4] devotes an entire chapter to showing why voluntarism cannot be the theist's fallback, precisely because it presupposes what it tries to ground. The present reply agrees with Leftow's diagnosis and presses the point one level further: the conditions voluntarism presupposes are T, S, and Φ, and once they are secured, no further appeal to divine will is needed to underwrite logical necessity.

A kindred deflationary move presses from outside theism entirely. Sober [@sober1993] argues, in a Humean spirit, that logical truths need no grounding at all: their status as truths is a matter of their formal character, not of any metaphysical relation to a ground. Sher's *Epistemic Friction* [@sher2016] develops a logical realism on which logic is objective but not grounded in any further entity; logical truths track formal features of reality the way mathematical truths track quantitative ones, and no rational author is required. The structural account agrees with Sober and Sher that no being is required to ground logic, and adds a constructive account of what does underwrite logical necessity: the structural roles. Where Sober stops at the formal character of logical truth and Sher stops at objective formal features of reality, the present account specifies which features those are and why they obtain necessarily. The convergence is on denying the theistic grounding; the divergence is on whether anything positive can be said about what logic describes. The structural account says yes, and says it is what the present book has been defending from [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1) on.

Two adjacent objections are addressed elsewhere. Divine simplicity as the doctrine that God is identical to the divine attributes (bearing directly on the conceptualist move) is [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1). Swinburne's case that the necessary ground must be a mind rather than a set of roles is [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4). The present section confines itself to the positive claim that logic requires a rational ground, and contests it on the three strategies available for what that ground could be.

*What the three moves show.* The three strategies receive different verdicts. Voluntarism faces the strongest internal difficulty, because an act of decree appears to presuppose the logical and modal alternatives it is meant to create. Presuppositionalism must explain how a necessarily rational Author grounds logic without merely describing that Author through logical predicates. The conceptualist view may coherently locate logical content in divine intellect, but then it becomes a rival metaphysical interpretation of the relation between logic and mind rather than a simple escape from structural constraints. The present account offers a non-theistic structural interpretation of logic; it does not establish by retorsion alone that no essence-prior or conceptualist account could be coherent. The remaining question is comparative: which account best explains the necessity and applicability of logic without adding an unearned grounding relation.

*The widened claim.* Pressed on logic, the presuppositionalist widens the target: the claim becomes not that logic requires a divine ground but that *intelligibility itself* does — that the very possibility of making sense of anything (logic, induction, the uniformity of nature, the fit between mind and world) presupposes God ([@vanTil1955]; [@bahnsen1998], whose 1985 debate with Stein ran the demand for logic, induction, and moral standards together). The widening looks like a strengthening. It is a category error, and naming the category dissolves it.

Intelligibility is not a substance that something must supply; it is a relation, the fit that obtains when a tracker converges on a structure already there. A text is intelligible to a reader who has acquired its language and opaque to one who has not, though the text is unchanged: what varies is not a quantity of intelligibility resident in the ink but the match between an acquired competence and an antecedent structure. The relation has two terms, and each is already accounted for. The objective term is structure — that there is something with determinate identity, distinction, and exclusion to be tracked at all — and that is what T, S, and Φ secure, the burden this chapter has already discharged. The subjective term is a competence that converges on the structure, acquired the way any tracking is acquired, through exposure and adjustment. Neither term, and so not the relation they compose, requires a further being to supply it.

The presuppositionalist's demand — *what grounds intelligibility?* — therefore mislocates its object. To ask what supplies the fit between a competence and a structure is to treat a relation as though it were a thing, on the model of asking what grants a key its fit to a lock: nothing grants it, the cut of the one matches the cut of the other, and the matching is not a third item in need of a donor. Once intelligibility is seen as the convergence of a tracker on a structure rather than a gift bestowed from above, the question that seemed to demand God as its answer turns out to have no place for an answerer.

The demand fails from the other side as well, once the relation is turned on the being the argument offers as its ground. To make sense of something is an achievement: a competence closing a gap, gathering a structure it did not already hold. The relation runs in a direction, from not-yet-tracking to tracking, and it presupposes a knower who lacked the structure before acquiring it. An omniscient being holds all structure already, so it has no gap to close and nothing it comes to track: nothing is intelligible *to* such a being, not through any deficiency but because *making sense of* names the work of a finite tracker meeting a structure it did not author. The argument has reached for the one being to whom the phenomenon it is built on cannot apply. The second reading of the phrase fares no better: if *to make sense of* the world were to *make* it, to author the structure rather than converge on it, that is voluntarism, and it collapses under the act of decree exactly as the third move showed. On the first reading there is nothing for an omniscient ground to make sense of; on the second the making already presupposes the structure it would produce. Intelligibility is left as nothing a divine being could supply.

The same dissolution handles the induction prong the presuppositionalist presses through Hume. That the future's resemblance to the past cannot be justified without circularity is a real problem, but a divine guarantor does not solve it: the belief that a sustaining God will keep nature uniform rests on exactly the inductive habit under examination, so the guarantor relocates the circle rather than closing it. T, S, and Φ provide conditions under which ordered inquiry and stable comparison are possible, but they do not entail that the contingent laws or regularities of nature remain uniform. The Humean problem of induction therefore survives the bare structural floor; a divine guarantor may not solve it without circularity, but the triad alone does not solve it either. The direction of support then runs opposite to the one the argument needs: we hold nature uniform because we meet it as uniform, not because anything announces its uniformity to us, so the regularity counts as evidence that the structure is all there is rather than as a trace of a guarantor standing behind it.

*The reliability rejoinder.* Grant that intelligibility is a tracker converging on structure — what makes the tracking *reliable*, apt to latch onto what is there rather than to misfire? The demand repeats the category error one level in. Reliability is not a further substance the relation must be given; it is the success-condition that individuates something *as* tracking. Tracking admits degrees of reliability: a competence can correlate with a structure while misfiring in some conditions. Reliability therefore requires an account of error rates, calibration, and the processes that sustain successful representation; it is not guaranteed by the definition of tracking alone. At the structural floor, though, the demand thins: whatever competence tracks T, S, and Φ at all already operates within them, as a key that opens the lock is already cut to it. The fallible work of exposure and adjustment is just the process by which non-converging candidates fall away; what the word “competence” picks out is what survives. Nor does the evolutionary debunker’s wedge — selection tracks fitness, not truth — find purchase here, for the structure tracked is not a contingent regularity from which fitness could come apart but the precondition of there being distinct representational states to select among at all: any competence operating on distinct states already operates within T, S, and Φ. The wedge bites on contingent first-order content, never on the structural floor.

*What converges.* The section closes on two prongs. The first, developed through the three moves, is that the structure logic describes is necessary and no theistic strategy has shown it to require a rational author. The second is that intelligibility — the broadened target to which the argument retreats once the first prong holds — is a learned relation to that structure, not a substance any being must provide. The first removes the need for a ground; the second removes the need for a giver. Together they block a quick inference from logic or intelligibility to God. The comparative question remains whether a theistic, realist, conventionalist, or structural account best explains logical necessity, induction, and cognitive reliability without circularity.

A final consideration, offered as illustration rather than argument: the case that logic requires a rational ground is itself made in logic, and even the logician's vocabulary is borrowed from the structure it evaluates. “Therefore” is *there + fore*, space and time fused; “necessarily” renders the Latin *ne + cedere*, not to withdraw, and withdrawal is a structured act: a succession of positions across a relational distance by something that persists. The etymology settles nothing; it only shows the structure surfacing in the very words built to describe it.

### 5.1.10 Moral Argument {#sec-5-1-10}

The moral argument reasons from the reality of objective moral facts to God as their necessary ground. It has proved resilient precisely because it leans on a premise few want to deny (that some things are genuinely right or wrong, independent of what anyone believes or desires) and asks what could underwrite it. It must be engaged where it actually pushes, not as a restatement of the ontological argument [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7) takes up: its force is axiological, not conceptual, and turns on the authority of obligation rather than the content of a concept.

The argument's contemporary forms tie moral obligation specifically to a personal will. Adams[@adams1999] identifies moral goodness with resemblance to God and obligation with God's commands; Evans[@evans2013] argues that obligations bear marks (authority, universal scope, inescapable bindingness) that only the commands of a personal, loving God adequately explain. Hare[@hare1996] presses the "moral gap" between the demand morality makes on us and our capacity to meet it, a gap divine assistance is needed to close. Craig[@craig2008] presses the argument in its most widely debated deductive form (if God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist; objective moral values and duties do exist; therefore God exists), the popular syllogism that fixes the argument's public profile, with all the philosophical weight resting on its first premise: that authority of the relevant kind requires a personal commander. Baggett and Walls[@baggettWalls2011; @baggettWalls2016] give the argument its strongest contemporary form, recasting it as an abduction rather than a deduction: theism is offered as the best explanation of the full moral landscape at once, its values, its obligations, its knowability, and the possibility of moral transformation, so that no single premise carries the inference and the cumulative fit is what is offered as evidence. Behind these stands Mavrodes's[@mavrodes1986] point that objective moral facts sit awkwardly, are "queer", in a world with no more than nature in it; and even Mackie[@mackie1982], no theist, allows that objective values, were there any, would fit more easily in a theistic universe than a naturalistic one. The shared structure is an inference to the best ground: moral facts are real and categorically binding; only a personal will supplies authority of that kind; therefore God.

Grant the realism in full. Moral facts are not projections, conventions, or sentiment got up as fact; that gratuitous cruelty is wrong is true, and true independently of any attitude taken toward it. Grant, too, that bindingness is the crux: an obligation that bound no one would not be an obligation, and a naturalism that reduces value to preference or fitness-tracking does struggle to recover the authority that genuine obligation carries. The argument's animating worry is legitimate, and the present account shares it rather than dissolving it.

*First.* The ground the argument seeks is real but mislocated. What the argument adds to that worry is a personal will to supply the authority, and the dependence of morality on such a will is exactly what the book contests. The ground of moral bindingness is located at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) in the structural constitution of persons and their standing toward one another, not in commands issued from outside that order; obligation is read off what persons are and how they stand to one another, not conferred by a will above them. If that identification holds, the argument's central premise (that objective morality depends for its existence on God) is false, with the ground already supplied structurally and no further person required to issue it.

This front must be drawn at the register Chapter 8 actually licenses. The argument of [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) proceeds by structural *identification*, not strict derivation: it exhibits where moral bindingness is seated, but does not derive the full content of obligation the way Chapter 2 derives modal status. A determined moral realist can decline the identification (holding that authority of the relevant kind still requires a commanding will, however well morality maps onto the structure of persons) and so keep the dependence premise alive. Taken alone, this front shifts the burden; it does not discharge it.

*Second.* The commanding will the argument names cannot be had for free. The argument's deeper trouble does not wait on Chapter 8. Grant, for the sake of the argument, that moral authority does require a personal ground: the ground the argument names still cannot supply it. The classical commanding will is typically described as atemporal, non-spatial, and immaterial. The revised [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7) result does not make such a being semantically empty by definition. The pressure is whether a timeless divine nature or will can ground directed obligations to distinct persons while preserving determinate authority and content. Ordinary commands are temporal acts. Divine-command theorists may instead ground obligation in God's eternal nature or standing will. That move avoids a temporal issuing event but still owes an account of the directed relation between commander, content, and obligated persons. Each is a condition of succession, relation, or persistence, and a ground precluded from time, space, and substance has not been shown able to supply any of them. Adams's resembling goodness, Evans's loving commander, Hare's assisting God each presuppose a personal agent doing personal things: willing, relating, sustaining. Pressed to name the will that obligates, the moral argument points at a ground whose standing to command is exactly what remains unexplained.

A defender might relax the ground to a personal agent that does instantiate the conditions: temporal, related, present to those it binds. Then the proposal departs from strict classical timelessness. It may still claim ultimacy, but it must explain how an agent participating in temporal and relational moral life grounds rather than merely exemplifies moral authority. The revision keeps a commander by giving up the commander's ultimacy.

The argument tracks something real. Moral facts are binding, and their bindingness is not self-standing: it is grounded. The mistake is the location: what grounds obligation is not a will behind the world but the structural constitution of persons within it ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)), the same inversion the book runs throughout, fixing on a genuine feature and mislocating its bearer. The doctrines this argument carries with it (divine-command theory as an account of where obligation is grounded, and Hare's moral gap) are taken up in their own right in the Excursus, where the structural account is in hand to reconstruct what survives once the existence argument falls.

The abductive form needs separate handling, since it rests not on the single commanding act the second front dismantles but on a comparative claim: that theism explains the moral landscape better than any rival. The comparison fails at both ends. On the theist's side, an explanation is only as good as the standing of its explanans, and the classical explanans enters the comparison owing the relation problem above: a ground precluded from time, space, and substance must account for the explanatory, sustaining, and commanding relations the abduction credits to it before its explanatory fit can be scored.

On the rival side, the inference is run against a strawman naturalism that reduces value to preference or fitness-tracking. The genuine rival is robust non-naturalist realism, worked out most fully by Wielenberg[@wielenberg2014]: objective moral facts as brute necessary truths standing in non-causal *making* relations to their base properties, requiring no commander and no reduction to preference. That account is the near-twin of the structural identification at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12), obligation seated in what persons are and how they stand to one another, and it blunts Mavrodes's queerness charge: necessary moral facts are a serious rival to divine-command accounts, but their normativity is not explained merely by analogy with necessary structural conditions. The non-naturalist still owes an account of authoritative reasons and their relation to natural persons.

Against that rival the abductive inference does not clear its comparative step, for the same reason the modal-grounding argument does not clear its own ([§5.1.8](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-8)): a personal ground is named as the best explanation only because the field of rivals was drawn to exclude the structural one.

*What is established.* The moral argument is right that objective morality is real and binding, and right that its bindingness must be grounded. It is wrong about the ground. Where Chapter 8's identification holds, obligation is seated in the structural constitution of persons rather than in a will above them ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)); and independently of that identification, the classical ground faces a substantive relation problem: its timeless nature or will must ground determinate obligations to distinct persons without relying on an unexplained command relation. What the argument sees (that morality is grounded) the structure supplies. What it added (that the ground is a divine will) names a being whose capacity to will and command is the very thing still owing an account.

### 5.1.11 Pascal's Wager {#sec-5-1-11}

Pascal's *Pensées*[@pascal1670] advances a prudential argument for theistic belief that has shaped the apologetic literature for three and a half centuries. The wager does not claim that the God of classical Christian theism exists, nor that the evidence weighs in favor of existence. It claims that, under uncertainty, belief is the rational bet: finite stakes are wagered against infinite expected return. Where the cosmological and ontological arguments engaged earlier in this cluster purport to establish a conclusion about what is the case, the wager purports only to settle a question about what to do under irresolvable uncertainty. Its appeal is that it appears to bypass the metaphysical disputes the other arguments inherit. The appearance is misleading: the wager does not bypass the metaphysics; it presupposes it, and what the presupposition invites and costs must be assessed on the wager's own decision-theoretic terms.

Contemporary reconstructions sharpen the wager's defended form. Jordan[@jordan2006] develops the canonical analytic treatment, treating the wager as a many-gods-robust decision under genuine option in the William James[@james1896] sense, and shows that the wager survives several classical objections when properly reconstructed: the principle of insufficient reason, the mixed-strategies dilemma developed by Hájek[@hajek2003], and the symmetric-payoff parodies. Lycan and Schlesinger[@lycanSchlesinger1989] press the dominance argument: granted any non-zero credence in the classical Christian God, no available strategy dominates belief. The load-bearing premise across these reconstructions is the same: *P*(God exists) > 0, where the God in question is the necessary-being God of classical Christian theism whose existence underwrites the infinite expected payoff.

*The modal smuggle.* The wager's prudential framing invites a modal reading it cannot pay for. Non-zero *objective chance* would require a genuine possibility, but Pascal's wager ordinarily uses epistemic credence. A rational agent may assign non-zero credence to a proposition that is in fact impossible because its modal status is unknown. Thus *P*(God exists) > 0 does not by itself entail metaphysical ◇(God exists). The wager therefore need not assert a metaphysical possibility premise; it needs a defensible epistemic credence. The God on whose existence the wager's infinite payoff depends (the God of classical Christian theism, omniscient and omnipotent and morally perfect across worlds) is a necessary being on the tradition's own commitment (Anselm, *Proslogion* II; Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I.2.3; Plantinga[@plantinga1974b]). The classical conception forecloses a contingent reading: *God exists* is therefore equivalent to □(God exists), with no contingent witness available. If metaphysical possibility of a necessarily existing God were independently established, S5 would yield necessary existence. The wager's epistemic credence does not establish that modal premise. The argument and its S5 defenses are carried at [§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), and the parallel line through the modal ontological argument's explicit possibility premise is closed at [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7). The wager's probability premise does not entail its metaphysical conclusion; it supports only a decision under uncertainty.

The wager resembles Plantinga's argument only if epistemic probability is conflated with metaphysical possibility. Kept distinct, the wager is a decision-theoretic argument under uncertainty, not a disguised S5 proof. Plantinga explicitly uses a metaphysical possibility premise and S5. Pascal uses credence and expected utility. Conflating the two would be an error; the wager must be assessed on decision-theoretic rather than modal-transfer grounds.

*The epistemic reading.* A defender might press that the wager's probability is epistemic, not metaphysical: Pascal is gambling under ignorance, not measuring credence over modal alternatives. This is the wager's standard interpretation, not a retreat. Decision theory routinely operates with epistemic credences under uncertainty. The harder problems are different: assigning coherent probabilities across rival religions and payoff schemes, handling infinite utilities, accounting for mixed strategies and finite costs, and determining whether belief is voluntarily controllable. The epistemic reading therefore preserves the wager while exposing it to the standard decision-theoretic objections.

*A further pressure.* The classical-Christian-God specification is not optional for the wager: it is what underwrites the infinite payoff. The payoff structure requires that the wagered-for being be such that its existence settles eternity in the manner the wager presupposes: omnipotent enough to deliver infinite reward, omniscient enough to recognize the wagered belief, morally engaged enough to honor it. A merely contingent god, or a god whose attributes fall short of the classical specification, does not deliver the payoff structure the wager needs. The many-gods objection presses this from one side: too many candidates fit the prudential frame, and the calculation cannot select between them. The present objection presses it from the other side: only the classical necessary-being God delivers the payoff at all.

*What closes.* The wager does not establish God's existence and should not be converted into an S5 derivation. As prudential reasoning, it depends on contestable epistemic credences, utility assignments, and a treatment of the many-gods problem. The classical-Christian specification supplies one payoff model but does not receive probability merely from being describable. The wager can remain a pragmatic recommendation for some agents under some credal states; it does not settle the rival-ultimate question. A second strand of the wager (Pascal's counsel that one may *cultivate* belief by acting as if, until assent follows) meets the account of the will at [§8.9](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9), which shows the will cannot install a conviction its field withholds; it is taken up where that result bears on inculpable nonbelief, in the divine-hiddenness entry (E.13). The strong claim that belief is uniquely rational does not survive without further decision-theoretic and theological premises.

## 5.2 Doctrines of the Divine Nature {#sec-5-2}

This cluster gathers the doctrines of the divine nature: the constructions built to keep the divine ground ultimate without regress, simple without composition, and independent of the structure it grounds. Divine simplicity ([§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1)) holds the ground free of all composition; the via negativa ([§5.2.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-2)) secures it by denial, saying only what it is not.

The question is the one the chapter presses throughout: can the doctrine hold its ground apart from structure without relying on structure to do so? The finding is again relocation rather than refutation. Each doctrine, in securing the ground's independence, reintroduces the very structural conditions it was meant to set the ground above.

### 5.2.1 Divine Simplicity {#sec-5-2-1}

Divine simplicity is the doctrine that God has no parts, not only no physical parts, but no metaphysical composition of any kind: no distinction between God and God's attributes, none between God's essence and God's existence. Where the other classical counter-moves contest how structure applies to God, simplicity denies that it applies at all.

It is not austerity for its own sake. It is meant to secure divine ultimacy by ruling out composition, dependence, and metaphysical parts in God: were God assembled from features more basic than itself, aseity would already be lost, for the more basic features would ground God rather than vice versa. The doctrine has two tightly linked expressions, simplicity proper and *actus purus* (pure act without potency), which classical theism treats as mutually entailing. Strict Thomistic simplicity takes both to their limit: *Deus est suum esse*, God's essence just *is* God's existence, without distinction.

The doctrine has a long history and a contested one. Augustine (*De Trinitate* VI) articulates an early form: God's attributes are identical to God's being. Maimonides (*Guide of the Perplexed* I.50–60) presses the most austere version: the divine attributes are equivocal with creaturely attributes, and positive predication of God is strictly impossible. Avicenna (*Metaphysics* VIII) develops the essence-existence identity later inherited by Aquinas. Aquinas (*ST* I.3–I.4) gives both doctrines full rigor and argues their mutual entailment. The doctrine was contested even within its home tradition: Duns Scotus [@dunsScotus1300] introduces the formal distinction as a middle ground, arguing that God's attributes are formally distinct though really identical, an internal concession that the strict reading generates problems.

Contemporary defenders: Dolezal's *God Without Parts* [@dolezal2011] defends strict simplicity; Brower [@brower2009] and Stump's *Aquinas* [@stump2003] refine it through truthmaker and phased-identity variants; Feser's *Aquinas* [@feser2009] defends the act/potency distinction as the metaphysical basis of simplicity; Kerr's *Aquinas's Way to God* [@kerr2015] reconstructs *esse* as the central Thomistic category; Pruss [@pruss2006] supplies contemporary PSR groundwork; Leftow's *God and Necessity* [@leftow2012] develops an alternative modal-theistic framework preserving key simplicity commitments; Rogers's *Perfect Being Theology* [@rogers2000] defends a contemporary Anselmian simplicity.

Against the doctrine: Plantinga's *Does God Have a Nature?* [@plantinga1980] presses the charge that strict simplicity either identifies God with a property (ontologically incoherent) or abandons the doctrine; Hughes's *On a Complex Theory of a Simple God* [@hughes1989] develops the analytic critique at length; Mann's "Divine Simplicity" [@mann1982] is sympathetic but catalogs the unresolved problems; Mullins's *The End of the Timeless God* [@mullins2016] presses the combination of simplicity and timelessness as internally inconsistent; Wolterstorff's "Divine Simplicity" [@wolterstorff1991] rejects the doctrine in favor of a richer divine psychology.

The structural account sits closest to the Plantinga–Mullins wing in finding a deep tension between strict simplicity and active divine predicates. Its narrower claim is not that every simplicity doctrine is immediately contradictory, but that any account on which a simple God grounds, donates, sustains, knows, or wills must explain how those relations acquire determinate content without the structural roles the account identifies.

Against the structural account, simplicity is the counter-move with the longest pedigree. The canonical line is run end-to-end at [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1), which defends Necessary Possibility and S5 invariance; Cartesian Certainty for change's bilateral witnesses is supplied at [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2); the necessary modal constraint, tying the possibility of change to T, S, and Φ, is established at [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4); that constraint is lifted to the unconditional Triconditional Necessity of the three Conditions at [§2.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-5); and those Conditions are identified with Nature through the Triconditional machinery at [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). Simplicity, in its strict form, denies the application of that whole structure to God.

The classical theist answers that a maximally ultimate being is precisely one that does not instantiate the structural roles: a being with no composition cannot be assembled from parts the way structured entities are. One coherent being lacking relational non-identity, causal persistence, and temporal succession is all the position requires.

Pressure turns on whether that one being is coherently specifiable. Nine questions take up the objection: one at the level of the commitment, eight across its forms. They test three connected matters: whether the divine subject can be distinctly specified, whether it can stand in a real relation to creation, and whether its predicates retain differentiated content. The replies test whether any form avoids dissolving into ∅ or reinstating the roles under a different name.

*First.* The commitment question asks what simplicity delivers beyond its negative specification. Simplicity names the absence of composition without naming the activity the doctrine performs with it. Negatively specified, the doctrine rules out parts, composition, potency, and any distinction between essence and existence. A position that did nothing beyond negation would be inert. Simplicity earns its place because the theist uses it to affirm: that God grounds creation, donates existence, sustains the created order, and is fully actualized without potency. Each operative verb is a positive predicate. *Ground* requires an asymmetric dependence relation and a distinction between grounder and grounded; *donate* requires directed source–recipient content, though not necessarily a temporal transition in the donor; *sustain* requires an enduring or counterfactually stable dependence relation; *fully actualized* must retain content beyond bare self-identity. These are thin role-level demands, not yet an identification with loaded physical Time, Space, and Substance. The doctrine is specified by negation and cashed out by positive structural operations. The remaining eight questions test whether any form of the doctrine can accommodate the affirmations the doctrine is used to make.

*Second.* The relational-extension form tests whether a being with no spatial extension can be a distinct existent. Strict Thomistic simplicity holds that God has no parts, no composition, no distinction between essence and existence. God is not assembled from features; God is God's features, wholly and undividedly. Structural categories (distinction, succession, persistence) apply to creatures, not to the ground of creatures.

The absence of spatial extension does not by itself prevent numerical distinctness: abstract objects, if admitted, supply an obvious countermodel. The sharper question is whether the simple being has enough determinate identity and relational content to be distinguished from creation and to ground it without composition. Pressed to this limit, the worry is whether the doctrine leaves in place the structural conditions under which a distinct existent can be picked out at all.

Even granting existence as a hypothesis, a simple being collapses the architecture required for causal power. For any being to be a causal agent (to ground, sustain, or relate to creation), it must be a distinct relatum capable of entering into relationships. Interaction requires a between. Simplicity removes the between. The result is a *Point-State* — a would-be existent contracted to a dimensionless point, with no extension across which anything could be held apart from anything else: no relational manifold to host distinct coordinates, no gap between divine will and divine act, no distinction between divine subject and object of knowledge. Without Space in its distinction-grounding role, no distinct relata; without distinct relata, Substance's interaction has nothing to connect. The advocate who strips all distinction performs one in the act of stripping: individuation requires exactly what absolute simplicity removes.

The classical theist has one reply left here: God's distinctness from creation is transcendent, not positional; numerical, not at a distance; God distinct as Being Itself rather than as one relatum standing off from another. Grant the reply for distinctness taken statically; it still cannot be purchased for the verbs the doctrine refuses to drop. To *ground*, *donate*, or *sustain* is more than merely to differ from the recipient: it requires determinate asymmetric dependence. Metaphysical grounding need not involve motion or transit across a spatial interval. The burden is therefore to explain the direction and content of the relation without introducing composition, not to supply a literal crossing. The move that rescues the static distinctness forfeits the active verbs, and those verbs were the doctrine's entire reason for asserting the distinctness to begin with.

*Third.* Brower's truthmaker simplicity and Stump's phased-identity simplicity refine non-compositional distinctness. Simplicity does not require God's properties be strictly identical in the strong Thomistic sense; it requires only that no composition grounds God. The properties may be distinct in some sense but not compositional; what is ruled out is metaphysical dependence, not distinctness as such.

The refinement concedes the structural point while relabeling the relation. If God's properties are distinct in some sense but non-composite in another, then some relational structure holds among them: a structure that distinguishes the properties while unifying them. That is exactly what relational non-identity within a unified manifold consists in. Space at the role-definition level does not require a unified whole be dissolved into its parts; it requires parts be distinct within the whole. Brower's truthmaker simplicity and Stump's phased-identity simplicity both concede distinct relata within a unified divine being, a description of a structurally unified substance with distinct aspects. The structural conditions the argument names are retained in the refinement; what changes is the vocabulary under which they are described.

*Fourth.* Dolezal's apophatic form pairs strict simplicity with the claim that creaturely concepts cannot fully articulate what it amounts to, and holds that structural categories do not apply to the uncreated ground. The categories of our thought (including the structural roles the argument invokes) apply to creatures, not to the uncreated ground. Simplicity is a truth affirmed of God even though the categories we use to describe God fall short; the structural objection applies a creaturely measure to a non-creaturely reality.

Apophatic simplicity makes the position immune to objection only at the cost of making it immune to assertion. If the structural categories do not apply to God, neither do the categories of existence, power, will, or ground, each of which the theist affirms. The apophatic move is selectively applied: negation is invoked against the argument's categories but suspended for the categories the tradition wants to preserve. Either the negation is global, in which case the doctrine says nothing about God at all, or it is selective, in which case its selectivity requires a justification apophaticism was meant to avoid. Selective apophaticism does work the doctrine needs done while exempting itself from the obligation to justify where the negation stops. The structural analysis does not apply a creaturely measure. It applies the measure any affirmation of existence requires.

*Fifth.* The *actus purus* form presses simplicity through its metaphysical architecture. God is pure act: the complete actualization of all perfections with no unrealized potential. Whatever has potency is partly not actual; whatever is pure act has no potency. God is therefore pure act and the unconditioned ground of everything partly actual.

Pure actuality generates its difficulty more specifically than the crude charge that “no potency” means “no power.” The Thomist is right to reject that formulation: potency in the act/potency scheme is not active power, and pure act is meant to be fully actual causal power rather than inertness. The problem is not active power as such. The problem is the transition from not-exercising to exercising, from no creaturely effect to creaturely effect, from source alone to source-related-to-recipient. If the effect is contingent, the exercise of power must be related to that effect in some determinate way; if the exercise is eternal and unchanged, the effect seems eternal with it; if the effect is not eternal, some relational asymmetry has entered the account.

Feser's refinement distinguishes pure act from static immobility: pure act is not absence of causal capacity but fully realized causal capacity, a being whose power is entirely actualized. The refinement sharpens the structural question rather than removing it. An act that genuinely produces, sustains, or donates being is an exercise of causal capacity. It requires determinate source–effect difference, asymmetric dependence, and a bearer of the causal role. Those thin requirements do not by themselves establish spatial extension, temporal succession, or physical substance; the stronger identification needs the independent arguments supplied elsewhere. *Sustains* is itself a maintenance relation: to sustain is to hold something in being across the relevant interval or dependence-structure. An atemporal pure act can be asserted; what remains missing is how it produces, sustains, or donates without the structured relation those predicates require.

What the Way–Possibility Convertibility ([§3.2](convergence.html#sec-3-2)) makes inescapable here is the way-side of the predicate. Pure act forecloses potency, and the Thomist can refuse the potency framing without contradiction: the act/potency scheme is internal Thomistic vocabulary, and *actus purus* declines the predicate on the Thomist's own terms.

The way-predicate is not declinable. The Thomist's own characterization of God as *ipsum esse subsistens* (subsistent being itself, a determinate manner-of-being rather than dependent or composed) is itself a *way* of being. To say God's mode of being is *subsistent rather than dependent*, *simple rather than composed*, *necessary rather than contingent* is to specify a way under each predicate (direction, difference, link). By the Convertibility, whatever bears a way bears the structural conditions a way decomposes into. The exit *actus purus* offers against potency is not available against way: the Thomist commits to God's way of being as part of the doctrine's positive content, and cannot then deny the structural conditions that way-talk presupposes.

Two Thomist replies deserve direct hearing. Dolezal's *God Without Parts* [@dolezal2011] apophatic move holds that *way* is creaturely vocabulary, predicated of God only analogically and not univocally, so the way-predicate does not carry its structural conditions across the analogy. The Fourth question above answers this in the general case: selective apophaticism cannot disqualify *way* while retaining *subsistent*, *simple*, *actus purus*, and *ipsum esse* as positive content. Either all the positive predicates the doctrine asserts of God fall under the apophatic disqualification (in which case the doctrine asserts nothing), or none of them do, in which case *way* stands with the rest. Brower's [@brower2009] and Stump's *Aquinas* [@stump2003] truthmaker-identity reply holds that one simple truthmaker can ground distinct predicates (*subsistent rather than dependent*, *simple rather than composed*) without those predicates introducing real distinctions in the truthmaker. The general form of that reply is met at the Seventh question below; the point that bears here is way-specific: as soon as the truthmaker is the condition under which *way of being* is correctly predicated, the truthmaker bears a way under the Convertibility, regardless of whether the multiplicity of senses is located on the creaturely-concepts side.

The same wedge applies to creation specifically. Classical theism reads creation as either a way *from* God (efficient donation outward, source-to-recipient) or a way *through* God (sustaining medium across which created being is held). Both readings require God to occupy a way-role: the former requires source-direction (T) and source/recipient distinction (S); the latter requires medium-as-carrier (Φ). The Convertibility forecloses both, because neither way-from nor way-through can be predicated of a being held outside the structural conditions ways decompose into. The doctrine cannot drop both readings, because dropping both abandons creation as a relation between God and creatures, which the doctrine is constructed to maintain.
