The underlying critique (that classical simplicity is in tension with creation as a real relation) is well-trodden ground: Mullins's *The End of the Timeless God* [@mullins2016] presses it as the modal-collapse argument; Schmid's "From Modal Collapse to Providential Collapse" [@schmid2022] sharpens the tension for atemporalist simplicity by showing that avoiding modal collapse forces providential collapse; Wolterstorff [@wolterstorff1991] rejects simplicity partly on the ground that it cannot accommodate God's responsive relation to creatures. The standard Thomist reply invokes the doctrine of mixed relations (real on the creature side, conceptual on the divine side, *ST* I.13.7) together with simultaneous causation (treated at [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3)); the atemporalist's further resource is the Stump–Kretzmann eternal-present account [@stumpKretzmann1981], whose ET-simultaneity is offered to dissolve the modal-collapse and timelessness tensions by denying the temporal sequence they presuppose; its eternal-present mechanism is handled at [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1), where the Boethian eternal present and ET-simultaneity are met directly.

The way-foreclosure framing isolates what these replies must still concede: even a relation merely conceptual *quoad nos* requires *some* way-role on the divine side to terminate the creaturely relation, and a pure terminus with no way-role at all is ∅ articulated in classical vocabulary rather than an alternative to it.

Feser's *Aquinas* [@feser2009] and subsequent work extends the *actus purus* defense through the Thomistic doctrine of the analogy of being (*analogia entis*): predicates like “ground,” “donate,” and “sustain” apply to God not univocally (importing creaturely conditions) nor equivocally (as mere homonyms) but analogically: in a mode proportioned to the divine being, tracking a real divine attribute without importing the full creaturely profile. This is a refined attempt to hold the positive predicates and the simplicity negations simultaneously: the analogy licenses the affirmations while the simplicity doctrine strips the structural conditions those affirmations normally presuppose.

The structural reply addresses the analogical mode directly. Analogical predication requires a real proportion grounded in something real about the divine subject: the predicate must track a real divine correlate that stands in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely counterpart. A feature that distinguishes God-sustaining from God-not-sustaining is a relational position, Space in its distinction-grounding role. To be the *source* rather than the *recipient* of sustaining is to occupy a directed role, Time in its ordering sense. To be the *medium* through which sustaining propagates is Substance's persistence role. The analogical mode does not eliminate these structural conditions; it reasserts them under a mode of predication that is itself a structural fact about the proportion between divine and creaturely attributes. The doctrine of analogy, taken seriously, presupposes the structural conditions it is designed to moderate. The same cluster recurs at [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3) (Feser's act/potency machinery under direct scrutiny) and [§5.2.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-2) (the analogical-apophatic complementarity); the structural question at each is whether an analogical-relational claim can be grounded without the structural conditions any relational claim presupposes.

*The eminent-containment retreat.* One form of the analogical reply is not yet exhausted. Pressed past predication to its ground, the classical theist may hold that the perfections are present in God not as ways God is (not as direction, difference, or link) but *eminently*: as the positive plenitude in which every perfection pre-exists in a higher mode than its creaturely realization (Aquinas, *ST* I.4.2). On this retreat God is neither a being among beings exhibiting the structural roles nor bare being, but positive fullness *containing* what creatures have in structured form, without the structure. The retreat concedes that *way*-talk carries the conditions the Convertibility names, and for that reason declines to predicate *way* of God at all: what is affirmed is content, not a way of being.

The Convertibility reaches the retreat through what positive content is. Content that is genuinely positive is determinate: it is thus and not otherwise, the fullness of being rather than its privation or limit. Determinacy is contrastive: to be the fullness rather than the privation is to exclude the privation, and a content that excluded nothing (compatible with every state, including its own absence) would not be content but an idle word (*omnis determinatio est negatio*, in its minimal logical form). To exclude is to stand in relational non-identity to what is excluded, and relational non-identity is Space in its distinction-grounding role, the same feature the analogical reply already conceded must distinguish God-sustaining from God-not-sustaining.

A defender may resist the step from determinacy to Space by pointing to abstracta: the number seven is fully determinate (seven and not eight) yet stands in no spatial relation, so determinacy alone seems not to force relational non-identity. The example is granted (the status of abstracta is treated in its own right at [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4) and conceded at [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7)), and it does not rescue the retreat. The contrastive determinacy of an abstract object describes what the structural conditions afford without grounding, donating, or sustaining anything; it is determinate the way a value is determinate, not the way an agent is. The eminent content the retreat needs is not inert in that way: it is the positive plenitude *from which* creation is grounded and sustained, and a determinacy that does grounding work distinguishes the source from what it grounds in the very act of grounding it. That distinction is relational non-identity in its concrete, distinction-grounding role, Space. The dilemma therefore re-presents one level up: either the eminent content is abstract-like, in which case it grounds nothing and the doctrine forfeits the creation, donation, and sustenance the retreat was invoked to preserve, or it does the grounding work, in which case its determinacy is the concrete contrastive determinacy that reinstates Space.

Eminent content is therefore not a *tertium quid* beside way-of-being and bare being. Either it is determinate, in which case it is contrastive and reinstates the structural condition under the name *eminence*; or it excludes nothing, in which case it is content-free and is ∅ after all. The *tertium quid* the retreat needs would have to be positive content that is neither contrastive nor empty, and there is no such option to occupy.

Before that premise is named, its reach is worth marking, because it is far narrower than the result it secures: it is load-bearing only here, against the eminent-containment retreat. Every form of the doctrine that keeps the active verbs (*ground*, *donate*, *sustain*) was already closed by the way-foreclosure, which needs no truthmaker premise at all; only the retreat that drops the verbs for pure content reaches this far, and only it forces the question of what then distinguishes that content from ∅. The closure rests on one premise worth making explicit: that what bears no feature discriminating it from ∅ is ∅, a discernibility principle for being. The classical theist's only coherent refusal is to hold that divine positive content is really distinct from the Null State while bearing no discernible differentiator from it, a primitive positivity distinct from nothing by no feature at all. That refusal is not free here, because [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) precludes the Null State on exactly this ground: a putative something with no feature to distinguish it from nothing is nothing described as if it were something. The eminent-containment retreat and the Null State stand or fall together; the doctrine cannot reject the principle for ∅ and keep it for God.

The principle is not a stipulation the argument helps itself to; it is the truthmaker demand the doctrine already honors. *God is not nothing* is either true in virtue of something on the divine side (a *fundamentum in re*, some feature answering to the distinction), or it is a distinction drawn in our concepts alone, with nothing in God answering to it. The seventh question below presses the first horn for the attribute-predicates: *good* and *omnipotent* are true of God only if they track something real about him. The existence-predicate is not exempt. If a *fundamentum* distinguishes God-existing from the Null State, that feature is a discriminating position (relational non-identity, Space in its distinction-grounding role), and the structural condition stands reinstated under the name *fundamentum*. If nothing answers to it, then nothing on the divine side makes *God is not nothing* true rather than false, and a distinction with no foundation in re is exactly the empty, merely-verbal distinction the tradition refuses when it insists the divine names are not synonyms.

So the primitive-positivity refusal is an exemption, and a local one: it asks that a single predication (*God is*, *God is not nothing*) be released from the truthmaker demand the doctrine accepts for everything else it says of God, and the release falls exactly where the doctrine needs it.

The exemption is neither free nor Thomist. A reader who rejects truthmaking outright can decline the demand; the classical theist, having already grounded the divine names in what is real about God, cannot withhold it for the one predication on which the simplicity of God and the reality of the Null State are made to part.

What stays genuinely open is one premise, and it is worth scoping exactly, because it is narrower than full truthmaker commitment. The closure needs no truthmakers for all truths, and none for negative or general truths, the contested precincts of truthmaker theory. It needs only that a single positive existential (*God is*, *God is not nothing*) be true in virtue of something on the divine side: that there be a difference in re between God-existing and the Null State.

Nor can the Thomist slip the demand by recasting this as a negative truth: *God is not nothing* read as the bare denial of a competitor, exempt the way negative and general truths are exempt. That recasting is foreclosed by the doctrine's own center: *Deus est suum esse*, God's essence is God's existence. On that thesis *God is* is made true by the divine *esse* itself, the most positive *fundamentum* the tradition recognizes, the act in virtue of which anything whatever exists; it is the one existential the doctrine can least afford to make costless. A theist who downgrades *God is* to an exempt negation has not reached for the negative-truth exemption but denied that God's essence is *esse*, which is to abandon simplicity at its root. That is the least controversial corner of the doctrine, and it is one the classical theist already occupies. Aseity is the claim that God's existence is grounded in God rather than in another; a theist who denies that *God is* has an ontological ground has not escaped the argument but abandoned aseity, the classical project's load-bearing commitment. So the closure holds as firmly as aseity, and no more firmly: which is as firmly as the doctrine needs, since aseity is not negotiable for the position under examination.

*Sixth.* The ipsum esse subsistens form holds that being itself precedes structural characterization. *Ipsum esse subsistens* (the sheer act of existing, prior to any structural characterization) is the version of the doctrine that goes deepest. God is not a being among beings but Being itself, the unconditioned ground in virtue of which beings are. T, S, and Φ are features of creatures, of beings that have existence. The source of that existence is not itself a being with structural features; it is the pure act of existing, which precedes every structural distinction. The stratification proposal makes this precise: created being exists within T, S, and Φ; uncreated being stands at a prior level; the two levels are related by the act of *esse*; God donates existence to creatures, and the donation is neither a structural event (which would place God in the structure) nor a non-event (which would leave the donation inexplicable). It is a transcendent act that stratifies being itself.

The stratification does not escape the structural conditions. It relocates them to the interface. For God to donate existence to creatures, there must be a relation between donor and recipient, and a relation is a structural fact. (The simultaneous-causation mechanism classical theism offers to explain this relation is [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3).) Donation is a causal relation connecting source to recipient across an ontological transition: distinction between donor and recipient (S), direction from source to product (T), structural persistence across which the donation runs (Φ). The Thomist who claims God's being is prior to structure must invoke structure to explain how that being relates to anything, which is to invoke structure to explain how what is supposedly prior to it grounds anything at all. Read charitably, the Thomist's deepest insight (that being is not a property added to an essence but the fundamental act making anything real) is precisely what the structural picture affirms. The disagreement is about whether that act is identical to the structural conditions or prior to them. The above establishes that the “prior to” reading is either vacuous or covertly structural.

*Seventh.* The multiple-descriptions form tests whether a strictly simple being can ground distinct true predicates. Strict simplicity holds that God has no real distinctions: God's goodness, power, and knowledge are not separate properties but identical with God's simple essence. The multiplicity is in our creaturely concepts, not in God.

This generates a dilemma the doctrine cannot discharge. If “God is good” and “God is omnipotent” describe genuinely distinct divine attributes, then the attributes are distinct, and distinction is composition. If they are not descriptions of genuinely distinct attributes (if both sentences describe the same simple fact), then they are informationally equivalent: swapping them out changes nothing, and the divine names the tradition treats as distinct turn out to be synonyms. The classical response (the multiplicity is in our concepts, not in God) does not close the gap. Even if the multiplicity is on the concept side, those concepts must be tracking something real about God to be true of him. “God is good” is true in virtue of something. If that something is numerically identical to what makes “God is omnipotent” true, the truthmaker-identity defender [@brower2009; @stump2003] replies that one simple truthmaker can ground distinct predicates the way one Venus grounds both “morning star” and “evening star”: same referent, distinct senses. The reply preserves distinct content only as long as the senses do no metaphysical work. As soon as “good” and “omnipotent” require even minimally different aspects of the divine essence to be the conditions under which the predicates apply correctly rather than incorrectly (as they must, on pain of becoming synonyms), those aspects are real features the predicates discriminate among. Discrimination among real features within one being is what relational non-identity within a unified manifold consists in.

The dilemma re-presents at the level of aspects: either the aspects collapse and the predicates are synonyms whose multiplicity is unprincipled, or the aspects are real and strict simplicity has conceded the structural condition under the name “aspect.” The doctrine of analogy ([§5.2.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-2)) addresses the linguistic question of how predicates apply; this question precedes it: what the predicates must track if they are to have multiple applications at all. A being of which only one thing can be truly said (because all descriptions collapse into one simple identical fact) is not a being the theological tradition has described. It is a being that exhausts itself in a single predicate the tradition has not been able to name.

*Eighth.* The softenings (Leftow, Scotus) preserve assertability by conceding enough structure to make the doctrine statable. A kindred softening is Leftow's [@leftow2012] divine-modality framework, which preserves key simplicity commitments while allowing some distinctions within God: specifically, between God's nature and God's will. The softer version does the work kindred deflations always do: it concedes enough structure within the divine being to make the being assertable, and the conceded structure is what the argument identifies as T, S, and Φ at the appropriate level. The line is independent of the apophatic reading's fate: grounding modality in divine nature and will places necessary-possibility-of-change inside God, which Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)) identifies with T, S, and Φ. Scotus's formal distinction, anticipating the contemporary softenings by seven centuries, makes the concession inside the Catholic tradition itself. Open-theist softenings (Hasker, Sanders) concede still more (temporal duration, genuine response, real relation to creatures) and concede the structural commitments most explicitly. The softenings rescue assertability at the cost of simplicity: the doctrine that remains is a structural doctrine with the word *simplicity* still on the label.

*Ninth.* The essence/energies form is the Eastern counterpart to the softenings, and it concedes the structural point more openly than any other while most insisting it has not. Gregory Palamas (*Triads* III.2), systematizing the hesychast tradition, distinguishes within God the imparticipable essence (*ousia*, utterly unknowable, beyond participation) from the uncreated energies (*energeiai*), the divine operations in which creatures genuinely participate: the deifying grace and the light of Tabor through which theosis occurs. The distinction is held to be real, *in re* and not merely in our concepts, yet to introduce no composition: the energies are God wholly in act, not parts of God, so simplicity is claimed to stand. Lossky's *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church* [@lossky1957] and Bradshaw's *Aristotle East and West* [@bradshaw2004] develop the position as the one account securing both divine transcendence (the essence withdraws absolutely) and real communion (the energies are genuinely God and genuinely shared), the pair strict Western simplicity is pressed on at the Fourth and Fifth questions. Taken at its strongest, it is the most direct rival to the structural account in the neighborhood, because alone among the forms it does not deny distinction in God: it affirms one and asks to keep simplicity anyway.

That affirmation is where the form supplies the structural conditions rather than evading them. The distinction between essence and energies is either real or not. If it is merely nominal (a distinction in our mode of access, essence-as-hidden against energies-as-revealed), it collapses into the strict simplicity of the Third and Fourth questions and inherits their verdict, at a cost Palamas cannot pay: theosis becomes participation in the bare essence, which the doctrine exists to deny. If the distinction is real, then God internally carries the inventory the argument names: a relational non-identity between essence and energies (S), a directed procession from essence as source to the energies as its uncreated activity (T in its ordering sense, directed origin without clock-time), and a participation across which the energies are conveyed to creatures (Φ, the carrier-role of an interval something crosses). A real distinction held in God, with a directed origin and a participable activity, is structure under the name *energies*.

The defender answers that this is a distinction *sui generis*: neither real as between two things nor merely logical, but the Palamite middle. That middle is the formal distinction of the Eighth question pressed one tradition over: Scotus's formal distinction and the essence/energies distinction are the same concession made in two tongues, and the structural conditions never required separability; a real but inseparable distinction, with a directed order and a carried activity, is the paradigm of an articulated structure rather than an exemption from one.

The plurality of the energies presses the point a second time, more bluntly. The energies are many (wisdom, power, foreknowledge, providence, deifying grace) and each is held to be uncreated. Either they depend asymmetrically on the essence, which is a directed dependence-order within the divine (T) and an internal articulation simplicity was meant to exclude, or they are co-primitive, in which case the uncreated is an irreducible manifold (S) and the unity that secured aseity is already surrendered. The doctrine multiplies the uncreated; the argument has only to register the multiplication. Read at its most careful, the essence/energies distinction does not bypass the structural conditions classical simplicity strips from divine being: it is the form that supplies them itself, uncreated, and names the supply *energies*.

A being denied every determinate distinction, dependence direction, and stable bearing role could not support simplicity's positive predicates. Mere lack of spatial extension or temporal succession, however, does not establish that stronger absence.

*What converges.* The nine questions survey the principal defenses considered here, and each returns to a common burden: the doctrine is specified by negation and cashed out by positive structural operations, so that strict identity secures at most a static distinctness that leaves the doctrine's active verbs without relational content; non-compositional distinctness retains the structural conditions under a different label; selective apophaticism does work it exempts itself from justifying; pure act still owes an account of the transition from source alone to source-related-to-recipient; *ipsum esse subsistens* relocates structure to the donation interface; multiple true descriptions of a strictly simple being collapse into informational equivalence or reinstate real distinction; the softenings concede the structural commitments explicitly; and the essence/energies distinction either collapses into the strict simplicity it meant to refine or, taken as real, supplies the structural conditions itself under the name *energies*.

All the ways necessary for possibility are held in place by the structural conditions classical theism strips from divine being. The doctrine asks the reader to grant every condition possibility requires while denying every one of them to the being possibility was supposed to terminate in.

What the doctrine calls simplicity may preserve a minimal structural floor whenever it retains determinate active predicates or real relations to creation. A defender may instead posit an essence-prior or apophatic ground; that move is not answered by merely repeating the floor, but owes an account of how the proposed ground and its relation to creatures are determinately specified. The chapter's conclusion is therefore a burden: strict simplicity does not by itself deliver a structure-free ground, and its strongest versions must discharge the relation and predication problems developed here.

Sibling theistic counter-constructions: Rasmussen's Limits-plus-Isomorphism derivation ([§5.1.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-1)), Swinburne's probabilistic simplicity ([§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4)), and the PSR-demand variant ([§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)). The downstream severance this defeat produces for classical predication (how the attributes come apart once simplicity no longer holds them together as one act) is [§6.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2).

### 5.2.2 Via Negativa {#sec-5-2-2}

The *via negativa* (the "negative way" of approaching God by denying predicates) is among the oldest theistic responses to the structural pressure [§3.5](convergence.html#sec-3-5) makes general. Pseudo-Dionysian unknowing (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1), Maimonidean predicate-denial (*Guide of the Perplexed* I.50–60) [@seeskin2000; @stern2013], and the later apophatic tradition (Eckhart, *Sermons*) [@marion1991; @turner1995; @davies2008] all approach God by stripping predicates away until what remains is supposed to exceed every structural category. Contemporary reconstructions [@sells1994; @turner1995] argue that apophatic discourse does not merely deny predicates but performs a linguistic self-subversion that transcends the predicate/denial framework altogether.

The general point has already been pressed at [§3.5](convergence.html#sec-3-5): the act of negating the structural conditions instantiates them in the very performance of the negation. The apophatic application brings the abstract pressure to ground. An apophatic move that subtracts time from divine being uses time to make the move, distinguishes what is subtracted from what remains, and persists as a negating act. The successive negation of T, S, Φ (Pseudo-Dionysius's ladder of unknowing, Maimonides's series of attribute-denials, Eckhart's *abyss beyond God*) does not reach a standpoint outside structure; it traces structure's contour from the inside, marking each condition by the act that tries to remove it.

The contemporary self-subversion reading marks a necessary distinction. Sells's *Mystical Languages of Unsaying* [@sells1994] and Turner's *Darkness of God* [@turner1995] argue that the apophatic move is not a simple negative proposition but a recursive undoing of its own enunciation. Granted in full: the practice of self-subversion is an activity unfolding through succession, distinction, and a continuing practitioner. That establishes an act-side structural fact. It does not by itself establish that the intended referent of apophatic discourse is structured, because the apophatic theorist may deny that the discourse represents a determinate object at all.

*A parallel front: the immutable-thinker dilemma.* The apophatic discipline pressures classical theism from one direction: every act of negation instantiates what it negates. A parallel pressure runs along the divine attribute of immutability itself. The classical-theistic God is, on the standard view (Aquinas, *ST* I.9; Anselm, *Proslogion* 18–22), immutable, atemporal, and omniscient.

The three attributes pull against one another when the question is whether God thinks. Either divine knowledge involves successive cognitive episodes, or it is one timeless act. The first option conflicts with strict immutability. The second is the classical answer and cannot be dismissed merely by assuming that every instance of thought must be episodic.

The classical responses to this horn, Boethian eternity (*Consolation of Philosophy* V.6); the Stump and Kretzmann ET-simultaneity reconstruction (a relation of co-presence between eternity and time without temporal succession on the divine side) [@stumpKretzmann1981]; Leftow's *Time and Eternity* [@leftow1991]; Helm's *Eternal God* [@helm1988], all attempt to dissolve the succession by relocating divine cognition outside time. The relocations preserve immutability by separating the mode of divine knowing from creaturely succession. They face a burden of explaining how one timeless act bears differentiated, tensed, and contingent content, but the proposal is not closed simply by redescribing that mode as non-successive.

If God has no cognitive state or relation at all, omniscience is lost. But dispositional and non-occurrent models of knowledge show that knowing need not consist in a stream of episodes. The live issue is what positive cognitive relation remains and whether it can distinguish its contents.

The Thomistic *actus purus* names fully actual actuality without potency rather than activity-as-transition; on that strongest reading ([§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1) develops the eternal-present and actuality-potentiality discipline; [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1) the classical divine simplicity case), the conditions [§3.5](convergence.html#sec-3-5) establishes are instantiated not in the *mode* of divine cognition (which is unitary act, not succession) but in the *content* divine cognition cognizes. 'Eternal knowledge' (Aquinas, *ST* I.14) is content-bearing: omniscience predicates determinate content over articulated objects (S-distinguishability); divine knowing of what-is-the-case inherits the temporal articulation of what-is-the-case (T at the level of what is known); the unity of the eternal act sustains its content (Φ as the structural carrying of the act, not the duration of a process).

Nor does recasting divine omniscience as second-personal knowledge (acquaintance with persons rather than grasp of propositions) lift the result clear of the conditions: the persons known are themselves distinct from one another and from their knower (S) and articulated across the times of their lives (T), so personal knowing bears determinate content no less than propositional knowing, and the content it bears carries the structure the relocation of mode was meant to escape. The Aristotelian and Thomistic frameworks (*Metaphysics* Λ 1072b14–30; *ST* I.3) shift where T, S, and Φ are instantiated; they do not extract divine cognition from the structural conditions any cognition's content requires. The classical-theistic account therefore faces a mode–content tension rather than a deductively closed dilemma: succession in the divine mode threatens immutability, while a timeless unitary mode owes an account of differentiated and temporally articulated content.

Feser's *Aquinas* [@feser2009] and *Five Proofs* [@feser2017] develop the most sophisticated contemporary integration of the apophatic and analogical modes: apophasis disciplines the excess of positive predication, and the analogy of being (*analogia entis*) supplies the positive content that apophasis alone cannot provide. On Feser's reading, "God is not composite" (apophasis) pairs with "God is subsistent being itself" (analogy), the two modes functioning as complementary faces of a single theological discipline.

The structural reply tracks both poles. The apophatic pole has been addressed above: every act of negation instantiates T, S, and Φ in the performance. The analogical pole is addressed in the engagement with the analogia entis at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1): analogical predication requires a real proportion grounded in something real about the divine subject: the predicates must track a real divine correlate that stands in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely counterpart, and such a correlate must at least support determinate difference, direction, and stable bearing. Whether those roles warrant the stronger labels Space, Time, and Substance is a further step rather than a consequence of analogy alone.

The complementarity places structural conditions on the act side and a determinate-content burden on the object side. It does not by itself prove that the apophatic referent instantiates the same structure as the discourse used to approach it.

*What converges.* The chapter's stance on the *via negativa* is disciplined rather than eliminative. The apophatic tradition tracks the inadequacy of univocal projection from creaturely concepts to divine being. Its enacted negations are structurally conditioned, but that act-side fact does not settle whether apophatic discourse succeeds in referring beyond determinate predication. The remaining issue is therefore not refuted by retorsion; it is a burden of apophatic semantics and theology. The general structural result sets the terms of that burden, while the religious and existential significance of the apophatic remainder is carried forward to [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3).

## 5.3 Non-Classical Ultimates {#sec-5-3}

This cluster gathers the accounts of the ultimate that are not classically theistic but make the same bid against structure: Spinozist pantheism ([§5.3.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-1)), Neoplatonism ([§5.3.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-2)), process theology ([§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3)), and Madhyamaka emptiness ([§5.3.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-4)). Each names or reconceives ultimacy—one infinite substance, the One beyond being, creative process, or emptiness. Some place the ultimate prior to familiar structure; others identify ultimacy with an immanent or dependent order rather than trying to transcend it.

The single question carries over: can the account reach its ultimate without leaning on the structure it was meant to stand free of? The finding is relocation rather than refutation. The candidates divide: articulated priority claims incur determinate-role burdens; immanent and process accounts may be compatible with the structural floor while revising ultimacy; strict apophatic and anti-thesis positions leave an open semantic or dialectical seam.

### 5.3.1 Spinozist Pantheism {#sec-5-3-1}

Spinoza's *Ethics* (Part I) identifies God with Substance: the single, infinite, necessarily existing reality of which all finite things are modes. Spinoza's God is not a person standing outside Nature but the totality of what is, expressed under the attributes of thought and extension (and infinitely many other attributes we do not access). On this view, God is the one necessary substance expressed through attributes and modes. That makes Spinozism a close comparison for the book's necessary structural ground, but not an automatic identification with it.

The Spinozist position is the non-classical counter-construction closest to the argument's own commitments. Unlike the classical theist, the Spinozist does not place God beyond Nature. The Spinozist can therefore regard T, S, and Φ as necessary features of the one substance's modal order. This is compatibility, not identity: Spinoza's attribute theory, necessitarian derivation of modes, and parallelism go beyond the book's structural result.

The alliance should be scoped, though. Spinoza's attributes are thought and extension expressed co-equally (the order and connection of ideas the same as the order and connection of things) whereas T, S, and Φ make Physicality fundamental and derive mind downstream, as recursive structural depth yields phenomenal interiority (Chapter 8). That downstream derivation of mind is a commitment this account owes rather than a result it can claim here: the defensive case that experience requires no non-structural ingredient is made at [§4.3.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-1), and the positive account of how structural depth yields interiority is earned, not assumed, in Chapters 7–8.

On the immanence-and-necessity axis the convergence is genuine; on the attribute taxonomy the present account is a physicalist necessitarian, not a parallel-attribute substance monist, and the parallelism that is Spinoza's third distinctive demand is precisely what it does not inherit.

*The half-necessitarian pressure.* A sharper Spinozist challenge presses not the identification but the prior consistency of the necessity verdict. If the engine behind the argument (the derivation in §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7 that closes the necessity of T, S, and Φ) carries any modal force, Spinoza's own reasoning suggests it should close modal space at the level of the modes as well.

Spinoza holds that finite modes follow from infinite Substance with the same logical necessity as theorems follow from axioms; contingency, on his view, is an epistemic effect of partial perspective, not a structural feature of reality. A half-necessitarian reading (necessary structure, contingent particular configurations) appears to split what Spinoza holds together.

This is not a worry read off the primary text alone: Melamed (*Spinoza's Metaphysics* [@melamed2013]), the most careful contemporary reconstructor of Spinoza's substance monism, defends the strict-necessitarian Spinoza against the moderate readings that would soften the modal claim, holding that on Spinoza's system there is no genuine contingency anywhere, the finite modes included, and that the appearance of contingency is wholly an artifact of inadequate ideas. The challenge is therefore pressed in its strongest current form: if the argument's modal engine carries the force claimed for it, the most defensible reading of Spinoza says it should leave no contingency standing at the level of the particular configurations either.

The reply is that the argument's modal engine is not a rationalist PSR that cascades from necessary ground to necessary consequence. It is a more confined demonstration: that T, S, and Φ are conditions on any concrete existent, derived from the incoherence of ∅ (the maximally undifferentiated configuration in which none of the conditions obtains), not from a principle requiring that whatever follows from the ground must follow necessarily. The modal PSR is confined at [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3) to the existence of contingents as a class, and the necessity claim is located at the structural level alone by [§2.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-8).

What is necessary is that there be a reality satisfying T, S, and Φ; what particular reality satisfies them is not determined by the necessity of the conditions.

The half-necessitarian position is therefore stable: the necessity runs to the conditions, not to the configurations meeting them. Spinoza's deeper necessitarianism requires a further principle (that the specific attributes and modes are uniquely determined by Substance) that the present argument does not need and does not accept.

The argument grants the Spinozist's structural commitment. What it contests is the identification. *Deus sive Natura* (God-or-Nature: Spinoza's formula identifying the two) is offered as a term-substitution. If "God" is just another name for the necessary ground, the substitution is harmless and the disagreement is verbal.

But the historical theological work the term *God* is asked to do (providing an object of worship, a source of moral obligation, a being to whom prayer is addressed, a guarantor of cosmic justice) does not transfer to the structural ground. The structural ground is not a being to whom one prays, a moral agent, or a loving person.

*What is established.* The Spinozist who accepts this pares the divine vocabulary down to something closer to reverence for what is. That position is coherent and may be theologically valuable; it is not what the analytic theology literature means by classical or personal theism. The argument's verdict is that Spinozism avoids the specific burden of locating God beyond structure because it identifies divinity with immanent Nature. The cost is the abandonment of most of what the term *God* was historically asked to deliver.

### 5.3.2 Neoplatonism {#sec-5-3-2}

Plotinus (*Enneads* [@plotinus270]) and the Neoplatonic tradition place the ultimate ground beyond being itself. The One (τὸ Ἕν) is not a being among beings, not even the supreme being; it is the source from which being emanates, lying beyond all predication, including the predicates of existence and unity in the strict sense. Plotinus is willing to push apophasis (the via negativa: approaching the divine by denying predicates rather than affirming them) past where classical theism stops. Where Aquinas's God is being-itself (*ipsum esse*), Plotinus's One is prior to being and to *esse* alike.

The position relocates the challenge rather than escaping it. If the One is the source from which Reality emanates, the account posits an ordering or dependence relation between source and derivative. Plotinian emanation is not ordinarily a temporal process, so succession cannot simply be assumed. The sharper burden concerns determinate sourcehood, derivative difference, and asymmetric dependence: how these obtain without turning the One into one relatum among others.

Nor does the henological motive for positing the One (that a manifold of conditions must derive from a prior unity to be one structure rather than a heap) find purchase here: T, S, and Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) are not an aggregate awaiting an external unifier but one Nature, identical under the Triconditional Identity ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)), so the unity the One is invoked to supply is already internal to the structural ground.

The same analysis covers the inward arm of the Neoplatonic cycle. The reply to this point runs on procession (the outward emanation from the One) but the reversion by which all things turn back toward their source fares no better: reversion likewise expresses an ordered dependence of the derived upon its source, not necessarily a clock-time journey. It requires intelligible difference and direction, while the Neoplatonist owes an account of how those roles apply analogically without compromising the One's priority.

Plotinus is alert to the difficulty, and the difficulty has able contemporary defenders, so the apophatic reply must be taken at full strength. Gerson (*Plotinus* [@gerson1994]) reconstructs the language of emanation as systematically analogical rather than literally predicative, and Perl (*Thinking Being* [@perl2014]) reads the One not as a further being standing behind beings but as the sheer intelligible presence in which beings consist, so that talk of a source names a relation of dependence internal to appearing rather than a process undergone by some super-entity.

The *Enneads* insist that the language of emanation, derivation, and procession is improper: that nothing can really be said about the One, including that it is the source of anything. The strategy of strict apophasis preserves the One's transcendence by withdrawing every predicate, including the predicate of being a ground.

The consequence should be stated with care. If the One is not asserted to stand in a determinate grounding relation, then the present argument has no object-level ground claim to refute. It can register that the philosophical practice of unsaying is structurally enacted, but that act-side point does not establish the One's structural character. If a Neoplatonist instead retains determinate claims of emanation, sourcehood, or dependence, those claims incur the grounding-role burden developed in this chapter. The engagement therefore yields a fork: apophatic silence leaves a theological or contemplative stance outside this chapter's positive grounding claims; articulated emanation enters the dialectic and must explain its relation.

The contemporary readings do not escape this. Analogical predication is still predication: an analogy holds between two terms in a respect, and to sustain it is to deploy distinction and relation, the very conditions at issue. And Perl's immanentist reconstruction concedes the point rather than evading it, for a presence in which beings consist, a dependence internal to appearing, just is a structural-dependence relation described from the inside, T, S, and Φ under another name, not a way past them.

*What closes.* The chapter closes only the articulated priority claim: a One described as emanating, grounding, or standing in determinate dependence relations incurs the structural burden of those relations. Strict apophatic silence is not thereby contradicted; it declines to supply the kind of ground claim this chapter adjudicates. The remaining disagreement is whether such silence can support the explanatory work Neoplatonism often asks of the One.

### 5.3.3 Process Theology {#sec-5-3-3}

Process theology, developed by Charles Hartshorne (*The Divine Relativity* [@hartshorne1948]; *A Natural Theology for Our Time* [@hartshorne1967]) from Whitehead's metaphysics in *Process and Reality* [@whitehead1929], abandons the classical attributes in favor of a God who is temporal, related, and changing. Hartshorne's central technical move is dipolar theism: God has two natures, a primordial nature that grasps the eternal possibilities and a consequent nature that grows with the world's becoming. Divine perfection is reconceived. Omniscience is knowledge of all that has become, not of what will be (which is genuinely indeterminate). Omnipotence is the maximal persuasive power compatible with creaturely freedom, not coercive control. Eternity is everlastingness within time, not timelessness outside it.

John Cobb and David Griffin's *Process Theology: An Introductory Exposition* [@cobbGriffin1976] gives the tradition its most influential systematic statement, and the position has been extended by Marjorie Suchocki (*God–Christ–Church* [@suchocki1982]; *The End of Evil* [@suchocki1988]), Joseph Bracken (*The Triune Symbol* [@bracken1985]; *Society and Spirit* [@bracken1991]) on social-trinitarian process theism, Roland Faber (*God as Poet of the World* [@faber2008]) on theopoetics, and Thomas Jay Oord (*The Uncontrolling Love of God* [@oord2015]) on essential kenosis.

The position's significance for the present argument is that it is the theistic family closest to the present account: both reject the classical attributes of timelessness, immutability, simplicity, and impassibility; both insist on the reality of time, change, and relation as features any adequate metaphysics must accommodate.

Where they part is over personhood and grounding. The process theist holds that the supreme exemplification of process is itself a person (the divine consequent nature is conscious, loving, and responsive) and that this person is the necessary ground of the world's becoming. The present argument is silent on the first claim and supplies a limited structural challenge to the second. Two distinct questions need separating, and each requires a distinct reply.

The first question is whether, within Nature, there exists a maximally inclusive person who experiences every event and to whom every event matters. On this the present argument is silent. It establishes Nature's necessary features; it does not settle which configurations within Nature actually obtain.

The choice between a process-theistic Nature (with a maximally inclusive divine person) and a non-process-theistic Nature (without) is downstream of what the argument settles, and turns on substantive empirical, phenomenological, and theological considerations rather than structural ones.

The phenomenology of religious experience, the problem of evil and theodicy, the coherence of divine consequent-nature consciousness, the question whether anything in nature exhibits the universal-prehension structure Whitehead's metaphysics requires (prehension being Whitehead's technical term for the non-cognitive grasping by which each occasion of experience takes up its predecessors): these are the considerations that bear on the first question, and the present account does not adjudicate them.

Hartshorne's argument from divine relativity, Cobb and Griffin's case for the religious adequacy of process theism, Suchocki's development of the eschatological consequent nature can stand or fall on their own terms. The present account neither requires nor forbids them.

The second question is whether such a being could be what classical theism wanted God to be: the necessary ground of T, S, and Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) rather than a configuration within them. On this the present argument is not silent, but its conclusion is limited: a process-theistic God clearly realizes temporal, relational, and active roles; whether those roles preclude every sense of divine ultimacy depends on the further theory of grounding and aseity the process theist offers.

Hartshorne's dipolar theism is the test case. The primordial nature, on Hartshorne's account, grasps the eternal possibilities timelessly; the consequent nature grows with the world's becoming. The question is which nature is supposed to ground the world's structural conditions.

If the primordial nature grounds them, the process theologian must explain how an abstract pole that orders possibilities grounds concrete becoming; this does not by itself collapse into classical theism. If the consequent nature grounds them, its growth with the world raises a circularity or mutual-dependence concern, though a process theorist may explicitly reject one-way classical grounding.

Cobb and Griffin's reply [@cobbGriffin1976, ch. 2] is that the dipolar God is the ground of the *order* of becoming rather than of the structural conditions of becoming, but the distinction does not save the position. Order presupposes the structural conditions, and a God who grounds order while presupposing the conditions is not the necessary ground the classical project required.

The dilemma tightens into a single result, one the attribute analyses of Chapter 6 rest on rather than re-derive. What makes the two poles *poles of one God*, on Hartshorne's own account, is a relation between them: the consequent nature prehends, includes, and grows from the primordial nature, and the primordial nature is the abstract ground the consequent nature concretely actualizes.

That relation is not static co-instantiation but a directed dependence: grounding and prehension run from the primordial ordering of possibilities to the consequent nature's concrete inclusion of the world.

The pole relation requires determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer that unifies the poles. These are the book's thin structural roles. Identifying them with loaded spatial interval, temporal succession, and physical substance requires further argument, but dipolar theism plainly does not describe a wholly structureless ultimate.

The same role-floor applies to the dipolar reconception of perfection as responsiveness. Perfect inclusion of and affectedness by the world require determinate receptivity and relation. This locates the divine consequent nature within an articulated process, but it does not by itself settle whether that process can be metaphysically fundamental.

Hartshorne's God avoids the classical tensions of timeless simplicity by instantiating the structural roles at both poles and in their relation. The remaining question is whether such instantiation makes God merely an inhabitant or instead a necessary, co-constitutive feature of the process order. This result is deployed attribute by attribute across Chapter 6: each section names the local form the pole-relation takes for its predicate and refers the structural verdict back here.

The second question is taken up at length in Chapter 6. The framework-invariant point is established at [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1): a temporally embedded, causally extended, relationally constituted deity instantiates the structural conditions and therefore owes an account of whether its relation to them is dependence, identity, or co-constitution. It is closed as a binding cost at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) (Horn 3): a God who exists in time and acts within the structure is a God who depends on the structure for that position.

Process theology avoids the charge that its divine candidate lacks determinate temporal, relational, or active roles. It carries a serious aseity burden: a temporal, relational God appears dependent on the conditions of the process it inhabits. Process theists may respond by revising aseity rather than denying dependency; the present account records that cost without treating the revision as a contradiction.

Suchocki's eschatological development of the consequent nature does not change this: an eschatological consummation is still a temporally extended event, and an eschatologically consummated God is still a configuration within Nature. Bracken's social-trinitarian extension multiplies the divine persons but does not relocate them outside Nature. Oord's essential kenosis specifies the modality of divine action without altering the metaphysical embedding. Each contemporary development of process theology preserves the central commitment (God is temporal, related, changing) and each, on the present analysis, preserves the consequence: such a God instantiates T, S, and Φ and owes the same account of whether its relation to them is dependence, identity, or co-constitution.

A kindred position worth marking is open theism (Pinnock et al., *The Openness of God* [@pinnock1994]; Hasker, *God, Time, and Knowledge* [@hasker1989]). Open theism shares with process theology the rejection of timeless omniscience and the affirmation of genuine creaturely freedom, but typically retains creation *ex nihilo* and divine independence in ways process theology does not. The present reply raises the same question: an open-theist God who exists in time and knows the past while leaving the future open is structurally embedded, and the theorist must explain how that is compatible with the proposed grounding role. The aseity question is the same question for both positions.

Process theology is the theistic position best positioned to accept the argument's structural commitments without contradiction, but the cost is a substantial revision of classical aseity (the divine attribute of existing from oneself alone, independent of anything else for one's being), and aseity is the load-bearing commitment of the classical project. Process theology provides a coherent way of being a theist after the present account; it does not provide grounds for accepting theism, and it does not preserve what the classical project was distinctively trying to secure.

Whether the further commitments of process theology are independently warranted (whether the consequent nature exists, whether divine persuasion is the right account of God's action, whether eschatological consummation is the right account of history) are questions for the philosophy of religion rather than for the present account. The present account leaves the first question open; on the second, it establishes the structural instantiation and records the aseity cost.

*What is established.* The process theologian who accepts the structural argument has a coherent position: a God who realizes temporal, relational, and active roles at maximum scope. This is not the classical aseity claim, and it requires either treating God as a configuration within Reality or articulating a revised account of ultimacy compatible with divine process. Hartshorne's move is therefore a genuine theological revision, not a mere preservation of the classical project. The present account records the cost: process theology does not straightforwardly preserve the grounding role classical theism assigned to God. Whether its revised religious and metaphysical picture is independently preferable remains a live philosophy-of-religion question.

### 5.3.4 Madhyamaka Emptiness {#sec-5-3-4}

Nāgārjuna's *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (c. 150 CE) [@nagarjuna1995] develops the doctrine of *śūnyatā* (emptiness) as a sustained critique of any view that attributes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to anything whatever. Nothing exists from its own side; everything arises in dependence on conditions. The tetralemma (A; not-A; both A and not-A; neither A nor not-A) exhausts the options and refutes each. The result is not nihilism but the deconstruction of any positive metaphysical thesis, including the theses of substance, time, and space as intrinsically existing.

The challenge is radical in a way no other challenge the argument faces is. The Madhyamaka position is engineered to dissolve precisely the kind of structural claim the present book defends, and contemporary Madhyamaka scholarship has sharpened the challenge rather than softened it. Garfield [@garfield1995; @garfield2002], Siderits [@siderits2003; @siderits2007], and Westerhoff [@westerhoff2009] defend a Madhyamaka (particularly in its Prāsaṅgika form) that is not the conciliatory Madhyamaka of Tsongkhapa's reading but a thoroughgoing rejection of *all* metaphysical theses.

On this reading, the *prasaṅga* (consequence-only) method is dialectical: the Mādhyamika (the adherent of the Madhyamaka school) does not advance any positive position, including the position that things arise dependently, but only draws absurd consequences from the positions of others.

The tetralemma is not a fifth alternative but the closure of all alternatives. The Mādhyamika has no thesis [@westerhoff2009, ch. 8], and the present argument, having theses, is precisely the kind of view *prasaṅga* targets.

Two replies must be distinguished, because they engage Madhyamaka at different scopes.

The narrower reply concerns *svabhāva*. *Svabhāva* in the technical sense is intrinsic, independent, self-existing nature. Nāgārjuna's arguments are devastating against the claim that any phenomenon has nature in that sense. They are not directed against (and do not refute) the claim that phenomena exhibit structural conditions that obtain dependently. The present argument here has never claimed *svabhāva* for T, S, or Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance). The structure is mutually constituting: each role requires the other two, and none has independent existence apart from the others. In the technical Mahāyāna vocabulary, T, S, and Φ are empty of *svabhāva* and dependently arisen with respect to one another.

The narrower reply observes the convergence: the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent arising) Nāgārjuna names is structurally isomorphic to the present argument's mutual requirement.

The wider reply must engage the Prāsaṅgika who refuses the convergence, who insists that even “structural conditions that obtain dependently” is *svabhāva* in disguise, because the assertion takes a stable form, picks out determinate roles, and survives translation across linguistic and conceptual schemes. On the strict Prāsaṅgika reading defended by Garfield and Westerhoff, the present argument is doing what *prasaṅga* targets: advancing a positive thesis (the Triunity holds across all possible worlds) under cover of denying *svabhāva* in name only.

The present argument resists the wider critique only at a limited point. It does not depend on assimilating Madhyamaka to a conciliatory reading; it distinguishes the practice of *prasaṅga* from the object-level thesis the Mādhyamika declines to assert.

*Prasaṅga* is a dialectical method: the Mādhyamika draws absurd consequences from an opponent's premises. The drawing-of-consequences is an activity. It occurs through succession, differentiates premises from conclusions, and persists through a reasoner or practice. *Prasaṅga* therefore exhibits T, S, and Φ at role-resolution in its operation.

That act-side fact does not force the Mādhyamika to accept an object-level thesis that the structural conditions exist inherently or independently. It establishes instead that the conditions of the dialectical practice are not dissolved by the practice. The structural account may claim those conditions are necessary; the Prāsaṅgika may deny that this is a final metaphysical description. Their dispute remains over the status of the positive structural thesis, not over whether the practice of reasoning takes place in a structured manner.

*The four corners, run explicitly.* The catuṣkoṭi is built to exhaust the options for any thesis and refute each in turn; run against □(T∧S∧Φ), it reaches no exit.

To affirm the first corner (that the conditions hold) is to perform an assertion that unfolds over time, distinguishes what is affirmed from what is not, and persists through the one affirming: the affirmation instantiates T, S, and Φ.

To affirm the second corner (that the conditions do not hold) is to perform a denial carrying the same three features, so the denial instantiates what it denies.

The third corner, both, must differentiate the respect in which the conditions hold from the respect in which they do not (Space), hold the two together in one bearer (Substance), and articulate them in sequence (Time); it presupposes the conditions in order to state its two conjuncts.

The fourth corner, neither (the refusal to occupy any corner, and the Prāsaṅgika's own dwelling) is itself a configuration: the withholding unfolds over time, sets itself apart from assertion, and persists through the one who withholds.

The tetralemma closes the space of positions one might take toward the modal claim; it does not close the space of conditions on taking any position at all. Each corner, the empty fourth included, is occupied by an activity that exhibits the very structure the corner was meant to dissolve: the catuṣkoṭi cannot be turned against □(T∧S∧Φ) except from within it.

*What is established.* The Tsongkhapa-Gelug reading distinguishes the negation of *svabhāva* from the negation of conventional existence: the structural conditions are conventionally real and ultimately empty of intrinsic nature, and the argument is compatible with that reading. The stricter Prāsaṅgika reading remains a live disagreement. The present account can establish that Madhyamaka practice is structurally enacted; it cannot settle the wider anti-thesis position by treating that enactment as a contradiction. The narrower reading yields accommodation; the wider reading leaves a genuine dispute over whether structural necessity is a positive metaphysical thesis or only a conventionally indispensable description.

## 5.4 What the Rival Ultimates Carried {#sec-5-4}

This is the chapter's reckoning. The rival ultimates do not all end with one verdict. Some descriptions subtract the conditions under which a determinate ground or relation can be specified, and on the book's analysis dissolve into ∅. Some preserve directed dependence, relational non-identity, and real grounding content under analogical, process, or apophatic vocabulary. Some remain live only by positing an essence-prior or transcendent ground whose relation to the structural domain requires independent metaphysical defense.

The point is not that theistic philosophers reasoned carelessly — they reasoned with great care, and the tradition's repairs are among the most carefully built constructions in the literature. The question is which verdict each repair earns: incoherence, relocation, compatibility, explanatory cost, or a remaining open seam.

The preceding sections examined the tradition's main repairs: the foundation and contingency arguments (Rasmussen, the Kalām), the simplicity constructions (classical divine simplicity, Swinburne), the modal and ontological arguments (Plantinga, the modal-grounding argument), the cosmological and design inferences (simultaneous causation, fine-tuning, intelligent design), and the apophatic, absolute-monist, and process traditions (the *via negativa*, Neoplatonism, Spinozist pantheism, Madhyamaka emptiness, process theology). Each arrived with its own apparatus and its own point of pressure.

A recurrent pattern from Chapter 4 emerged here: some constructions presuppose structural roles they were built to transcend, while others revise ultimacy or leave an explanatory seam rather than collapse.

The Spinozist identified God with immanent Nature and accepted structural articulation rather than classical transcendence. The Neoplatonist placed the One beyond being and described emanation. The process theologian made God temporal and embedded: the revised theist's option, named differently. Plantinga's maximal greatness raises a compossibility and possibility-premise burden; the strongest negative classical attributes are additional commitments rather than part of that definition. The Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna's middle-way Buddhist school) emptied *svabhāva* (Sanskrit: “own-being” or self-existence) and left the dependent-arising structure intact. The resulting verdicts differ: compatibility for some immanent accounts, a grounding burden for articulated transcendence, and an open dialectical seam for strict apophasis or anti-thesis positions.

Three interlocutors deserve to be taken slowly, because each presses back in a different way: the revised theist, who accepts the structure and keeps the name; the Thomist identifier, who accepts the result and claims the tradition reached it first; and the Kalām objector, who grants the structure as actual and asks for a cause outside it.

Consider the revised theist. The philosopher who abandons classical theism and redefines God as temporal, extended, and causally embedded (a necessary person who instantiates the structural roles rather than lacking them) has escaped ∅. That much the argument grants. The revision places God within the structural order. That creates a burden for classical aseity, but embeddedness alone does not prove non-fundamentality: the revised theist may propose a necessary, co-constitutive, or priority-bearing configuration and must defend that grounding account.

Consider the Thomist identifier. Distinct from the revised theist, this interlocutor does not modify the classical attributes. The identifier accepts the argument's structural result and identifies it with God under the classical description intact: Thomas's *ipsum esse subsistens*, Feser's Pure Act, Dolezal's being-itself: these, the identifier says, just are □(T∧S∧Φ) under another name. If the argument proves a necessary structural ground, Thomism was right. The ground exists and deserves the name the tradition gave it. The book has not refuted classical theism; it has renamed it.

The identification requires what it denies. *Ipsum esse subsistens* was specified by Thomas as being without temporal succession, without spatial extension, without material composition: the *via negativa*'s long labor was precisely to mark what the necessary ground lacks. The structural account specifies the ground by what it instantiates: succession, relational non-identity, causal persistence. These are opposing specifications of the ground's character, not two descriptions of one fact. The identifier cannot hold both.

Drop the classical attributes to preserve the identification and the move collapses into the revised theist's option above. Keep the classical attributes and the argument's result (that a ground lacking T, S, and Φ is ∅) reapplies without remainder. No third position.

Analogical predication does not supply a non-T/S/Φ articulation. The Thomist reply at this junction is that the “requires” in the reduction above smuggles in *univocal* predication: it treats the source–recipient relation as if it had to be articulated in the same kind of temporal, spatial, and physical terms that creaturely causal relations require, whereas the Thomist insists on *analogical* predication for God-talk.

Grant the point: God-talk is analogical, and the divine act is not one more event inside the world.

The structural claim is not that the divine act must be *creaturely* T/S/Φ, but that any determinately contentful “source–recipient” relation must still carry (i) an ordering (before/after, priority/posteriority, dependence direction), (ii) a non-identity between relata (this rather than that), and (iii) a persistence or invariance that makes it the same source across the relation. Those are exactly the role-definitions of T, S, and Φ.

If the Thomist denies all three at once (no ordering, no non-identity, no persistence/invariance) then the “relation” has no determinate content and collapses into the Null State-style limit: not a higher articulation, but no articulation at all. If the Thomist grants that the relation has determinate content (which requires all three), the *via negativa* no longer specifies a ground lacking T/S/Φ; it specifies a ground instantiating them under analogical description, which is just the revised-theist relocation in different vocabulary.

So the analogical/univocal distinction does not open a third option: it either leaves the reduction intact (no determinate relation, hence ∅) or reintroduces the structural roles under another name (hence in-Nature rather than beyond it).

::: {.corollary}
**Thomist-Identifier Variant** · **R14** · *Result of the Drop/Keep Dilemma*

The Thomist identification of □(T∧S∧Φ) with the classical *ipsum esse subsistens* cannot be sustained. Either the classical attributes are dropped, in which case the identifier collapses into the revised theist (configured within Nature, not above it); or the classical attributes are kept, in which case the ground specified by what it lacks reduces to ∅ under the Null State definition ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)). No third option. The local Chapter 5 summation rests on the Chapter 2–4 machinery already established; the Result form anticipates Supernatural Preclusion ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)) as a variant routing through Horn 3 of the Trilemma Closure, where the same result is restated under Supernatural Preclusion once that result is in place downstream. ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1), [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1))


:::

::: {.untyped}
*Proof (Thomist-Identifier Variant).* Notation: Drop = drop the classical attributes; Keep = keep the classical attributes (the two options developed above).

1. Drop ∨ Keep: exhaustive over the identifier's options on the classical attributes.

1. Drop → collapses into revised theism: the structural ground is configured within Nature, not above it.

1. Keep → a ground lacking T, S, Φ is ∅; the argument's result reapplies without remainder.

∴ the Thomist identification cannot be sustained. ∎


:::

The identifier who presses anyway applies the tradition's name to a ground specified by the features the tradition defined its own ground against. The structural ground is specified by what it instantiates: succession, relational non-identity, causal persistence; *ipsum esse subsistens* is specified by what it lacks. The identification holds only if one of the two specifications is silently dropped.

Consider the Kalām objector. The Kalām is the contemporary research program dedicated to denying necessity-of-T on independent grounds: the conceptual impossibility of an actual infinite past (Hilbert and traversal arguments), the empirical claim that the universe has a past boundary (BGV), and the cosmological inference from beginning to a transcendent personal cause.

It fits the chapter's pattern differently from Chapter 4's deflationary, change-skeptical, and modal-variants clusters: the Kalām does not arrive at the structural conditions by presupposing them in its denial; it accepts T, S, and Φ as actual and contingent and asks for an originating cause outside the order.

The chapter pressures the Kalām along a different seam. [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) distinguishes objections to an actual infinite past, evidence for a finite cosmic boundary, and the further inference to a timeless personal cause. A first temporal boundary need not be a moment prior to T, and [§5.1.6](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-6) no longer treats an ordinary historical Fall as requiring such a categorial origin. The composition view of Temporality is marked at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), separating the quantitative question of how far the past extends from the metaphysical question of what grounds the order.

The destination the Kalām pursues (a necessary ground for the contingent series) is adjacent to where the structural argument lands; the line taken to that destination, and the personal-cause specification of what is found there, are what the chapter contests.

The same structural ground constrains accounts of miracles. It does not by itself establish their logical impossibility, because classical theists can construe a timeless cause as producing temporal effects without undergoing a temporal episode. (This local summation draws only on the Chapter 2–4 machinery already in place: the Principle of Modal Invariance and the structural-condition requirement on any act of intervention; the parallel to the Supernatural Preclusion of [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1) is anticipatory, restated under that result once it is established downstream.)

A miracle is ordinarily a change in a state of affairs attributed to divine intervention. The effect has temporal, spatial, and bearing conditions. The disputed question is whether the cause must instantiate those conditions in the same mode or can ground the effect timelessly.

The Principle of Modal Invariance, if established, forecloses an effect that literally lacks all structural conditions. It does not without further premises foreclose an unusual event within those conditions or settle the mode of its cause.

A being defined as atemporal, aspatial, and immaterial faces an interface problem: the account must explain how it stands in a determinate causal relation to physical events without simply assuming that cause and effect share one mode of being. “Intervention” is a content-laden notion. The event described as intervention occurs to something, at a time and place, through T, S, and Φ. Whether its cause must share that mode is precisely the interface question, not a premise the analysis may assume. The structural analysis therefore does not foreclose miracles merely from the classical attributes. It imposes a burden on the causal interface and on the evidential identification of an event as divine intervention.

The difficulty pressed here is chiefly structural, though several arguments also carry evidential burdens: classical claims must retain determinate content and explain their relation to the structured domain.

The book inherits from these repairs the question it turns: not whether a necessary ground exists — the argument grants that it does — but whether what stands there is a being beyond Nature or the structure of Nature itself.

The theistic rivals carried the question further than anyone. Their active grounding descriptions commonly carry ordered dependence, relational non-identity, and real grounding content. A ground defined by the absence of every such condition dissolves on the book's analysis; a ground that grants them has conceded a structured ground. What remains open is not merely whether *God* is its name, but whether an essence-prior or transcendent proposal can make its grounding relation intelligible without collapsing into either a structured relation or an unexplained primitive. That is the residual burden Chapters 5 and 6 continue to test.
